title: Tactile wheel with one notch
new_elements: Single-detent dial (One dial that only turns between Heat and Stop.)
rationale: There is only one thing to do with the dial, so nothing needs to be explained.
judge_comment: A single-detent Heat/Stop dial is radically simple and cheap, but it may sacrifice control over time and power.

title: Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Recipe card slot (A slot on the front accepts a card that carries power and time for one dish.)
rationale: Inserting a card works like playing a film, so the user just chooses a card and no settings.
judge_comment: A card carrying power and time removes all settings and is easy to understand, though it needs a supply of cards and a reader.

title: Three Pictogram Buttons
new_elements: Food-picture buttons (Three large buttons showing soup, drink and frozen meal.)
rationale: Choosing by picture needs no understanding of power levels or timings.
judge_comment: Picture buttons directly remove the need to learn settings, are easy to build, and are clear, though not very radical.

title: Picture-card control cartridge
new_elements: Picture-card cartridge (Slide-in cards each show one food and set all controls.)
rationale: Inserting a card for the food sets everything, so no setting ever needs remembering.
judge_comment: Food-specific picture cards replace the control panel with an obvious slide-in action, which strongly removes the learning curve and is easy to build with simple sensing.

title: Pictogram Knob Faces
new_elements: Pictogram dial (Dial with icons for steam, snow, and sun instead of numbers.); Icon-driven choice (Shows the effect of each setting with a picture.)
rationale: Pictures explain what each setting does without any reading.
judge_comment: Icon dials directly remove the need to learn settings, are cheap and easy to make, though the idea is fairly incremental.

title: Temperature Target Dial
new_elements: Serving-temperature dial (A dial marked hot, warm and cold that sets a target food temperature instead of power.); Infrared food-temperature sensing (An IR sensor reads the food surface and adjusts heating until it reaches target.)
rationale: Choosing a serving temperature in plain words is far easier than choosing a power level.
judge_comment: Hot/warm/cold target with IR sensing removes the need for power or time knowledge, and IR sensors are feasible though surface reading is imperfect.

title: Auto-Start on Door Close
new_elements: Door-close start sensor (Closing the door starts the last-used cook program.); Starts cooking when the door closes (One action, no start button.)
rationale: Closing the door is already the last step of loading, so it is the natural moment to start.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes the start step and is easy to build, though the last-used program could surprise users and carries some safety concerns.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Food pictogram ring (A ring of simple icons (egg, pizza, soup, leftovers) that sets everything at once.); Select food type (Choosing a picture selects the power and time automatically.)
rationale: Users pick what they are cooking instead of how to cook it.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial removes the need to pick power and time, so it directly meets the no-learning-curve need, and it is simple and buildable, though not very radical.

title: Picture-Menu Dial
new_elements: Food-icon selector (A rotary dial with pictures (popcorn, leftovers, frozen pizza) that set time and power together.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of the food removes the need to know what numbers or power levels mean.
judge_comment: An icon dial that sets time and power together removes the need for numbers, though similar presets already exist.

title: One-Button Heat
new_elements: Single HEAT button (One press starts 60 s of cooking; each extra press adds 30 s; no numbers or power settings.)
rationale: A single repeated press is the simplest possible interaction for a first-time user.
judge_comment: A single button is very simple and clearly specified, but it is not radical, and similar quick-start buttons already exist.

title: Sensing Stop, No Timer
new_elements: Humidity-based doneness sensor (A humidity sensor detects steam release and stops cooking when the food is hot, with no time to set.)
rationale: The machine decides when food is done, so the user never sets a time at all.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensing auto-stop removes time setting entirely; sensor cooking exists in high-end units but is a strong fit for zero learning curve.

title: Fixed-Cycle Reheat
new_elements: Single-length reheat cycle (A fixed 90-second cycle with a stop button replaces the imprecise short-time timer.)
rationale: A fixed cycle removes the need to set any time for the most common use.
judge_comment: A single fixed 90-second reheat cycle with a stop button makes the most common use effortless and is very easy to implement, though it is limited to one use case.

title: Egg-Timer Shell
new_elements: Egg-shaped timer (A dial shaped like an egg timer that turns to a heat level and ends with a spring stop.); Familiar timer (Reuses the look of a classic kitchen timer.)
rationale: People already know how a timer dial works, so the learning curve is zero.
judge_comment: A familiar single dial substitutes for the keypad and removes the learning curve, though mechanical timer dials already exist on microwaves.

title: One Button Means Everything
new_elements: Universal single button (A single button that opens, starts, and stops depending on the context.)
rationale: One button with context-based meaning has nothing to memorize beyond pressing it.
judge_comment: A single context-sensitive button substitutes many controls and directly removes the learning curve, though it is fairly obvious and leaves open how cook time is chosen.

title: Single Flat Glass Panel
new_elements: Flat touch-glass pictogram panel (A flat glass face shows three large pictograms for cook, reheat and defrost.)
rationale: Three pictograms replace a crowded panel, so the choice is obvious at a glance.
judge_comment: Replacing the crowded keypad with three large pictograms directly removes the learning curve and is easily built.

title: Egg-Timer Mechanical Cam
new_elements: Spring-wound egg-timer dial (A classic egg-timer spring dial with a bell that rings at the end.)
rationale: Users already know how to turn a timer dial and hear it ring.
judge_comment: A familiar mechanical timer dial substitutes for a digital keypad, giving zero learning curve, though it's a known retro approach.

title: Single-Button Reheat Dock
new_elements: Reheat dock tray (A tray that sits on the unit; placing a plate on it starts a reheat, and taking it off stops.)
rationale: Placing the plate is the only action, and lifting it off ends the cycle, so no button is needed.
judge_comment: Placing a plate to start and lifting it to stop removes all controls and needs no learning, which is plausible with a weight sensor, though it gives little control over the cycle and has safety issues.

title: Food-Photo Power Selector
new_elements: Four-picture power pad (Printed pictures of popcorn, leftovers, frozen meal and reheat drink replace the numbered 5-step knob.)
rationale: Choosing by picture of the food removes the need to understand power levels or duty cycles.
judge_comment: Picture-based selection directly removes the need to learn power levels and is cheap and easy to implement.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retractable pull cord (The user pulls a cord to the length they want, and it slowly retracts while cooking runs.)
rationale: A longer pull means more time, which is understood directly by physical length.
judge_comment: Pull length mapping directly to time is intuitive and needs no learning, and it replaces the keypad cheaply, much like a kitchen timer.

title: Food-Type Slider Replacing Power
new_elements: Frozen-to-leftover slider (A slider running from frozen to leftover that sets power by food state.)
rationale: Choosing by food state is more natural than choosing an abstract power percentage.
judge_comment: Choosing by food state removes the abstract power concept, which directly serves zero-learning-curve use, though similar presets already exist.

title: Stepless Slider to Picture Modes
new_elements: Three-icon mode bar (Icon bar with Heat, Cook, and Defrost.); Chooses mode by icon (The user taps an icon and cooks.)
rationale: Three icons replace the numbered knob with choices a child can understand.
judge_comment: Replacing the numbered knob with three icons directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though the idea is not very radical.

title: Tray-as-Controller
new_elements: Smart food tray (Tray with an NFC tag that sets the program when placed.); Sets program by placing the tray (Putting the tray in starts the right cook.)
rationale: The tray carries the instructions, so the user never has to type them.
judge_comment: Placing a tagged tray to auto-start the correct program removes the need to enter settings, which directly serves zero-learning-curve operation, and NFC is cheap and proven.

title: Food-shaped dial
new_elements: Food-type selector tray (Tap a picture of soup, bread, or frozen pizza and the cooking profile is set.)
rationale: Users choose what they are cooking instead of guessing minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Pictorial food presets are very intuitive and easy to build, though common on existing microwaves and not radical.

title: Stickers instead of settings
new_elements: Tap-to-cook stickers (A sticker on a packet, when tapped on the oven, starts the right cook.)
rationale: Packaging does the teaching, so the user only taps.
judge_comment: NFC-style stickers substitute settings with a tap, which is nearly zero learning, though it depends on packaging adoption.

title: Sticky-note timer
new_elements: Magnetic timer tag (A magnet with a time printed on it sticks to the door and counts down.)
rationale: A time tag is physical and obvious, so no dial needs to be learned.
judge_comment: A magnetic time tag replaces the dial with an obvious physical object, which is cheap, simple and fits the no-learning-curve need well.

title: Hand-cranked backup
new_elements: Analog timer hourglass (A sand timer on top that the user flips to start a cook.)
rationale: Flipping a sand timer is a universal action that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Substituting a flip sand timer for digital controls is simple, intuitive and radical, though the fixed durations limit power and precision control.

title: Cook by Photo
new_elements: Food recognition camera (Camera identifies the food and sets the cook automatically.)
rationale: The user shows the food to the machine instead of translating it into settings.
judge_comment: A camera that identifies the food removes settings entirely, though recognition accuracy and cost are hurdles.

title: Cooking Tray Does the Thinking
new_elements: Smart pre-programmed tray (Tray carries an identifier that sets the cook program when placed.)
rationale: Placing the tray is the only action, so the cook settings are never seen by the user.
judge_comment: A tray carrying an identifier that sets the program makes placing it the only action, which is simple and buildable, though it ties users to proprietary trays.

title: Dinner Pods Replace Settings
new_elements: Pod recognition ring (Food pods carry an RFID tag that drives the cook.)
rationale: Packaged food configures the machine so the user only inserts and closes.
judge_comment: RFID pods make operation insert-and-close with no learning, which is feasible with proven tech, though it's tied to a pod ecosystem.

title: Package-Reads-Itself
new_elements: Printed food-pack code reader (A printed code on the packaging is read by a sensor, which loads the timing and power settings.)
rationale: The manufacturer sets the cooking instructions, so the user never programs anything.
judge_comment: Reading cooking instructions from packaging removes all user input, but it depends on industry adoption of the code and does not work for unpackaged food.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity-based food sensing (Gas sensor detects steam release and ends cooking once the food is ready.)
rationale: The machine decides when to stop, so the user does not need to watch a clock.
judge_comment: Humidity or gas sensing for auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, but it does remove the need to set a time, which fits the no-learning-curve need well.

title: Two-Button Feast
new_elements: Two-button control bank (Just a Warm button and a Cook button; duration and power are automatic.)
rationale: Two obvious buttons remove every decision except the one between warm and cook.
judge_comment: Two buttons with automatic duration and power are very easy to use and simple to build, though the idea is not very radical and the auto settings are vague.

title: Phone-Free Pairing Remote
new_elements: Single-button wall remote (A wall-mounted remote with one large button starts the last recipe the user used.)
rationale: One button that repeats the last used recipe means the user never has to set anything again.
judge_comment: A single repeat button removes setup entirely and is simple to build, but it assumes a first use that has already happened.

title: Weight-Loads-Recipe Plate
new_elements: Recipe-by-plate (Each plate has a set weight and shape, and the oven reads its load and runs the matching recipe.)
rationale: Putting food on a plate starts the right program, so the user never chooses anything.
judge_comment: Plate-identified recipes remove all choices and are plausible via weight or shape sensing, though accuracy and the need for dedicated plates are concerns.

title: Everyday Cook Companion
new_elements: Cook-for-me button (One press runs a stored default for the last food, with no setup.)
rationale: A single press that repeats the last successful cook needs zero learning and suits older users.
judge_comment: A one-press repeat of the last cook needs zero learning and is easy to build, though similar features already exist.

title: Ingredient Pod Reader
new_elements: RFID reader (Reader that scans a tag on the food container.); Cooks from the container tag (Sets power and time from the tag written by the food maker.)
rationale: The food itself carries its instructions, so the user only places the container.
judge_comment: A tag-reading container removes all settings input, which fits zero learning curve well, though it depends on food makers adopting the tags and the idea resembles existing barcode-scan microwaves.

title: One Heat button with food sensing
new_elements: Single Heat button (One button starts cooking and sets time from food sensing.); Food-mass and humidity sensing (Estimates load to pick time automatically.)
rationale: One button with no numbers to set means the cooking process has no learning curve.
judge_comment: A one-button start with automatic sensing directly removes the learning curve, and sensor cooking already exists, though it is not truly a substitution of a cheaper part.

title: Weight-based auto timer
new_elements: Load-cell tray (Tray weighs food and sets time from its mass.)
rationale: Placing food on the tray sets the cook automatically, so the user only loads and closes.
judge_comment: Load-cell auto timing removes the need to enter anything, which directly serves a no-learning-curve goal, though food weight alone doesn't determine cook time well.

title: Steam Sniffer Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor cavity (Humidity sensor that detects when food is steaming and ends the cycle.); Automatic doneness stop (Stops heating when the food is ready, without a timer.)
rationale: The machine decides when to stop, so the user never has to estimate a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop is already used in sensor-cook microwaves, so it works well but is not new.

title: Preset Shape Plugs
new_elements: Shape key plug (A physical plug shaped like a dish; inserting it selects the matching programme.); Physical preset selection (Selects the programme by insertion of a matching shape.)
rationale: A shape fits only one way, so no one can choose the wrong setting.
judge_comment: Mechanical shape plugs are foolproof and cheap, but they limit the number of presets and add loose parts.

title: Ready-Meal NFC Sticker
new_elements: Printed NFC sticker (Sticker printed on ready meals that holds the heating programme.); Packaging-driven programme (Programme comes from the packaging, not the machine.)
rationale: The food maker sets the cooking, so the user only has to place the meal.
judge_comment: Packaging-driven NFC programs replace the user interface with a cheap sticker; this is a clever substitution, but it only works for compatible ready meals.

title: Fold-Out Turntable Blank
new_elements: Stationary mode stirrer (A rotating metal fan in the cavity ceiling spreads the field, so the tray and motor are not needed.)
rationale: Food can be placed anywhere, so the user never has to think about position.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, so the idea is feasible and removes the placement decision, though it is not very radical.

title: Color-Coded Food Ring
new_elements: Colour-coded ring dial (A coloured ring matches the food category, with no numbers at all.)
rationale: Colours match food categories, so the user chooses by recognition alone.
judge_comment: Recognition-based colour dial removes numbers and learning, simple and cheap, though colour coding is a known idea.

title: Shared Office Badge Mode
new_elements: RFID badge reader (A staff badge loads that person's favourite programs and does not require any setup.)
rationale: A badge tap loads the user's own programs, so shared use needs nothing to learn.
judge_comment: An RFID badge that loads personal programs is concrete, cheap and removes setup in shared settings, though its benefit is narrow.

title: Preloaded Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Recipe card slot reader (A slot reads a printed card with a large code and starts the matching program.)
rationale: Sliding in a card is a physical, familiar gesture with no programming needed.
judge_comment: A physical card with a code that starts the right program is a familiar gesture and a real substitute for a keypad, though it means buying cards.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Four-picture food dial (One dial with pictures: frozen, leftovers, drink, snack. Each picture sets time and power automatically.); Selects cooking program by picture (Maps a visual food category to a preset time and power.)
rationale: Users choose by recognising a picture of their food, so no timer or power numbers need to be understood.
judge_comment: Directly removes number-reading and is easy to build, but picture-based presets are already common, so it is not radical.

title: Close-to-Cook Auto-Start
new_elements: Starts cooking when door closes on loaded food (Closing the door with a plate inside starts the last-used or preset cycle.)
rationale: The action of closing the door is the start command, so there is no button to find.
judge_comment: Closing the door as the start command removes the button search entirely, though accidental starts and safety need handling.

title: NFC Food-Tag Cooking
new_elements: NFC food packaging tag (Tag on packaging carries time, power and cavity settings.); Reads cooking program from packaging (Oven reads the tag when the food is placed on the tray.)
rationale: The food package sets the oven, so the user never needs to know any settings.
judge_comment: The package sets the oven, which removes the need for any settings and directly serves zero learning curve, though it depends on packaging adoption and an NFC reader in the oven. It is also more an addition than a substitution.

title: Ring Countdown
new_elements: LED ring countdown (A ring of LEDs around the cook button shrinks as time runs out.)
rationale: Time is shown as a shrinking shape, which can be read at a glance by anyone.
judge_comment: A shrinking LED ring replaces a numeric display with a glanceable, universally readable form that directly supports no-learning-curve use.

title: Three Food Presets
new_elements: Three-button presets (Three large buttons labelled Drink, Reheat and Cook, each with a fixed time and power.)
rationale: Three clear choices are far easier to learn than a range of minutes and power levels.
judge_comment: Three labelled presets strongly reduce the learning curve and are easy to build, but the idea is common and not radical.

title: Voice Says Popcorn
new_elements: Offline voice command (A small offline speech module starts a preset when the user says the food name.)
rationale: Speaking the food name requires no buttons, labels or reading.
judge_comment: Offline voice presets by food name remove nearly all operating steps and are workable with current embedded speech modules, though noise and accents are a risk.

title: Single Dome Button
new_elements: One-button dome (One big domed button that starts cooking and opens the door when pressed again.); Single-action control (Every operation is one press, with the same action each time.)
rationale: One button that always does the same job removes the need to learn any control panel at all.
judge_comment: A single always-same-action button directly eliminates the learning curve, though cook time and power setting handling is unclear.

title: Ready-Meal Barcode Tray
new_elements: Barcode reading tray (The food tray has a printed barcode; a reader sets time and power when the tray is placed.); Optical barcode reading (A low-cost optical reader built into the cavity wall.)
rationale: Placing the food on its tray is the only step, because the tray tells the machine what to do.
judge_comment: A tray that sets the program itself needs no user input, but it requires special trays and a barcode reader that tolerates heat and steam.

title: NFC Meal Tap
new_elements: NFC food pack reader (The user taps the food packet on the front; the packet's NFC tag sets the program.); Near-field tag reading (Short-range wireless reading of a printed tag on packaging.)
rationale: Tapping the packet does the whole job, so the user never sets anything by hand.
judge_comment: Tapping a pack to set the program is effortless and technically possible, but it needs NFC tags on food packaging, which depends on food makers adopting them.

title: Hot-Plate Sticker Guide
new_elements: Colour-coded food stickers (Stickers placed on the food packet that match a colour on the machine's panel.); Matches food to setting by colour (Pairs packaging with the machine setting through colour, not numbers.)
rationale: Matching colours on packet and panel means the user never has to interpret power levels.
judge_comment: Colour matching replaces numeric settings with a simple cue, which suits no-learning-curve use, though it needs packaging cooperation.

title: Voice-Only Setup Mode
new_elements: Spoken-command microphone (A microphone that accepts simple spoken commands such as heat soup for two minutes.); Keyword spotting speech (On-device recognition of a small set of spoken keywords.)
rationale: Speaking the task in plain words means the user needs no panel, dial or manual at all.
judge_comment: Voice commands remove the learning curve directly, and on-device keyword spotting is practical, though voice control in appliances isn't new.

title: Door-Pop Finish Signal
new_elements: Spring-loaded door popper (Small spring cracks the door open a few millimetres when cooking ends.); Physically signals cycle end (Door movement is the signal.)
rationale: A door that visibly pops open at the end needs no understanding of sounds or lights to know the food is done.
judge_comment: The physical door pop gives an intuitive finish signal and is mechanically plausible, though it replaces a beep rather than any control.

title: Close-to-Start Door
new_elements: Door-closure magnetic reed switch (Detects the door latching shut and begins heating.); Start on close (Closing the door is the only action needed to cook.)
rationale: A natural action (closing a door) replaces an unlabelled start control.
judge_comment: Reed switch start-on-close is cheap and intuitive, but it needs a duration default and carries a risk of accidental starts.

title: Single Rocker Control
new_elements: Two-position rocker switch (Left side warms, right side cooks; press and hold to run.); Binary intent input (Reduces every action to one of two choices.)
rationale: Only one control exists, so there is no panel to decode.
judge_comment: A single two-position rocker removes nearly all decisions and is easy to build, though it sacrifices control over time and power.

title: Soup Steam Stop
new_elements: Steam density sensor (Monitors steam from the food and stops when it stabilises.); Gas-phase sensing (Detects water vapour concentration.)
rationale: Steam level tells the machine when liquid food is hot, so no time needs setting.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on steam sensing removes time setting entirely; humidity sensors already exist in some ovens, but the approach is sound and workable.

title: Tap-the-Plate Programs
new_elements: NFC-tagged plate (Dishes carry an NFC tag; placing the plate on the turntable loads the correct time and power.)
rationale: Placing the food on the plate is the only action, so no settings ever need to be chosen.
judge_comment: NFC plates remove all setting choices and are plausible, but they need special dishes and tags that match each food, which limits flexibility.

title: Frozen-Meal Sleeve Reader
new_elements: Packaging light-code strip (A printed reflective strip on frozen meal sleeves that the cavity's light sensor reads to set cooking.)
rationale: The user simply inserts the packaged meal and the microwave handles every setting.
judge_comment: Inserting the meal and having it cook automatically is a zero-learning experience, but it depends on packaging standards and only works for compatible meals; the code reading by a cavity sensor is plausible.

title: Clearing Electrochromic Window
new_elements: Electrochromic window (The window is dark when cooking and clears when the door is opened or cooking ends.)
rationale: The window itself communicates cooking state, with no switches or lights needed.
judge_comment: A window that darkens while cooking and clears afterward shows state intuitively with no extra controls, which fits the no-learning-curve need.

title: Music-Box Crank Timer
new_elements: Wind-up crank timer (A hand crank winds a spring; the longer you turn it, the longer it cooks, with no electronics.)
rationale: Turning a crank for more time is a tactile action anyone understands, with no display to read.
judge_comment: A wind-up mechanical timer is a real substitution with an intuitive action, and similar mechanical timers have long been used in microwaves.

title: Preset Shelf Memory
new_elements: Preset shelf buttons (Three large preset buttons for common foods, each with a printed photo of its food.)
rationale: Three photo presets cover most daily needs with one press each.
judge_comment: Photo preset buttons directly remove the learning curve and are easy to build, though fairly conventional.

title: Pour-In Weight Auto-Set
new_elements: Load cell in turntable (Weighs the food and sets time and power from the weight.); Derives cook settings from mass (Weight is converted into time and power automatically.)
rationale: Placing the food on the plate is enough, so no numbers have to be set.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-settings remove number entry, directly serving zero-learning operation, though weight alone is an imperfect basis for cook settings.

title: Food Picture Dial
new_elements: Photo menu dial (A single rotating dial shows photos of common meals and starts the matching program.)
rationale: Choosing a photo of the meal needs no knowledge of times or power levels.
judge_comment: A photo-menu dial maps meals directly to programs with no learning curve, which is very intuitive and easy to build, though accuracy depends on the portion and the food.

title: Magnetic Cook Tokens
new_elements: Magnetic preset tokens (Small tokens that stick to the door and select a program when placed.); Magnetic detection (Hall-effect sensor reads the token's position.)
rationale: Sticking a token on a door is a physical act that needs no understanding of settings.
judge_comment: Magnetic tokens replace the keypad with a simple physical act and are very buildable, though they only partly address timing and add loose pieces to lose.

title: Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Recipe card slot (A slot where a card with cook settings is inserted to program the machine.); Card reader (Reads the settings encoded in the card.)
rationale: Inserting a card is simpler than programming, and cards can be shared among users.
judge_comment: A card reader that swaps manual programming for inserted cards is simple and workable, similar to existing barcode or RFID cooking devices, though it needs a card for each food.

title: Humidity-Driven Cooking
new_elements: Steam sensor (Measures steam from food and ends cooking when it stops rising.); Humidity sensing (Detects moisture to judge when cooking is complete.)
rationale: Steam tells the machine when food is ready, so no time setting is required.
judge_comment: Steam sensing enables zero-input cooking, which closely matches the need, though sensor cooking already exists in some models.

title: Hand-Over-Plate Sense
new_elements: Proximity sensor (Starts heating when a hand is held over the plate, then stops when the hand is removed.); Hold-to-heat (Heating happens only while the user holds a hand over it.)
rationale: Holding a hand over food is a direct gesture that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A radical gesture-based hold-to-heat control is intuitive and safe, but it is tiring for long cooks and the sensing is tricky near a microwave.

title: Food-Pack NFC Auto-Program
new_elements: NFC food-pack tag (Passive tag on packaging carries power level and time, read by the oven on placement.)
rationale: The user never sets a dial because the food package tells the oven what to do.
judge_comment: Package-driven programming removes all input, though it requires industry-wide tag adoption and is not a true substitution for the controls.

title: Single Scroll Wheel Panel
new_elements: Scroll wheel with three icons (One wheel with icons for hot, warm and defrost)
rationale: One control with three icons is easier to read than two knobs and a dial.
judge_comment: A single wheel with three icons directly simplifies operation and is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Shell Cooking Companion Cup
new_elements: Self-timing cup (Cup that signals the microwave when liquid is at the right temperature)
rationale: The container tells the machine what to do so the user does not have to.
judge_comment: A container that tells the microwave when to stop removes the need to set anything, which fits the no-learning-curve need well, though wireless temperature sensing in a microwave is hard.

title: Dish Name Printed on Dish
new_elements: NFC-tagged packaging (Ready meal packaging carries a tag that sets the cooking program when placed inside.)
rationale: The food itself carries its instructions, so the user never has to program anything.
judge_comment: NFC-tagged packaging removes programming entirely and is plausible, though it depends on food makers adopting it and it doesn't cover non-tagged food.

title: Plate-Sized Button Field
new_elements: Full-width touch strip (A wide strip along the front where any tap starts or stops cooking.)
rationale: A large target that accepts any tap means the user cannot press the wrong button.
judge_comment: A single wide tap-anywhere strip removes button choice and is easy to build, though it gives up control over power and time.

title: Microwave Reads the Label
new_elements: Camera label recognition (A camera reads the printed name or barcode on the food package.)
rationale: The user shows the package, and the machine handles the rest.
judge_comment: Showing a package to a camera that reads the barcode removes nearly all operation learning and is plausible with existing tech, though a cooking-instruction database is needed.

title: Single Dial With Three Words
new_elements: Three-word dial (One dial with the words Reheat, Cook, Defrost in large letters.)
rationale: Three plain verbs cover almost every need with no numbers to interpret.
judge_comment: A three-verb dial replaces the numeric keypad with something instantly understood and easy to build, though it is not very radical.

title: Tap the Plate to Reheat
new_elements: Tap-to-start plate tag (Tapping the plate's rim on the microwave triggers the stored reheat program.)
rationale: Tapping an object the user already holds is the simplest possible gesture.
judge_comment: Tapping an NFC-style plate tag to start a stored reheat program is nearly zero-learning, though it needs special plates and the tag must survive microwave exposure.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Food pictogram dial (Single rotary dial with large icons (popcorn, leftovers, frozen veg, drink) that sets time and power together.)
rationale: Replacing the timer and power knobs with one icon dial removes the need to understand time and power levels.
judge_comment: Very clear fit for no-learning-curve operation and easy to build, but icon-based presets already exist on some ovens and it is not radical.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity and VOC gas sensor (Detects steam and aroma release to judge when food is hot and stops heating.)
rationale: The user never sets a time because the oven stops when the food smells and steams ready.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto-stop already exists in premium ovens, yet it does remove the need to set a time and is a fairly concrete mechanism.

title: Thermal-Camera Doneness
new_elements: Low-res thermal imaging (Cheap thermopile array reads the surface temperature of food to decide when it is done.)
rationale: The machine reads the food directly, so the user never has to guess power or time.
judge_comment: A thermopile array is cheap and plausible, though it reads only surface temperature and has to cope with the cavity environment and with covered food.

title: Floor-Weighed Auto-Cook
new_elements: Load-cell turntable base (Turntable sits on a load cell that reads food weight and sets time automatically.)
rationale: Weight alone tells the machine the right settings, so the user just places the food and presses nothing.
judge_comment: Load-cell weight sensing can remove all setting input, though weight alone is a crude proxy for the right cook settings and a load cell on a rotating turntable is difficult.

title: Barcode Cook Programs
new_elements: Barcode scanner window (Scans the food packet barcode and loads the correct cooking program.)
rationale: The packet tells the oven what to do, so students never have to read or set anything.
judge_comment: Scanning the barcode removes all settings and is feasible, though it relies on a program database and is not entirely new.

title: Single Big Button Oven
new_elements: One-button control (One large button starts a default auto-cook that reheats most foods.)
rationale: A single button with a sensible default means there is nothing to learn at all.
judge_comment: A single-button default cook directly delivers zero learning curve and is easy to build, though one-button designs already exist and a default may not suit all foods.

title: Steam-sensing auto-stop
new_elements: Steam-sensing auto-stop probe (Humidity sensor in cavity ceiling detects steam rise and ends cooking when food is done.)
rationale: The user never sets a time, so there is nothing to learn or misjudge.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop exists in sensor-cook microwaves, but it fully removes time setting and is very practical.

title: Camera food recognition
new_elements: Cavity camera with food classifier (Small camera identifies the food on the turntable and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: Both knobs disappear, so the only task left is putting food in and pressing start.
judge_comment: Camera recognition truly eliminates settings, though it's costly, and misclassification and steam on the lens are concerns.

title: Large sealed membrane panel
new_elements: Raised membrane button (A sealed, wipeable panel with one large raised button that clicks when pressed.)
rationale: A large tactile button is easy to find and press, and the sealed surface resists spills.
judge_comment: One large tactile sealed button is very easy to use and easy to build, though how it sets time or power is left unclear.

title: One-Dome Start Button
new_elements: Single domed start button (One large dome press starts cooking at a default setting; pressing again adds 30 seconds.)
rationale: A single obvious button means nothing needs to be learned before the first use.
judge_comment: One button with a default start and +30s is the simplest possible interface and trivially feasible, but it is not very radical.

title: Humidity-Ended Cooking
new_elements: Steam humidity sensor (A humidity sensor in the vent stops the cycle when steam output peaks and falls.)
rationale: The user never sets a time because the food itself signals when it is done.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensing auto-stop removes the need to set a time, directly serving zero-learning operation, though some microwaves already use sensor cooking.

title: Food Package Lid Reader
new_elements: Barcode window in cavity roof (A scanner reads a barcode printed on the meal tray and loads its cooking profile.)
rationale: Scanning the packet is the only step, so no cooking knowledge is needed.
judge_comment: Scanning a barcode for the cooking profile is plausible and nearly zero-learning, though it only works for labeled packaged meals.

title: Colour-Coded Power Wheel
new_elements: Colour-band power wheel (A wheel with four colour bands from pale to deep orange sets power by colour intensity.)
rationale: Colour intensity maps naturally to heat, so no numbers need to be understood.
judge_comment: A colour-band wheel replaces numeric power levels with an intuitive visual mapping, is cheap to make, and goes straight at the no-learning-curve need.

title: Barcode Cook
new_elements: Packaging barcode reader (Scans a printed code on food packs and loads the cooking program automatically.); Auto-program from package (Sets time and power without any user input.)
rationale: The user never sets a time or power level, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Package barcode scanning removes all settings and is plausible, though it only works for packaged foods and is not a strong substitution of a part.

title: Food Category Dial
new_elements: Four-position category dial (Dial with four pictograms: drink, bread, frozen, leftovers.)
rationale: Four physical positions with pictures replace five unlabelled power levels.
judge_comment: A four-pictogram dial is simple, cheap and directly replaces confusing power levels, though it is only mildly radical.

title: Auto-Defrost by Weight
new_elements: Weight-driven defrost (Load cells estimate the frozen mass and select a defrost curve without asking the user.)
rationale: Defrosting happens by pressing one button, so nobody has to guess a time for frozen food.
judge_comment: One-button defrost with automatic weight sensing directly removes the guesswork of setting a time, though it doesn't really substitute a part and similar products exist.

title: Dish Tag Auto-Program
new_elements: Dish-embedded RFID tag (Each reusable dish carries a tag that tells the machine its contents and program.)
rationale: Placing the dish is the only action a user takes, because the machine does the rest.
judge_comment: RFID auto-programming directly removes the learning curve and is readily feasible, though not very radical, and it needs tagged dishes.

title: Voice Says It, Oven Does It
new_elements: On-device speech command module (Hears plain phrases like 'warm my soup for two minutes' and sets the timer.); Offline speech recognition (Small neural model runs on a low-cost microcontroller with no cloud link.)
rationale: Speaking a request in ordinary words needs no dial, numbers or manual, so an elderly user can start cooking immediately.
judge_comment: Natural-language voice control removes the learning curve, and offline recognition on a microcontroller is plausible, though voice microwaves already exist and it is not a cheap substitution.

title: Squeeze to Heat
new_elements: Pressure-sensing front plate (Pressing harder on the front panel increases power and time, releasing stops.)
rationale: Pushing harder to cook and letting go to stop is a direct physical action that needs no reading or learning.
judge_comment: Pressure-to-heat is a radical, intuitive interface, but holding pressure for minutes is tiring and potentially unsafe or impractical.

title: Packaging Sets the Oven
new_elements: Package NFC tag reader (Reads a tag printed on food packaging and sets time and power automatically.); Passive NFC tags (Printed tags carry cooking instructions with no battery.)
rationale: Tapping the packet to the oven lets the food itself supply every setting, so the user chooses nothing.
judge_comment: Packaging-supplied settings by NFC tap remove all choices, which directly gives zero learning curve, and the parts are cheap and proven.

title: Voice-Free Meal Menu Wall
new_elements: Photo menu panel (Shows large photos of common meals to tap.)
rationale: Tapping a photo of the meal is the most direct way to cook for a new user.
judge_comment: A tap-a-photo menu directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Preset Snack Cartridge
new_elements: Cartridge reader slot (Inserting a pre-set cartridge loads the cooking program; no panel changes are needed.)
rationale: Users insert the food's cartridge and press nothing, so no settings are ever seen.
judge_comment: A cartridge reader that loads the program makes operation zero-learning and is practical, though similar to barcode or RFID cooking systems.

title: Food-Shaped Tokens
new_elements: Food token tray (Small chunky tokens shaped like pizza, rice, or soup; placing one selects the program.); RFID tagging (Passive tags inside tokens that the tray reads.)
rationale: Physical shapes match food types, so choosing a setting is the same as choosing a meal.
judge_comment: RFID food tokens make program choice physical and intuitive, are cheap and feasible, and are concrete, though tokens can get lost.

title: Dinner Dial Plate
new_elements: Single hunger dial (One dial with three marks: snack, meal, feast.)
rationale: Choosing how hungry you are replaces timing and power, which are harder to judge.
judge_comment: A single three-position dial replaces the keypad and is very simple, though it is imprecise for different foods and quantities.

title: Ring-Light Countdown
new_elements: Shrinking LED ring (Ring of lights around the door that goes dark one segment at a time as cooking finishes.)
rationale: A ring that empties is a visual countdown anyone can read at a glance.
judge_comment: An intuitive visual countdown that is cheap and readable, though it covers only status, not input.

title: Snap-On Food Caps
new_elements: Snap-on cap (A cap on the food container that clicks into place and sets time and power through its shape.)
rationale: A cap that only fits one way cannot be set wrong, so no learning is needed.
judge_comment: Physical caps that encode time and power replace the keypad with a shape-coded, error-proof interface that directly removes the learning curve, though the oven must read the cap and every food needs its own cap.

title: Steam-endpoint sensing
new_elements: Humidity and steam endpoint sensor (Stops heating when the moisture curve shows the food is hot, with no timer needed.)
rationale: Stopping on the food's own signal means no time to guess, which serves.
judge_comment: Humidity-based endpoint sensing already exists in sensor-cook models, but it removes timer guesswork and fits the need directly.

title: Shape-Recognising Cavity
new_elements: Overhead depth camera (Recognises the food on the tray and selects the cooking profile automatically.)
rationale: The machine sees what the food is and handles the settings itself.
judge_comment: A camera that identifies food and picks the profile removes nearly all user input, though recognition reliability and heat or steam on the camera are challenges.

title: Tag-Your-Bowl
new_elements: NFC food-container tag (Printed tags on bowls and cups send the required power and time to the oven on contact.)
rationale: The container carries its own instructions, so the user only places it on the tray.
judge_comment: Containers that carry their own cooking instructions remove nearly all operation, but they need ecosystem adoption and a safe way to handle non-microwave-safe items.

title: Hold-To-Run Timer Bar
new_elements: Capacitive slider bar with LED fill (Slide finger along bar; fill level shows minutes elapsed.); Displays and sets duration visually (A progress bar that doubles as a control.)
rationale: A visible bar that fills as you slide gives immediate feedback, which removes guessing and fixes short-duration imprecision.
judge_comment: A capacitive slider with an LED fill is simple, cheap and gives clear feedback, though it is only a modest departure from existing controls.

title: Timer-Free Fixed-Cycle Oven
new_elements: Fixed-recipe firmware (Runs one tested cycle that suits common foods.)
rationale: A single cycle that works for most foods removes all setting decisions.
judge_comment: A single fixed cycle removes all settings and directly serves zero learning curve, though one cycle for all foods risks poor results and is a fairly known concept.

title: Smell-Stop Gas Sensor
new_elements: Metal-oxide humidity and gas sensor (Detects steam and volatile compounds and ends cooking when they peak)
rationale: Cooking stops on its own at the right moment, so the user never needs to guess the time.
judge_comment: Auto-stop via humidity/gas sensing removes the need to choose a time, though it substitutes a sensor for a timer rather than something cheaper, and sensor-based cooking already exists on some microwaves.

title: Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: Mechanical wind-up spring (A crank winds a spring that unwinds slowly, with the visible coil showing the remaining time.)
rationale: A crank that unwinds needs no electronics, and the coil shows how much time is left.
judge_comment: A wind-up dial with a visible coil is simple and cheap and shows remaining time, though mechanical timers already exist on older microwaves.

title: Pre-Cooked Pod Oven
new_elements: Sealed meal pod reader (The oven runs the full cycle for a sealed pod, using the code printed on it.)
rationale: Putting in a pod and pressing start is the only action required.
judge_comment: Pod reader with a one-action start nearly eliminates the learning curve and is technically feasible, though pod-based systems exist and limit flexibility.

title: Food Pack Programming
new_elements: Packaging NFC programming tag (A tag on the food pack sends the correct time and power when the pack is tapped on the unit.)
rationale: The food manufacturer does the setting, so the user only taps the pack.
judge_comment: Tapping the pack removes all settings and uses proven NFC, though it relies on food manufacturers adopting it.

title: Single Start Knob
new_elements: One-turn start dial (A single dial with one position per food type and a press to start.)
rationale: One dial that does everything gives the user one place to look and one action to take.
judge_comment: A single dial with one position per food type directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though it is not very radical.

title: Package Tap Tray
new_elements: Printed-code reader tray (Reads a barcode or pictogram printed on the food packet and loads its recipe.); Recipe by packaging (Cooking instructions come from the packaging, not from knobs.)
rationale: Manufacturers print the instructions, so the user only places the packet on the tray.
judge_comment: Reading codes printed on packaging replaces the controls and is plausible, but it only works for packaged food and depends on manufacturers adopting it.

title: Pre-Programmed Cartridges
new_elements: Dish cartridge (A snap-in cartridge that carries the full cooking program for one dish.); Program by insertion (Inserting a cartridge sets all cooking parameters.)
rationale: Snapping in a cartridge is as simple as loading a game, and it needs no knowledge of power levels.
judge_comment: Cartridges eliminate parameter choices entirely, though they add consumables and limit flexibility.

title: Fridge-Door Magnet Presets
new_elements: Magnetic preset tokens (Tokens that stick to the door and each carry a program.); Program by magnet (Placing a token on the door selects its program.)
rationale: Stick-on tokens work like a fridge magnet, which is a familiar and effortless action.
judge_comment: Magnetic program tokens are intuitive and plausible with Hall sensors, and they substitute for a keypad, though the door placement has some practical issues.

title: NFC Food Tag Self-Programming
new_elements: NFC food-tag reader (A reader pad that reads a tag on the food packaging and sets time and power automatically.); Passive NFC tag encoding (Ready meals carry a cheap printed NFC tag that stores their cooking profile.)
rationale: Placing the packaged meal on the pad is the only action required, with no settings to understand.
judge_comment: Reading NFC tags on packaging gives true zero-input cooking, but it depends on food manufacturers adopting the tags and does nothing for untagged food.

title: Steam-Sensed Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor (A humidity sensor in the vent stops cooking when steam output drops off.); Vapour-based closed-loop control (Steam output is used as a proxy for food doneness.)
rationale: The machine decides when food is done, so the user needs no timing decisions at all.
judge_comment: Steam-sensed auto-stop removes timing decisions entirely and matches the need directly, though similar sensor-cook features already exist.

title: Two-Button Hot and Done
new_elements: Hot and Done buttons (Two large buttons: Hot heats a standard portion, Done stops the cycle.)
rationale: Two self-explanatory buttons remove every decision except whether to heat or stop.
judge_comment: Two-button Hot and Done design directly removes the learning curve, though a fixed standard portion limits flexibility and the concept is fairly close to existing one-touch models.

title: Packet-Programmed Cooking
new_elements: NFC tag on food packaging (Tapping the packet on the fascia loads the manufacturer's cook program.)
rationale: The packaging does the programming, so the user only taps and presses start.
judge_comment: Tap-and-start is nearly zero learning and plausible with NFC, but depends on food manufacturers adopting tags and only covers packaged food.

title: Picture-Dial Power
new_elements: Food-picture power dial (Power dial printed with pictures of food (soup, bread, ice) instead of numbers.)
rationale: Users choose by picture rather than by understanding duty cycles.
judge_comment: Directly replaces numeric power levels with pictures, removing the main learning hurdle, but it is a modest rather than radical change.

title: Raised Tactile Icon Panel
new_elements: Raised icon tiles (Large raised tiles with clear icons replace printed labels and small text.)
rationale: Large raised icons can be read by touch and by eye, so they need no manual.
judge_comment: Directly targets no-learning-curve operation with a simple, buildable substitution, but tactile icon panels are fairly familiar.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Stop
new_elements: Humidity steam sensing (A humidity sensor in the vent stops cooking when steam output shows the food is done.)
rationale: The oven stops itself, so no timer needs to be set or watched.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto stop removes timer setting, which directly serves zero-learning-curve use, and humidity-sensor cooking already exists in some ovens.

title: Smell-Done Auto-Stop
new_elements: Food VOC gas sensor (Metal-oxide sensor that detects aroma change as food reaches doneness.); Stops cooking at doneness without a timer (Ends the cycle when the smell peaks and then drops.)
rationale: Users never set a time, because the machine judges doneness from the food itself.
judge_comment: Auto-stop from food aroma removes time-setting entirely, though VOC sensing varies by food and is hard to make reliable; some microwaves already use humidity sensors.

title: Dishware that programs itself
new_elements: Passive RFID plate ring (A tag on the plate or bowl tells the oven the right time and power.)
rationale: Placing the food on a tagged plate is the only action the user takes.
judge_comment: A tagged plate that programs the oven is novel and zero-effort, but it needs special dishware and the plate does not know what food is on it.

title: Steam-sensing stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor (Detects moisture rising from food and ends cooking when it peaks.)
rationale: The oven decides when food is done, so nobody has to judge time.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, but it directly removes the need to pick a time; it's a weak fit for 'substitute' and not radical.

title: Cook from the fridge door
new_elements: Cloud recipe sync (The oven pulls the cooking plan from the packet's barcode via the cloud.)
rationale: Scanning a packet ends the need to set any settings.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning that sets cooking automatically removes settings entirely, though it relies on cloud data and a scanner, and the brief's SUBSTITUTE operator fits only loosely.

title: Pre-cooked meal kiosk
new_elements: Pre-set cook cartridge (A cartridge with the entire program inside is inserted to cook.)
rationale: Inserting a cartridge is the only action, so the oven needs no settings.
judge_comment: Inserting a cartridge as the only action eliminates settings entirely, though it needs a cartridge ecosystem and is akin to barcode or RFID cooking.

title: Radio-tagged food sleeve
new_elements: NFC food tag (Tapping the food packet to the oven sets the right cook program.)
rationale: A single tap is the simplest interaction possible.
judge_comment: NFC tap-to-cook removes nearly all operation steps and is plausible, though it needs packaging adoption and is not a true substitution of a part.

title: Hold-to-start
new_elements: Press-and-hold start (Holding a single button for one second starts a default cook.)
rationale: One deliberate action with one clear result is easy to learn.
judge_comment: A single hold-to-start button replaces the keypad and is simple and very feasible, but it is not radical.

title: Microwave as a cookbook
new_elements: Embedded e-ink recipe panel (A low-power e-ink panel displays a simple step-by-step recipe.)
rationale: Instructions appear on the appliance, so nothing needs to be memorised.
judge_comment: An e-ink recipe panel replacing the keypad is concrete and cheap, but reading recipes adds steps rather than removing them.

title: Cook Is Ready When You Are
new_elements: Auto-stop on doneness (Sensors detect steam and end the cook at the right moment.)
rationale: Users never guess a time because the machine judges doneness itself.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto-stop removes the need to set time and directly serves the need, but steam sensing already exists in many microwaves.

title: Door Hinge Is the Timer
new_elements: Door-angle timer (Opening the door by a set amount sets the time.)
rationale: A physical action that already exists becomes the control.
judge_comment: Using the door opening angle as a timer is intuitive and replaces a dial with a mechanical hinge sensor, though precision and the mismatch with how people open doors are concerns.

title: Stacking Cups That Cook
new_elements: Nested cook cups (Cups nest and carry a built-in cook profile.)
rationale: The container carries the instructions, so there is nothing for the user to set.
judge_comment: Containers that carry the cook profile remove all settings, but they need a reader (RFID or similar) and lock users into proprietary cups.

title: Hold-to-Heat Pad
new_elements: Large press-and-hold heat pad (Cooking runs only while the pad is pressed; releasing stops heating.)
rationale: Removes the need to understand time settings, so the user only has to hold a button for as long as they want heat.
judge_comment: Dead-man's-switch heating is zero-learning and simple, though holding for minutes is tiring and it only loosely fits a substitution of the timer.

title: Icon Dial of Foods
new_elements: Food-picture dial (One dial with pictures of popcorn, leftovers, frozen meal, and drink, each mapped to a preset cam profile.)
rationale: Users choose by recognising the food, not by reading numbers or power levels.
judge_comment: A pictorial dial with cam presets is cheap and intuitive, but it is a familiar approach and not radical.

title: Gentle-to-Go Slider
new_elements: Single detent slider (One slider with tactile detents from gentle to fast, with no numbers.)
rationale: A slider that moves in one direction only needs a glance and a touch, with no numerical scale to learn.
judge_comment: A detent slider with no numbers is intuitive and cheap, but it still leaves the user to guess at duration.

title: Frost-to-Clear Window
new_elements: Smart-glass state window (The window frosts while cooking and turns clear when heating ends, using electrochromic film.)
rationale: The window itself shows the state of the oven, so the user needs no status display to understand it.
judge_comment: Window state signalling replaces a display intuitively and is plausible with electrochromic film, though the film must be shielded against microwaves and heat.

title: Ring-Light Status Halo
new_elements: Door-edge LED halo (A coloured LED ring round the door edge: amber while cooking, green when done.)
rationale: Colour is understood without reading, so the user knows whether the oven is busy or finished.
judge_comment: A colour halo is an intuitive status cue that needs no reading, and it is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Timer-Free Clockwork Bell
new_elements: Fixed-count cam sequence (A non-adjustable cam runs one fixed heating sequence for each food selected.)
rationale: A fixed cam removes the setting step, so the mechanism is simple and cannot be set wrongly.
judge_comment: A fixed cam sequence is a concrete, cheap substitute for a digital timer, though food selection still needs some input.

title: Photo-Recognition Auto-Cook
new_elements: Food-recognition camera (Wide-angle camera above the plate that identifies the food.); On-device image classification (Small neural network that maps a food image to a cooking profile.); Selects power and time from a glance (Sets power and duration automatically from the recognised food.)
rationale: The user places food and presses nothing, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking strongly serves the need, but camera misrecognition and a lack of weight or state information limit reliability; it is also not especially cheaper or simpler.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable plate (Strain-gauge plate under the glass that measures food mass.); Strain-gauge weighing (Measures load and converts it to a mass reading.); Infers heating duration from mass (Maps the measured mass to a cook time.)
rationale: Users never set a time because the plate weighs the food and decides.
judge_comment: Load-cell weighing is plausible and removes time entry, but mass alone poorly identifies food type or desired heat.

title: Single Big Button
new_elements: Large pressure pad (One large pressure-sensitive pad on the front face.); One press starts a standard heat (A single press runs a default heat cycle that adjusts itself.)
rationale: One large target with one outcome is the simplest control possible.
judge_comment: A single large pad is as simple as it gets and is very easy to build, though the self-adjusting default is vague.

title: Voice Heat Command
new_elements: Offline speech recognition (On-device speech model that understands plain phrases.); Heats from spoken phrase (Starts heating when the user says something like heat this.)
rationale: Speaking a plain phrase is already known to everyone, so it needs no learning.
judge_comment: Offline voice control needs no learning and is plausible, but it is noisy in kitchens and the substitution is not cheaper or simpler.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor (Measures moisture in the cavity air.); Stops when steam peaks and falls (Ends heating when moisture shows the food is done.)
rationale: The machine decides when to stop, so the user never judges doneness.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensing auto-stop is already used in sensor-cook microwaves and removes the doneness judgement, but it is not radical.

title: Infrared Surface Done-Sensor
new_elements: Infrared surface thermometer (Non-contact sensor that reads food surface temperature.); Ends cycle at target temperature (Stops heating when the food reaches a safe serving temperature.)
rationale: Reaching a safe temperature replaces guessing at time and power levels.
judge_comment: An IR sensor that ends cooking at a target temperature replaces time and power guessing, though surface-only readings limit accuracy.

title: Pictogram Glass Presets
new_elements: Printed pictogram glass (Door glass with four printed icons such as bread, soup, frozen and leftover.)
rationale: Four pictures replace numeric power levels, so the choice is obvious.
judge_comment: Four icons on the door glass are simple and cheap to build, but they are a modest, incremental change rather than a radical one.

title: Tap-to-Reheat Pad
new_elements: Reheat tap pad (A single pad on the top that reheats the last thing cooked.)
rationale: One tap repeats the last cook, which is the only action most users ever need.
judge_comment: A single-pad repeat reheat is very simple and easy to build, but it is a modest idea and covers only repeat use.

title: Spring push-to-open door
new_elements: Push-to-open spring latch (Gentle push on the door face springs it open without a handle or button.)
rationale: Pushing a door is the default human reaction, so the mechanism matches what people already do.
judge_comment: Push-to-open latches are already common in cabinets and some appliances, so this is highly feasible and intuitive, but not very radical.

title: Three-picture food knob
new_elements: Picture-icon dial (Dial with three pictures: Reheat, Cook, Defrost.)
rationale: Choosing by picture of the task replaces abstract settings with words and numbers.
judge_comment: Pictorial task selection removes the learning curve, though similar preset-button designs already exist.

title: Food-icon power presets
new_elements: Food-icon preset buttons (Buttons labelled Melt, Simmer, Boil, Reheat set power automatically.)
rationale: Choosing the job instead of a power level means users never need to know what a number means.
judge_comment: Task-based presets replace abstract power levels with familiar jobs, which is intuitive and easy to build, though presets already exist on many microwaves.

title: Power set by tapping a food photo
new_elements: Food-photo selector (Door screen shows food photos; tapping one sets power and time.)
rationale: Tapping a picture of the food is faster and clearer than any scale of settings.
judge_comment: Photo-tap selection directly removes the learning curve, though it adds a screen rather than substituting a cheaper part and food-photo menus already exist in some ovens.

title: Auto-start on door close
new_elements: Close-to-start sensor (Closing the door starts a default cook from food sensing.)
rationale: Closing the door is already a natural final step, so it can serve as the start command.
judge_comment: Close-to-start removes the start step entirely and is plausible, though it risks accidental heating and the food-sensing mechanism is vague.

title: Barcode Auto-Program
new_elements: Package barcode reader (Flat scanner under the glass that reads the ready-meal barcode and loads time and power automatically.); Auto-set cooking program (Sets time and power with no user input.)
rationale: The user never sets a time or power level, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Barcode auto-programming removes all input for packaged meals, but it needs a barcode database and does nothing for non-packaged food.

title: Weigh-and-Go Plate
new_elements: Load cell turntable (Turntable that weighs the food and sets duration from mass.); Mass-based timing (Estimates heating time from how much food is on the plate.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate is the only step, so no timing decision is needed.
judge_comment: A load cell turntable is plausible and removes the timing decision, but mass alone is a poor predictor of heating time for different foods.

title: RFID Meal Cards
new_elements: RFID card reader (Reads a card or sticker placed on the food dish and runs its programme.); Card-based programme (Runs the heating programme encoded on a tag.)
rationale: Tapping a card is simpler than setting a dial, and tags can be printed on any meal.
judge_comment: Tap-and-go RFID cards are very simple and technically easy, though they depend on meals being tagged and RFID tags can be a hazard in microwaves.

title: Weigh-and-Go Tray
new_elements: Load-cell food tray (Strain-gauge base under the turntable reads food mass and auto-sets time and power, replacing both dials.); Load-cell mass sensing (Strain gauge bridge converts weight to a cooking-profile lookup.)
rationale: The user only places food and presses start, so there are no dials to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-setting removes dials, but mass alone poorly identifies food type, and a load cell under a rotating turntable is a hurdle.

title: Tap-and-Heat Food Packs
new_elements: NFC food-pack reader (Reads a tag printed on the packaging and loads its cooking program.); Passive NFC tag (Powerless tag on packaging stores time and power settings.)
rationale: Pressing a pack to the oven replaces every setting decision with one gesture.
judge_comment: Tap-to-cook is simple and feasible with cheap NFC tags, but it only works for packaged food that carries tags, and barcode cooking exists already.

title: Single Start Pebble
new_elements: One-button start pebble (A single large tactile dome; each press starts a default reheat and a long press opens the door.)
rationale: One button with one meaning removes the menu entirely.
judge_comment: A single button gives zero learning curve and is trivially buildable, but it's a minimalist idea more than a radical one, and a default reheat fits few foods.

title: Spoken Heat Command
new_elements: Far-field microphone array (Hears natural phrases such as 'warm up my coffee' and maps them to programs.); On-device speech intent recognition (Small offline model maps spoken intent to a cook program without cloud access.)
rationale: Users speak in ordinary words, so no panel needs to be learned.
judge_comment: Natural speech needs no learning and offline models are viable, but noisy kitchens and the microwave's own sound make it less reliable, and voice microwaves already exist.

title: Doneness by Smell
new_elements: VOC gas sensor (Detects volatile compounds as food heats and stops cooking at the right moment.); Metal-oxide gas sensing (Resistive sensor whose output changes with food volatiles.)
rationale: The oven stops itself, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Auto-stop by VOC sensing is truly hands-off and somewhat novel, but metal-oxide sensors are noisy, drift, and are hard to calibrate across foods.

title: Infrared Doneness Eye
new_elements: IR thermal eye (Low-cost thermopile reads surface temperature and ends cooking when the target is reached.)
rationale: Cooking ends on temperature, so no timer setting is needed at all.
judge_comment: Removes the timer step entirely, which serves zero-learning-curve operation, but a surface IR reading is unreliable for microwave heating and varies by food, so it is only moderately feasible.

title: Three Tactile Heat Positions
new_elements: Three-detent heat ring (A physical ring with clicks: low, medium, high, with no numbers to read.)
rationale: Three clicks cover every everyday case, and the feel of each click gives the setting away.
judge_comment: Simple, intuitive and easy to build, but it is a modest idea, not a radical one, and the three levels limit control.

title: Projected Control Surface
new_elements: Countertop laser projector (A small projector paints the controls on the worktop; the oven has no buttons.); Pico-projection with gesture sensing (Projected controls are read by a time-of-flight sensor.)
rationale: Controls are shown where the user is already looking, so no panel needs learning.
judge_comment: A radical idea with a projector and ToF gesture sensing, though projected controls on a worktop are sensitive to glare, clutter and heat, and gestures may add a learning curve.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Load-cell turntable weighing (Strain gauges under the glass tray estimate food mass and set cook time.); Load-cell tray sensor (Replaces the timer cam. Reads mass and sets duration automatically.)
rationale: Put food on the plate and press start; the machine works out how long it needs.
judge_comment: Press-start operation with no settings fits the need well, though mass alone is a poor predictor of cook time and load cells under a rotating tray are tricky.

title: Warm-Handle Done Cue
new_elements: Warms the handle when cooking ends (The door handle gently warms and softly pulses when food is ready.); Heated door handle (Low-power thermal strip in the handle.)
rationale: The handle itself says the food is ready, which suits users who cannot hear a bell or see a display.
judge_comment: A warm handle is a novel, accessible done cue, but it only signals completion and does little to simplify operation.

title: Single Big Button Fascia
new_elements: One large start button (A single oversized button that starts the default program.)
rationale: One obvious button is the simplest possible interface for anyone.
judge_comment: A single start button directly removes the learning curve and is very easy to build, though it is not really a substitution of parts and is not very radical.

title: Packet Barcode Cooking
new_elements: Package code reader (A scanner in the door reads a code printed on the food packet and sets power and time.)
rationale: Scanning the packet is the same action people use at a supermarket checkout.
judge_comment: Scanning the packet code sets power and time automatically with a familiar action, and the technology is mature, though it relies on codes printed on packaging.

title: Sticker-Start Cooking
new_elements: NFC food sticker (Tapping a sticker on the packaging against the door sets time and power together.)
rationale: Tapping a sticker is one action, and it needs no reading or number entry.
judge_comment: A single tap sets both time and power with no number entry, and NFC is cheap, but it needs stickers on the food packaging.

title: Sear-Melt-Warm Modes
new_elements: Mode picker (Three modes named Warm, Melt and Sear replace the five numbered power levels.)
rationale: Named cooking jobs are easier to choose than numbers that mean little to the user.
judge_comment: Named modes replacing numeric power levels make choices more intuitive and are easy to implement, with moderate novelty.

title: Open-Loop Off Switch
new_elements: Steam-stop detection (A humidity sensor detects when the food stops steaming and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The machine decides when to stop, so the user does not need to set or check a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop removes the time-setting step entirely, and the sensor idea is known, but the steam signal is unreliable for dry or covered foods.

title: Hands-Free Mode
new_elements: Gesture-free auto mode (The oven picks time and power from a camera view of the food, with no controls used.)
rationale: The machine chooses for the user, so the only learning needed is to put the food inside.
judge_comment: A camera-driven auto mode removes all learning, and it is plausible with existing food recognition, though accuracy in a microwave is hard.

title: Pull-Cord Duration
new_elements: Pull-cord timer (A cord the user pulls out; its length sets the cooking time and it retracts as the timer runs.); Spring-retract cord metering (A spring reel that returns the cord at a fixed rate.)
rationale: Pulling a cord out as far as the time you want is a physical gesture everyone already understands.
judge_comment: A pull-cord whose length sets duration is an intuitive physical metaphor and mechanically plausible, though retracting at a precise rate needs a governor.

title: Food-Card Slot
new_elements: Food-card slot (A slot the user slides a printed card into; the card's notches set time and power.); Notched-card mechanical reading (Mechanical feelers read the card notches without any electronics.)
rationale: Sliding in a card that matches the food replaces dials, so there is nothing to interpret.
judge_comment: A notched card read mechanically is a concrete low-tech replacement for dials, but it needs a card per food and loose cards get lost.

title: Pictogram Food Plate
new_elements: Food-icon press plates (Raised plates with food pictures; pressing one loads the matching time and power.); Selects food preset by picture (Chooses a complete cooking program from a single picture.)
rationale: Users choose by recognising food, not by reading numbers or understanding power levels.
judge_comment: Picture-based preset buttons directly remove the need to read numbers, but food-preset buttons already exist on many microwaves.

title: Door-Opens-Itself Finish
new_elements: Spring-eject door (The door springs open a few centimetres when cooking ends.); Electrically released spring latch (A solenoid releases the latch at the end of the cycle.)
rationale: The door opens by itself when the food is ready, so the user never has to find the release button.
judge_comment: Auto-opening door removes the release-button hunt at the end and is mechanically simple, though it doesn't address the start-up controls.

title: Handle-Is-The-Button
new_elements: Pull-handle latch (A large handle that releases the latch when pulled; no separate button.); Pull-to-release lever (A mechanical lever that moves the latch as the handle is pulled.)
rationale: The handle that people already grip doubles as the release, so there is nothing to search for.
judge_comment: Pull-handle door is intuitive and feasible, but it's already common on many microwaves and so is not radical.

title: Top-Lift Lid
new_elements: Gas-strut top lid (A top-opening lid lifted by gas struts that stays open on its own.); Gas-strut lift (Gas springs that carry the lid's weight so it lifts with one finger.)
rationale: Lifting a top lid is the same motion as opening a kitchen cupboard, so users already know how.
judge_comment: A gas-strut top lid mimics a familiar motion and is feasible, but a top-loading microwave raises spill and ergonomic issues.

title: Heavy-Dial Tactile Power
new_elements: Detented big-grip power knob (A large knob with a click at each of three clear settings, felt through the fingers.); Tactile three-step power (Shows power level by the number of clicks felt when turning.)
rationale: Felt clicks in the hand make three settings obvious even without reading any labels.
judge_comment: A detented three-step knob is simple and easy to build but fairly incremental.

title: Ready-Bowl Pad
new_elements: Heating pad sensor (A flat pad under the food that switches the cycle on when food is placed and off when it is removed.); Starts and stops by placement (The machine runs only when food is on the pad.)
rationale: Turning on is just putting food down and turning off is just taking it away.
judge_comment: Placement-triggered start and stop removes controls entirely and is very simple, though it needs safe detection and doesn't set power or time.

title: NFC Pack-Tap
new_elements: NFC tag reader pad (Reads a tag printed on food packaging and loads its cook program.); Near-field communication tag (Passive RFID-style tag, about 1 cent per pack.)
rationale: Tapping the food pack sets the correct time and power automatically, so the user never has to think about settings.
judge_comment: Tapping the pack is a clever, concrete way to remove settings, but it depends on food makers adopting the tags.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Cook
new_elements: Humidity sensor in cavity (Detects steam rise and stops the cycle when food is hot.); Capacitive humidity sensing (Low-cost polymer humidity sensor.)
rationale: The machine senses when food is ready, so the user never guesses at a time.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing is well proven and removes time guessing, but sensor cooking is already common on microwaves.

title: One-Tap Heat Me
new_elements: Weight plate under turntable (Measures food mass and chooses power and duration automatically.); Single-action start (One big button starts the right cycle for whatever is inside.)
rationale: A single button removes the choice of power level and time entirely.
judge_comment: A weight plate with a single button is plausible and simple, though mass alone gives imperfect cooking results.

title: NFC Food Card
new_elements: Packaging NFC tag (Food packaging carries a tag with cooking instructions that the oven reads on contact.); Near-field communication (Short-range wireless data transfer.)
rationale: The manufacturer sets the cooking time, so the user only places the packet on the tray.
judge_comment: Reading cooking instructions from packaging by NFC makes operation nearly zero-effort, but it depends on food manufacturers adopting tags and does nothing for food without them.

title: Phone-as-Remote Cook
new_elements: Scan-to-cook camera (Camera reads a food barcode and sets the cycle automatically.); Computer vision recognition (Identifies the food from its packaging or shape.)
rationale: The oven adapts to the food, so the user never has to translate a meal into settings.
judge_comment: Barcode and vision scanning to set the cycle is workable and removes the need to translate a meal into settings, though scanning is an extra step and the name mismatches the content.

title: Winding Clockwork Timer
new_elements: Wind-up cooking spring (User winds a spring to set cooking time, like a toy.); Mechanical spring energy (Stored energy released over time.)
rationale: Winding a spring is a tactile act with no numbers, which is easy to understand.
judge_comment: Wind-up mechanical timers are used in older microwaves, and they are intuitive and cheap, though less precise.

title: Glowing Wall Clock Face
new_elements: Analog clock face display (A large clock face whose hand shows remaining cooking time as a slice of pie.); Pie-chart time display (Time shown as a shrinking wedge.)
rationale: A shrinking pie slice shows time left without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A shrinking pie wedge is an intuitive, easy-to-build time display that replaces numbers, though similar timers already exist.

title: Hug Handle Door
