new_elements: Full-width grip bar (A wide bar across the door that opens it when pushed from either side.); Push-anywhere open (Pushing any part of the bar opens the door.)
rationale: There is no small button to miss, so opening the door is effortless.
judge_comment: A push-anywhere grip bar makes opening simple and is mechanically plausible, but it only addresses the door.

title: Pull-Tab Cooking
new_elements: Pull-tab heat trigger (A colored tab on the front; cooking runs while it stays pulled out and stops when released.)
rationale: A pull-and-release gesture needs no numbers, dial reading, or prior knowledge of times.
judge_comment: A hold-to-run pull tab is intuitive and safe, but it is awkward for long cooks and its mechanism is only loosely described.

title: Magnetic Click Heat Dial
new_elements: Magnetic detent knob (A knob with strong magnetic detents that click into place, so the setting is felt rather than read.)
rationale: Positive clicks confirm each choice by feel, so the user never needs to read the setting.
judge_comment: Tactile detents aid usability, but the user must still understand what the settings mean.

title: Push-Anywhere Latch
new_elements: Spring push-to-open latch (A door that springs open when pushed at any point on its edge, with no button.)
rationale: A push-to-open door is the most natural action and needs zero instruction.
judge_comment: A push-to-open latch replaces the button with something simpler and cheaper, and it is highly feasible, though similar doors already exist.

title: Flat-Panel Timer Glow
new_elements: Shape-based timer light (A shape that grows as time passes, shown on the light instead of numbers.)
rationale: A shape that changes with time needs no numeric understanding.
judge_comment: A growing-shape timer display removes the need to read numbers, serves the no-learning-curve need directly, and is easy to build with LEDs.

title: Ice-Pop Simple Mode
new_elements: Single-action reheat (One physical button that reheats whatever is inside at a set safe level.)
rationale: One button that always does the right thing is the zero-learning-curve answer.
judge_comment: One button that reheats at a safe preset directly delivers zero learning curve and is readily buildable, though the mechanism for sensing the food is vague.

title: Humidity-Sensing Auto-Cook
new_elements: Humidity and gas sensor array (Detects steam and volatiles to judge when food is done and stops automatically.); Auto-determines cook time without user input (Replaces manual time selection entirely.)
rationale: The machine decides when food is done, so the user never has to learn a time or power setting.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto-stop already exists in some premium microwaves, but it directly removes any need to learn settings and is plausible.

title: Single Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Food-picture dial (One dial with four pictures (drink, leftovers, frozen, popcorn) that each set power and time.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of the food is easier to understand than reading numbers and power levels.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible, but it is a modest, familiar simplification, not a radical one.

title: Scan-the-Packet Cooking
new_elements: Packaging code reader (Reads a printed code on food packaging and loads the correct settings.); Printed machine-readable code on packaging (Low-cost code printed on food packs that carries cook instructions.)
rationale: The user only places the pack and presses start, with no settings to remember.
judge_comment: Barcode-driven cooking is concrete and gives zero-setting use, but it depends on food manufacturers adopting it.

title: Stick-On Cooking Sticker
new_elements: Thermal sticker tag (A sticker on the food package that changes colour and tells the oven what it contains.)
rationale: The food tells the oven what to do, so the user has nothing to set.
judge_comment: Food packaging that tells the oven what to do removes all settings, but it needs a reader and depends on packaging adoption, and a thermal colour change is a vague way to encode instructions.

title: Infrared Doneness Eye
new_elements: Infrared food thermometer (Reads food surface temperature and stops when food is hot enough.)
rationale: The oven decides when food is ready from its temperature, so the user does not need to judge.
judge_comment: An IR thermometer that stops cooking automatically takes judgment away from the user and is plausible, though it only reads surface temperature and sensor-based microwaves already exist.

title: Subscription Food Auto-Cook
new_elements: Cook settings delivered with groceries (Each meal delivery sends settings that the oven loads automatically.)
rationale: Students never need to set anything because the settings come with the food.
judge_comment: Settings delivered with the food remove all operation, which is highly relevant, but it needs a package-to-oven data standard and ecosystem.

title: Weigh-and-Go Plate
new_elements: Load-cell food weighing (A strain-gauge plate estimates food mass and sets heating time automatically.)
rationale: The user only places food on the plate, so no timer or power settings need to be learned.
judge_comment: A load-cell plate removes the need to set time, and it's plausible, but weight alone is a poor proxy for heating needs and a rotating plate complicates the sensor.

title: Barcode Meal Pods
new_elements: Packaging barcode reader (A scanner in the cavity reads a barcode and loads the matching cook program.)
rationale: Scanning a barcode replaces every manual setting with one passive action.
judge_comment: A barcode scanner is cheap and proven (some existing models use it), but it needs a compatible barcode database and only works for packaged food.

title: Ambient Done Glow
new_elements: Edge-lit door glow (The door edge glows green when food is ready and stays dark while cooking.)
rationale: A single colour state gives status at a glance without any display to read.
judge_comment: An LED edge glow is cheap and easy to build and gives an intuitive status, but it only covers the done state and is not radical.

title: Snap Thermostat to Sensor
new_elements: Infrared food thermometer (A thermopile reads surface temperature and ends cooking at the right point.)
rationale: Reading the food directly removes the need for the user to understand cooking times.
judge_comment: An IR thermopile that ends cooking automatically removes the need to set a time and is plausible, though it reads only surface temperature, and the idea is not very radical.

title: Cloud Recipe Hub
new_elements: Delivery service (The delivery service sends the cooking program with the meal.)
rationale: The meal provider sets the program, so the user never configures anything.
judge_comment: Meal-supplied cooking programs remove all configuration, which directly serves zero learning curve, though it needs ecosystem and connectivity support.

title: Weight-Sensing Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Turntable that weighs the food and sets cook time automatically.); Automatic time setting (Cook time is chosen from measured food mass with no user input.)
rationale: The user places food and presses nothing, so there is no timer to learn.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation fits the need perfectly, but weight alone poorly determines cook time for different foods, and load cells in a rotating turntable add cost.

title: Tap-a-Picture Menu
new_elements: Food photo tiles (Large tiles showing a photo of the food, such as rice, pizza, or soup.); Recognition by picture (The user taps the picture of what they are cooking, and the machine sets power and time.)
rationale: Choosing by picture needs no knowledge of power levels or numbers.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and very buildable, though preset food menus already exist on many microwaves.

title: One-Press Cook
new_elements: Single heat button (One large button that opens the door when pressed once and starts cooking when the door closes.); Unified start and open (Opening and starting are merged into one gesture.)
rationale: A single button with one meaning removes the question of which button does what.
judge_comment: A single button simplifies operation, but it gives no control over time and risks starting accidentally.

title: Package-Reading Cook
new_elements: Package code reader (Scans a printed code on the food packet and loads its cook settings.); Printed-code cook data (Food makers print the right power and time on the packaging.)
rationale: The packet does the thinking, so the user only has to show the food to the machine.
judge_comment: Scanning packaging for cook settings removes all user input, though it depends on food makers adopting it (similar barcode microwaves exist).

title: Thermochromic Food Label
new_elements: Heat-reveal sticker (A label stuck to the food that changes colour when it is hot all the way through.); Thermochromic ink (Ink that changes colour at a set temperature.)
rationale: The food itself reports when it is done, so the user doesn't need to judge timing.
judge_comment: A heat-reveal label on the food shows doneness with no settings, but it needs a consumable sticker that survives microwaving, and it does not replace the controls.

title: Crumb-Free Smart Tray
new_elements: Disposable food tray (A tray with a built-in code that sets the machine and is thrown away after use.); Tray-based setup (The tray brings its own settings.)
rationale: The tray arrives ready to cook, so the user only places it and presses start.
judge_comment: A coded disposable tray that carries its own settings is feasible and reduces operation to place-and-start, though it creates waste and depends on tray supply.

title: Dial-Free Voice Ready
new_elements: Spoken choice buttons (Large buttons with spoken labels such as 'soup' and 'bread' that read aloud.); Audible choice (Hears the choice before cooking.)
rationale: Hearing what each button does removes any need to read or memorise.
judge_comment: Spoken button labels are highly accessible and easy to build, though not very radical and the button-press learning is still needed.

title: Simple Flat Switch Stove
new_elements: Single rocker switch (A flat rocker: up means heat, down means off.); Binary control (On and off are the only states.)
rationale: A rocker switch has two obvious states and nothing else to learn.
judge_comment: A single on/off rocker is extremely simple and cheap, but it is an obvious idea, and with no timer or power control it may not cook well.

title: Tap-a-Picture Control Strip
new_elements: Pictogram touch strip (Single capacitive strip showing pictures of rice, soup, pizza, frozen, reheat.)
rationale: Users recognise food pictures faster than they read numbers or dial positions.
judge_comment: A pictogram strip is very easy to use and cheap, but it is an incremental idea rather than a radical one.

title: Weigh-to-Cook Platter
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Turntable sits on load cells that read food mass and set time automatically.)
rationale: The oven decides how long to cook by weighing the plate, so no timer has to be set.
judge_comment: Load cells are plausible and automate time, but mass alone poorly predicts the cooking time for different foods.

title: Steam-Sense Auto Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor vent (Vent sensor detects steam rise and ends heating when steam drops off.)
rationale: Stopping when the food stops steaming means the user never guesses a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto stop is proven in sensor-cook ovens and removes the guessing, though the user still has to start it.

title: Ambient Done-Glow Cavity
new_elements: Edge LED glow ring (Ring of light around the cavity pulses slowly while cooking and turns green when done.)
rationale: The light shows status without any reading, so nothing has to be interpreted.
judge_comment: A simple glow ring that changes color on completion is easy to build and understand with no reading, though it isn't very radical.

title: Stackable Pictogram Trays
new_elements: Stacking food tray (Trays stack by picture, each carrying its own cooking profile.)
rationale: Picking the tray for the food sets the cook, so users never think about settings.
judge_comment: Tray-based cook profiles directly remove settings and learning, though it needs tray recognition (e.g. RFID or a mechanical key) and microwave-safe electronics, which the idea does not spell out.

title: Turntable-Free Mode Stir
new_elements: Stirring mode vane (Fixed vane in the cavity moves microwave modes so food heats evenly with no turntable.)
rationale: No rotating glass means nothing to take out, wash, or put back on the spindle.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves and are a feasible, cheap substitute for the turntable, though the link to a no-learning-curve interface is indirect.

title: Voice-Free Shape Picker
new_elements: Food shape camera (Camera recognises the food and proposes one setting for confirmation.)
rationale: The oven picks the program itself, so the user only presses one confirm.
judge_comment: A camera that identifies food and proposes one setting needs only a confirm press, which is very low learning curve, though recognition accuracy and cost are concerns.

title: Doorstop Power Switch
new_elements: Door-closing power (Power starts when the door closes and stops when it opens.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only step, which people already do without thinking.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is extremely intuitive, but it needs a default duration and raises safety and accidental-start concerns, so it is not fully workable as stated.

title: NFC Meal Tag Programming
new_elements: NFC tag reader (Reads a tag on the food packet and loads the cook program)
rationale: The user taps the packet to the oven and the correct settings load themselves.
judge_comment: Tapping the food packet to load the program removes the need to enter settings, which directly targets a no-learning-curve operation, but it depends on packets carrying tags.

title: Shared Cook Recipe Card
new_elements: Recipe card reader (Reads a printed card with a food picture and loads the cook program)
rationale: A printed card is faster and clearer than any manual.
judge_comment: Substituting a printed picture card for manual programming gives a strong no-learning-curve interaction and is feasible with a barcode or QR reader.

title: Stored Program Dial Only
new_elements: Program presets (Five fixed programs on one dial, each named by food type)
rationale: Five named choices is simpler than a timer with unknown numbers.
judge_comment: A five-preset food dial directly cuts the learning curve and is easy to build, but similar auto-cook buttons already exist.

title: Single Big Start Pebble
new_elements: One large tactile pebble (A single raised, glowing pebble that starts cooking whenever it is pressed.)
rationale: One obvious control removes every decision about which button to press.
judge_comment: A single start control is very simple and easy to build, but it leaves open how time and power get set, and similar one-button designs already exist.

title: Food Tells the Microwave
new_elements: Smell-based food detection (A gas sensor identifies the food type from its aroma and sets the program.)
rationale: The machine works out what to do from the food, so the user never has to decide.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting food would remove nearly all decisions, but gas-sensor identification of food is unreliable and the mechanism is vague.

title: Ambient Light Done Ring
new_elements: Ring light progress (A ring of LEDs around the top fills as cooking progresses and turns green when done.)
rationale: A visual progress ring explains the state of the oven at a glance.
judge_comment: The LED progress ring communicates state at a glance and is cheap and feasible, though it is a familiar pattern.

title: Food-photo button menu
new_elements: Four large food-photo buttons (Raised buttons showing photos of popcorn, rice, soup and leftovers, each starting a preset.)
rationale: Users recognise a picture of their food faster than they read a number on a dial.
judge_comment: Easy to implement and intuitive, but preset buttons are an incremental, familiar approach.

title: Door-close starts, door-open stops
new_elements: Door-closure sensor (Magnetic reed switch starts cooking when the door shuts and stops it when the door opens.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed, which matches the habit of shutting something to make it work.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes button use, but there is no way to set time or power and an accidental start with an empty cavity is a safety concern.

title: Single heat slider with food icons
new_elements: Food-icon heat slider (One slider moves between a soft icon, a bowl icon and a steak icon, setting power to match.)
rationale: Choosing by what the food is replaces understanding of power percentages.
judge_comment: Choosing by food icon replaces power percentages with something intuitive and is easy to implement, though it is not radical.

title: Smell-sensing reheat
new_elements: Volatile-gas sensor (Gas sensor detects aroma rising from food and lowers power when it peaks.)
rationale: Sensing the food itself means the user never sets power at all.
judge_comment: Aroma sensing removes power setting entirely, which strongly serves no-learning-curve use, though the gas sensor is noisy and the details of the control logic are thin.

title: One-button auto-program
new_elements: Single start button (One large button starts cooking, using sensors to choose time and power.)
rationale: A single button means the whole control panel is one action and nothing else to learn.
judge_comment: A single start button directly removes the learning curve, and the sensor-based auto-cook is plausible, though one-touch designs already exist.

title: Rotating icon drum replaces both knobs
new_elements: Food-icon drum (A single rotating drum shows food icons, and turning it sets both time and power.)
rationale: One control with pictures replaces two dials with numbers, which is simpler to use.
judge_comment: A single icon drum that sets time and power is a clear, intuitive substitution for two numeric dials, though the icon-to-setting mapping needs design care.

title: Food Card Slot
new_elements: Printed food-card slot (Slide a credit-card-sized printed card showing the food; its magnetic stripe sets time and power.)
rationale: Inserting a card that matches the food removes all settings the user must learn.
judge_comment: A card with a magnetic stripe is concrete and workable, but users must find and keep the right cards, which adds friction.

title: Food-Weight Auto Power
new_elements: Load-cell turntable sensor (Strain gauges under the turntable weigh the food and choose power and time automatically.)
rationale: Placing food on the plate is the only action, because the machine works out the settings from its weight.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto settings need no user action, but weight alone says little about food type, and strain gauges in a microwave are tricky.

title: Spring-Push Door
new_elements: Spring-loaded push door (A spring-loaded hinge opens the door a few centimetres when pressed, no latch needed.)
rationale: A gentle push is the natural way to open a door, so no mechanism needs learning.
judge_comment: A push-to-open spring hinge is a proven, cheap, intuitive substitute for the latch, though it is not radical.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Sliding drawer front (The cavity slides out like a drawer on guide rails, with no hinge swing.)
rationale: A pull-out drawer matches how people already open kitchen storage, so it needs no instruction.
judge_comment: A drawer matches existing mental models and is more radical, but it brings sealing, rail and cost challenges.

title: Infrared Food Reader
new_elements: Infrared thermopile surface reader (An infrared sensor reads the food surface temperature and ends cooking when it is hot.)
rationale: The machine finishes the job by itself, so the user does not have to judge when food is ready.
judge_comment: Automatic cooking by infrared sensing removes the need to set time or power, directly serving a no-learning-curve goal, though sensing through the cavity is challenging.

title: Projected Countdown Ring
new_elements: Floor-projected countdown ring (A light ring projected onto the turntable floor shrinks as cooking progresses.)
rationale: A shrinking ring on the floor shows time left in a way anyone can understand.
judge_comment: A shrinking projected ring gives an intuitive time-left display, though projecting inside the cavity and keeping it visible are challenges.

title: Ask-Before-Starting Magnet
new_elements: Food-type magnetic tile (A magnet tile on the food dish tells the unit what food it holds and sets the program.)
rationale: Placing the right tile on the dish is an intuitive act that sets the cycle with no menu.
judge_comment: Magnetic food tiles replace menus with a tangible act and are plausible with Hall sensors, though the user must keep track of the tiles.

title: Scent-Done Detector
new_elements: VOC gas sensor (Detects when food releases the aroma of being cooked and stops the cycle.); Gas-sensing chemistry (Metal-oxide sensing of volatile organic compounds.)
rationale: The machine decides when food is done, so the user never has to judge or set a time.
judge_comment: A VOC sensor replaces the timer with automatic doneness detection, which is plausible, though reliability across foods and false stops are concerns.

title: Tray-as-Controller
new_elements: Shape-coded tray (Tray notches and shape encode the cooking program, read by the cavity.)
rationale: Choosing the right dish is the same action as choosing the setting, so there are no controls to learn.
judge_comment: Shape-coded tray removes the need to choose settings and is a novel, concrete mechanism, though it requires dedicated trays and a reader.

title: Close-the-Door Start
new_elements: Door-closure sensor (Closing the door with food inside starts the default cook cycle.)
rationale: Closing a door is an action everyone already knows, so starting the oven needs no new skill.
judge_comment: Door-closure start eliminates controls entirely and is highly intuitive, though the default cycle risks overcooking or unsafe empty starts.

title: Auto-Sense Cook Button
new_elements: Humidity and IR food sensor (Reads moisture and surface heat to pick time and power without input.)
rationale: A single press is the whole interface, because the sensors make every other decision.
judge_comment: One-press operation with sensors is the ideal zero-learning interface, but sensor-cook features already exist and accuracy is a concern.

title: Plate Chip Instructions
new_elements: NFC plate tag (Plates or containers carry an NFC tag that tells the oven how to cook them.)
rationale: The instructions travel with the food, so the user never has to look anything up.
judge_comment: Instructions embedded in the plate removes all input, though it requires special tagged dishware and a reader, and it is only partly a substitution.

title: Tap-to-Heat Counter Panel
new_elements: Capacitive wood-grain surface (Flat, button-free surface where a tap on the printed food icon starts cooking.)
rationale: A flat surface with no moving parts looks like a countertop, not a control panel.
judge_comment: Replacing buttons with a flat capacitive surface and food icons is simple and feasible, but it is a fairly familiar touch-panel approach.

title: Projected Counter Status
new_elements: Counter projector (Projects a large countdown bar onto the worktop beside the oven.)
rationale: Status appears where the user is already looking, so there is no display to decode.
judge_comment: A projected countdown is practical and easy to read, but it only improves status feedback and not the controls.

title: Phone-Free Scanner Pad
new_elements: Tap-card reader (A pre-loaded card or fob with the chosen program, tapped on the door.)
rationale: A tap starts a known program, so the user learns nothing beyond a single habit.
judge_comment: NFC tap cards replace the control panel with one gesture and are very feasible, though cards must be managed and the idea is a bit like phone-app control.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell weighing turntable (Glass tray sits on strain-gauge load cells that read food mass and set time and power automatically.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate becomes the only step, because the machine reads the load and chooses the settings.
judge_comment: Weighing removes all settings, but mass alone cannot tell food type or desired temperature, so accuracy is limited.

title: Tap-a-Photo Food Panel
new_elements: Large photo-tile touch panel (Six big photos of common foods (rice, soup, pizza, milk, veg, frozen meal) replace numeric dials.)
rationale: Users recognise pictures faster than they decode time and power numbers, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive, but picture-based presets are an incremental, already-seen approach.

title: Radar Wave-to-Open Door
new_elements: 60 GHz radar gesture sensing (A low-power radar in the fascia detects a hand approaching the door and releases the latch.)
rationale: A wave of the hand opens the door, so nobody has to find or press a small button.
judge_comment: Radar wave-to-open is plausible and removes the button hunt, but it does not simplify the actual operation (settings), and accidental triggers are a risk.

title: Single Start Button Appliance
new_elements: One-button smart preset (A single big button starts a learned default program that adapts to what was cooked last.)
rationale: Pressing one large button is the simplest possible interface, so beginners get good results immediately.
judge_comment: A single-button appliance directly removes the learning curve, though one-button microwaves are not new and the learned default is vague.

title: Gas-Sniff Auto-Stop
new_elements: Metal-oxide VOC sensing (A gas sensor detects steam and aroma rising from food and ends cooking when they peak.)
rationale: Food tells the machine when it is ready by smell, so nobody needs to watch a clock.
judge_comment: Sensor-based doneness detection removes time setting entirely, though steam/VOC sensors exist in some ovens and reliability varies by food.

title: Dial-Free Ambient Hob Ring
new_elements: Turn-ring control halo (A ring around the door turns left or right to change power, lit to show the level.)
rationale: Turning a ring is the same movement people use on a cooker, so it feels obvious.
judge_comment: A turn-ring borrows a familiar cooker gesture and has a concrete lit-ring mechanism, though the ring is more complex to build than a button.

title: Shrink-Wrap Cooking Pouch
new_elements: Self-venting steam pouch (A pre-cut pouch goes straight into the cavity and vents steam through a built-in valve.)
rationale: Food goes in the pouch and nothing else, so cooking involves no cleaning or venting decisions.
judge_comment: The self-venting pouch replaces covers and venting decisions with one concrete mechanism, which is fairly novel and simplifies use, though it needs consumables.

title: One Press Cooks Whatever Is Inside
new_elements: Infrared food-surface scanner (Reads temperature and moisture of the food and sets time and power automatically.); Thermal-image food classification (Low-resolution IR array maps heat and classifies the load.)
rationale: A single START button with automatic settings means the user never has to make a choice at all.
judge_comment: A single button with automatic sensing is ideal for zero learning, but IR surface scanning cannot reliably gauge interior doneness or food type, and it adds cost.

title: Door Turns Colour When Done
new_elements: Thermochromic door window ring (Ring around the window changes colour when the cavity reaches serving temperature.); Thermochromic pigment (Colour-changing ink reacts to heat without power or electronics.)
rationale: A colour change on the window signals completion without any numbers or bells, so the user knows when to stop.
judge_comment: A passive thermochromic ring gives an intuitive done signal with no electronics, but it reflects the cavity rather than the food temperature and the pigment may degrade.

title: Two Buttons Only
new_elements: Warm and Hot buttons (Two large buttons select pre-set duty cycles for reheating and cooking.)
rationale: Reducing five power steps to two clear words removes the choice that causes most confusion.
judge_comment: Two plain-word buttons directly remove choice and learning, and are highly feasible, but the idea is fairly obvious and not wild.

title: Sound of Popping Ends It
new_elements: Acoustic doneness sensor (Microphone hears popcorn popping or sizzling stop and ends cooking.); Audio event detection (Simple sound classifier listens for change in cooking noise.)
rationale: Stopping when the food's natural sound changes requires no judgment, just letting the food speak.
judge_comment: Acoustic end detection is plausible and already exists for popcorn, but it covers only a narrow set of foods.

title: Single Hungry Button
new_elements: VOC gas sensor array (Detects steam and aroma to estimate food state.); Auto-selects heating time and power (Removes manual timer and power setting.)
rationale: One button that cooks by sensing the food removes every setting the user must learn.
judge_comment: One-button sensor cooking directly removes the learning curve, though sensor-cook exists and VOC accuracy is limited.

title: Silhouette Presets
new_elements: Tactile silhouette keypad (Raised icons of mug, bowl and plate.)
rationale: Users pick a picture of their container and the machine handles the rest.
judge_comment: Pictorial tactile presets are easy to build and intuitive, though they are incremental and fairly common.

title: Auto-Eject Door Done Signal
new_elements: Physical done signal (Door cracks open a few millimetres when cooking ends.)
rationale: Opening the door is the notification, so no sound or light needs interpreting.
judge_comment: A door that cracks open is an intuitive, no-learning done signal and easy to build with a latch solenoid, though it addresses only the end of the cycle.

title: Infrared Food Thermometer Stop
new_elements: Infrared thermopile sensor (Reads food surface temperature without contact.)
rationale: The machine stops when food is hot, so overcooking is no longer the user's problem.
judge_comment: An IR sensor that stops cooking automatically removes the need to set times, which directly helps simple operation, though surface-only readings limit accuracy.

title: Dial-Free Single Wheel Control
new_elements: Single detent wheel (One wheel with three labelled positions.)
rationale: Three positions replace many settings, so the control is easy to learn.
judge_comment: A three-position wheel directly cuts complexity and is very feasible, though not very radical.

title: Thermal Camera Auto Mode
new_elements: Thermal imaging array (Maps food temperature across the cavity.)
rationale: The oven sees whether food is hot, so the user needs no judgement.
judge_comment: Thermal sensing enabling automatic cooking removes the need for any input, though cost and accuracy are challenges and it is not cheaper.

title: Preloaded Meal Capsule
new_elements: Meal capsule reader (Reads a pre-sealed meal pack and runs its program.)
rationale: Pressing a sealed meal into the oven is the only step needed to cook it.
judge_comment: Sealed packs that carry their own program make cooking a single insert-and-go step, though capsule-based appliances already exist and it ties users to specific packs.

title: Hourglass Timer Dial
new_elements: Sand-drain hourglass timer (A clear chamber of fine sand drains visibly; when empty, heating stops and a soft thud is heard.)
rationale: Users read remaining time at a glance by watching sand, which needs no numbers, no dial calibration, and no learning.
judge_comment: A visible sand hourglass is intuitive, but it is imprecise and needs a mechanism that cuts heating when the sand empties, which is awkward to build.

title: Tap-to-Start Single Surface
new_elements: Single capacitive tap pad (One flat touch area starts a standard reheat cycle; tapping again adds more time.)
rationale: One tap with a sensible default means the user never needs to set anything at all.
judge_comment: Directly removes all settings with a one-tap default, highly relevant and easy to build, though not very radical and a fixed default may overheat or underheat some foods.

title: NFC Meal Tag Autoprogram
new_elements: NFC food-package tag (A tag on each frozen meal tells the oven the power and time to use.)
rationale: The user taps the packet on the oven and nothing else, so cooking settings never have to be known.
judge_comment: A package tap removes settings entirely, but it depends on food makers adopting tags and fails for untagged foods.

title: Portion Plate Sensor
new_elements: Infrared food-surface camera (A low-cost IR sensor reads the surface temperature and stops at the right point.)
rationale: Stopping when the food is hot, not after a fixed time, means users cannot ruin a meal by guessing.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on surface temperature removes the need to choose time or power, though IR reads only the surface and the idea resembles existing sensor cooking.

title: Magnet Latch Door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch (A strong magnet holds the door shut and releases it with a light push.)
rationale: The door closes with a soft click and opens with a push, with no lever to find or understand.
judge_comment: A magnetic push-open door is simple and intuitive, but magnetic latches are already common, so it is not radical, and it does not address the controls.

title: Stove-Top Inspired Dial Only
new_elements: Single hot-cold dial (One dial runs from cold to hot, with no numbers or timer.)
rationale: People already know a dial that goes from cold to hot, so no instruction is needed.
judge_comment: A single cold-to-hot dial closely matches existing user knowledge and removes the learning curve, though it lacks mechanism detail and is a little imprecise for cooking.

title: Fold-Down Tray Start
new_elements: Closing-tray trigger (Closing the fold-down tray starts cooking, so the act of loading starts it.)
rationale: Closing the tray is the only step, and it is the same as closing any drawer.
judge_comment: Loading and closing the tray as the single start action is very intuitive, though cook time still needs a default or sensing method.

title: Voice Command Only
new_elements: Local voice recognition (The user says 'heat soup' and the oven picks the program.)
rationale: Speaking the food name is simpler than knowing any control or setting.
judge_comment: Speaking the food name removes nearly all controls, and local recognition is feasible, though the voice-control idea is already known.

title: Say-It Cooking
new_elements: Voice microphone (Far-field mic that takes plain requests like 'warm my coffee' and sets time and power automatically.); Interpret natural request (Maps everyday speech to cook duration and power level.)
rationale: Speaking a goal removes the need to learn any dial logic at all.
judge_comment: Voice input removes the need to learn controls, but voice-controlled microwaves already exist and mapping a request to cook settings is imprecise.

title: Scan-and-Go Packaging
new_elements: Package reader (Reads a printed code on ready-meal packaging and loads the cook program.); Printed cook code (Low-cost machine-readable mark printed on food packaging.)
rationale: The packaging does the setting, so the user only places the food and presses start.
judge_comment: Package-coded cook programs are plausible and simple to use, but they only work for coded ready meals and similar scan-to-cook products exist.

title: Weigh-and-Heat Plate
new_elements: Load-sensing plate (Turntable underside weighs the food and sets cook time from mass.); Auto-set duration (Calculates cook time from the measured load.)
rationale: Weight tells the machine how long to cook, so no time has to be guessed or entered.
judge_comment: A weighing turntable that sets time automatically is a clear idea, though mass alone is a weak predictor of cook time and the load cell must work inside a microwave.

title: Steam-Stop Sensor
new_elements: Humidity sensor (Stops when steam from the food drops off, signalling the food is done.)
rationale: Steam is visible and intuitive, so the machine stops on what the user already watches for.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensing auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, yet it does remove the need to set a time.

title: Cook Card Slot
new_elements: Card slot (A slot that accepts a credit-card-sized card; each card is a pre-set meal.)
rationale: Inserting a card is a familiar action that does the setting for the user.
judge_comment: Inserting a card is a familiar action and it replaces the keypad, but it means buying and managing cards, and similar ideas already exist, such as barcode scanning.

title: Cook-Anything Puck
new_elements: Smart puck (A flat puck placed on the food; it sends the food type and time to the machine.)
rationale: The food itself carries its own settings, so the user only places it.
judge_comment: A puck that carries the food settings removes most decisions and nearly eliminates learning, though it needs a communication method and a puck for each food type.

title: Recipe Stripe Labels
new_elements: Colour sticker code (A coloured band on packaging that the door reads to choose the cook.)
rationale: Matching colour stripes is easier than reading any settings at all.
judge_comment: Colour-coded packaging read by the door is simple and workable, but it needs packaging adoption and doesn't cover non-packaged food.

title: Mug-Bottom Sensor
new_elements: Container contact pad (A pad under the cup or bowl that reads its material and fill and starts a matching cook.)
rationale: Putting the mug on the pad is a single natural action with no setup.
judge_comment: Placing a mug on a pad to auto-start a matching cook is very low-effort, though reliably sensing material and fill level is difficult.

title: Paper Cook Card
new_elements: Printed cook card (A paper card with a single printed image and no text; scanning it selects the cook.)
rationale: A printed picture is cheaper than a control panel and needs no learning.
judge_comment: A picture card replacing the control panel is simple, cheap and intuitive, though it requires cards for each food.

title: Shake-To-Heat
new_elements: Motion sensor cup (A cup with a sensor that starts heating when it is picked up and shaken.)
rationale: Shaking to start is a natural action that needs no buttons or instructions.
judge_comment: Shake-to-start is intuitive and truly radical, but a microwave cannot heat a cup while it is being shaken, and the safety logic is unclear.

title: Package-scan cooking
new_elements: Packaging NFC/QR reader window (Reads a tag printed on ready-meal packs and loads the manufacturer's cook program.)
rationale: Tapping the pack means the user never reads a dial or number, which fits directly.
judge_comment: Packaging tag reading is technically easy and reliable, but it only works for tagged ready meals and needs industry adoption.

title: Pictogram dial instead of numbers
new_elements: Three-icon dial (snowflake, plate, flame) (A single dial with three pictograms replaces the five numbered power steps.)
rationale: Icons need no reading or translation, so people who do not read numbers can still use it.
judge_comment: Very cheap and simple and a true substitution of numbers with icons, but incremental rather than radical, and time is still not handled.

title: Tangible preset pucks
new_elements: Shaped preset pucks that dock on top of the unit (Each puck, shaped like a mug, bowl or bread, sets a program when placed on the lid.)
rationale: Placing a physical object that resembles the food is a direct action with no menu to navigate.
judge_comment: Physical shaped pucks make program selection intuitive and menu-free, though they can be lost and cover a limited set of foods.

title: Solid-state phased-array heater
new_elements: Phased-array RF emitters (Several small emitters steer the field to avoid hot and cold spots, with no moving parts.)
rationale: Even heating without stirring or turning means the user never has to rotate or stir food.
judge_comment: Steering the field removes the need to stir or rotate food, which directly lowers user effort, and solid-state RF arrays exist though they are costly.

title: Teach-once learning plate
new_elements: Teach-by-example mode (User heats a food once and the machine stores that time and power for future use.)
rationale: Teaching by doing means the machine learns the user's habits rather than the user learning the machine.
judge_comment: Teaching by example directly removes the need to learn settings, though memory-preset features exist in some form.

title: Whole-front touch skin
new_elements: Capacitive touch skin with tactile dots (Smooth front panel with raised dots and a few large zones; every zone does one clear thing.)
rationale: Large tactile zones that each do one thing are easy to find by touch with no reading.
judge_comment: A tactile single-function zone panel is simple to use and plausible, but fairly incremental and still a control panel.

title: Aroma-Sensed Stop
new_elements: Volatile-organic gas sensor (Detects the rise in food aroma and ends heating when the food is ready.)
rationale: The machine judges doneness itself, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: A VOC sensor to detect doneness replaces time guessing and is feasible, though similar humidity sensors already exist and accuracy varies by food.

title: Printed-Preset Lid
new_elements: Four-preset printed fascia (Four large printed buttons: Reheat, Defrost, Drink, Popcorn. Each runs a fixed cycle.)
rationale: Four named buttons cover most tasks, which makes the machine simpler to operate than a timer and power pair.
judge_comment: Four labeled preset buttons are highly usable and cheap, but this is a common approach and not radical.

title: Cook-Pod Cavity
new_elements: Disposable pre-scanned cook pod (Food comes in a pre-scanned cardboard pod that is the cook chamber; the cavity is a shielded slot.)
rationale: Users insert a ready-made pod, so the machine's settings and the cooking method are already decided.
judge_comment: A pre-scanned pod removes all decisions and is a radical substitution, but it needs shielded disposable packaging and a food ecosystem.

title: Glowing Puck Control
new_elements: Dial-puck knob (A chunky, glowing puck is turned to set time and pressed to start.)
rationale: One chunky, glowing object does the job of several small controls, so there is only one thing to learn.
judge_comment: A single dial-and-press puck replaces a keypad and is easy to learn, though it is similar to existing dial microwaves and only moderately radical.

title: Voice-Only Cooking
new_elements: On-device keyword speech recognition (Recognises a few phrases like reheat, soup, or two minutes without internet.); Far-field microphone array (Hears spoken commands from anywhere in the kitchen.); Accepts spoken cooking commands (Converts plain speech into a cooking program.)
rationale: Speaking a request needs no reading, no dial mapping, and no memory of settings, which removes the learning curve.
judge_comment: Voice commands remove the need to learn controls, though they bring misrecognition and kitchen-noise issues and are a fairly common concept; the substitution of controls with speech is clear.

title: Single Smart Button With Steam Sensing
new_elements: Humidity and VOC gas sensor (Detects steam and aroma rise to judge when food is ready.); Gas-sensor doneness classification (Maps humidity curve shape to a stop decision.); Stops cooking when food is ready (Ends the cycle automatically without a timer.)
rationale: Users press one button and the oven decides when to stop, so no time or power setting needs to be understood.
judge_comment: One button with automatic stop is very simple to use, but humidity sensing is an existing feature and accuracy across foods is hard.

title: Wrap-Pack NFC Cooking
new_elements: Passive NFC tag in food packaging (Tag stores the manufacturer cook program and needs no battery.); NFC reader pad on the top panel (Reads the package by simply placing it on the oven.)
rationale: Tapping the meal pack sets the whole program, so the user never selects a time or power level.
judge_comment: Tapping the package to set the program is effortless, but it depends on food makers adopting the tags, and it only works for packaged food.

title: Weigh-And-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (Measures food mass and rough placement on the glass plate.); Auto-calculates time and power from mass (Uses mass and food category to set the duty cycle.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate is the only action, so no settings need to be known in advance.
judge_comment: Placing food on the plate as the only action is very simple, but mass alone cannot reliably identify food type, so the program may be wrong.

title: Squeeze-To-Add-Time
new_elements: Squeezable soft-touch side grip (Each squeeze adds 30 seconds to the timer.); Force-sensitive resistor array (Detects squeezing pressure with no moving parts.)
rationale: Squeezing is a natural, unlabelled gesture, so it removes the need to learn a dial.
judge_comment: The gesture is intuitive and cheap to build, but it gives no feedback and the 30-second increments are not obvious without learning.

title: Door-Close-To-Cook
new_elements: Magnetic reed door sensor (Detects when the door closes fully.); Starts last-used program on door close (Closing the door begins the saved default cook.)
rationale: Closing the door is already a natural action, so cooking begins with no extra button.
judge_comment: Very simple and feasible with a reed switch, but auto-starting on close risks unsafe or unintended heating and is not very radical.

title: Single Cook Card Slot
new_elements: Credit-card-style program card slot (Insert a card with a printed meal picture to start a program.); Printed magnetic stripe program card (Stripe encodes the cook recipe.)
rationale: Inserting a picture card is a simple tactile action that replaces knowing any setting.
judge_comment: Picture cards make starting a cook a zero-learning action, though they need a card ecosystem and magnetic stripes are outdated.

title: Food-Shaped Puck Settings
new_elements: Shaped cook puck with contact pins (Puck shaped like pizza, rice, or potato sits in a socket to set the program.)
rationale: Choosing a physical shape you can see replaces picking an abstract power level.
judge_comment: Food-shaped pucks give a very intuitive, radical way to set programs, but the puck supply and the range of foods they cover are practical limits.

title: Snap-On Control Cartridge
new_elements: Plug-in control cartridge (A single cartridge sets the program for one food type and is swapped out as a unit.)
rationale: Removing the whole settings panel and replacing it with one cartridge means the user has one thing to do.
judge_comment: Swapping a cartridge for a control panel is a real simplification that substitutes a part, though it needs a cartridge for each food and is awkward in use.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable platter (Strain-gauge platter reads food weight and sets cook time automatically); Infers cook time from food mass (Replaces manual minute-setting with a single Start press)
rationale: The user places food on the plate and presses one button, so no time has to be guessed or set.
judge_comment: Load-cell platter is plausible and removes time-setting, though weight is a weak proxy for cook time across food types and it's not much cheaper.

title: Package-Reads-Itself RFID Ring
new_elements: Passive RFID tag printed on food packaging (Tag stores cook time and power for the product, read by a cavity antenna)
rationale: Setting the correct time and power becomes unnecessary because the packaging carries its own instructions.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking is highly relevant, but it needs packaging adoption and RFID inside a metal cavity is problematic.

title: Heat-Until-Ready Sensor Eye
new_elements: Infrared thermopile food sensor (Non-contact sensor reads surface temperature and stops when food reaches serving heat)
rationale: The appliance decides when food is done, so the user only has to choose Heat and walk away.
judge_comment: IR sensing to auto-stop is feasible and truly simplifies, though surface-only temperature readings can be inaccurate.

title: Embossed Food Knob
new_elements: Tactile food-icon dial (Molded dial with raised icons for soup, drink and reheat that can be felt in the dark)
rationale: Raised shapes can be found by touch, so visually impaired users can operate it without sight.
judge_comment: A tactile dial with raised food icons is intuitive and accessible, and it is cheap to mold, so it replaces complex keypads well.

title: Freeze-Aware Auto Defrost
new_elements: Weight-based auto defrost (Load cell reads frozen mass and runs a defrost program with no setting)
rationale: The user puts frozen food in and presses one button, so defrosting needs no knowledge of times or power levels.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto defrost with one button directly removes the need to know times or power levels, though it is an established concept.

title: Food Picture Drum
new_elements: Rotating picture drum (A single dial showing pictures of rice, soup, popcorn and leftovers; each picture sets time and power together.); Selects food preset (Chooses duration and power in one turn by recognising the food shown.)
rationale: Replacing two numeric dials with one picture drum removes the need to know times or power levels, so anyone can cook without instruction.
judge_comment: A picture dial is simple and effective, though similar to existing preset-based microwaves and not radical.

title: Heat-Until-Done Button
new_elements: Steam-humidity sensing (A humidity sensor in the vent detects when food releases steam and stops heating automatically.)
rationale: One button that starts cooking and stops it when food is ready means the user never needs to guess a time.
judge_comment: One-button operation with automatic stop is the ideal no-learning-curve solution, and humidity sensors already exist in sensor-cook models, though accuracy varies by food.

title: Hanging Hook Timer
new_elements: Pegboard timer pins (The user pushes a pin into a row of holes; the pin count sets the minutes.)
rationale: Pushing a pin into a visible hole is a direct and tactile act that needs no reading.
judge_comment: A tactile pegboard timer substitutes the keypad with a visible, no-reading input, though pin counting is clumsy for longer or fine-grained times and needs a reliable pin-detection method.

title: Sealed Container Cooking
new_elements: Sealed cooking jar (A sealed jar with a built-in heat setting that the microwave reads from its base.)
rationale: The container handles power and time, so the microwave needs no user input.
judge_comment: A container that carries its own cooking program removes user input entirely, which is a strong substitution, though it needs a reader and a proprietary jar.

title: Cook-Time Strip Calendar
new_elements: Pictogram time strip (A strip with pictures of food and a time line; the user slides a marker to the picture.)
rationale: Sliding a marker to a picture is intuitive and needs no understanding of units.
judge_comment: A pictogram slider replaces numeric time entry in an intuitive way and is easy to build, though not radical.

title: Snap-and-Cook Camera
new_elements: Food-recognition camera (Small camera in the roof identifies the food and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: The user places food inside and presses one button, so no settings need to be learned.
judge_comment: Camera-based food recognition with one-button start nearly eliminates learning, though recognition accuracy and cost are concerns and the substitution is not cheaper.

title: Plate NFC Auto-Cook
new_elements: NFC tag on food packaging (Ready-meal packs carry a tag that tells the oven the exact cook profile.)
rationale: Tapping the pack to the oven replaces all manual settings, so there is nothing to figure out.
judge_comment: NFC tapping removes settings for packaged meals, but it needs packaging adoption and doesn't cover non-packaged food.

title: Single Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Four-icon food dial (One dial with icons for drink, leftovers, frozen meal, and popcorn.)
rationale: Choosing a picture is more intuitive than reading numbers or power levels.
judge_comment: A four-icon dial is cheap, intuitive and very feasible, but it is incremental and far from radical.

title: Dial-Free Touch Surface
new_elements: Single-option touch panel (Only one choice is shown at a time, with a large Next arrow.)
rationale: Showing one choice at a time removes overload for new users.
judge_comment: One-choice-at-a-time guided flow lowers cognitive load and is easy to build, but it may slow experienced users and is not very radical.

title: Colour-Coded Tray Cook
new_elements: Colour-ring tray (Each tray colour maps to a fixed cook program.)
rationale: Matching colours is easier than reading settings, and children can do it too.
judge_comment: Colour-ring trays that map to fixed programs replace settings with matching, which is simple and feasible with RFID or a color sensor, though it limits flexibility.

title: Sound-Cooked Oven
new_elements: Acoustic doneness sensor (Listens to food sounds such as popping or bubbling to decide when to stop.)
rationale: The oven decides when food is done, so the user never needs to check it.
judge_comment: An acoustic doneness sensor removes the need to set time and power at all, which serves the need strongly, though sound-based detection is unreliable for many foods.

title: Ask-the-Food Scanner
new_elements: Barcode scanner (Scans a food barcode on any packet to load its cook program.)
rationale: Scanning the packet uses a familiar supermarket gesture to set everything.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning to load a cook program is concrete and feasible, although it depends on a database and is not very radical.

title: Stove-Style Knob Ring
new_elements: Single ring selector (One ring dial shaped like a stove knob with a clear Off and On.)
rationale: People already know how to use a stove knob, so the oven needs no new skill.
judge_comment: A familiar stove-style knob is highly feasible and intuitive, but it is close to existing mechanical-dial microwaves.

title: Door-Close Start
new_elements: Magnetic reed sensing of door closure (A magnet in the door and a reed switch in the frame detect closing and start cooking automatically.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed, so there is nothing to learn and no start button to find.
judge_comment: Very simple and feasible, but it removes only the start button and still leaves the time to be set (a default would be needed); closing the door is also a bit of a safety concern.

title: Weighing Plinth
new_elements: Load-cell turntable plinth (A load cell under the glass plate reads food mass and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: The user places the food and the machine sets everything else, so no settings are needed.
judge_comment: Removes all settings by sensing mass, which fits the need well, though mass alone does not give the right time for different foods, and a load cell in a microwave is tricky.

title: Hold-to-Cook Ring
new_elements: Dead-man hold-to-run control (Cooking runs only while the user holds the ring, and releasing it pauses at once.)
rationale: Holding a control and seeing the food respond makes cause and effect obvious.
judge_comment: Hold-to-run makes cause and effect obvious and is quite radical, but it is tiring for long cooking times and the time control is unclear.

title: Three-Icon Power
new_elements: Three-pictogram power selector (Three large icons (gentle, normal, hot) replace the five numbered steps.)
rationale: Three pictures are simpler to choose between than five numbers.
judge_comment: Pictogram power selection is easily built and cuts choices, but it is an incremental change and hardly radical.

title: Door Pull Release
new_elements: Spring-loaded pull handle (A pull handle that opens the door directly, releasing the latch mechanically with no separate button.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is the most natural action a person can take, so no button needs to be found.
judge_comment: A pull handle that opens the door directly is intuitive and already common, and it replaces the button with a simpler part, which fits the substitute operator.

title: Humidity Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity-based doneness sensing (A humidity sensor in the vent stops cooking when steam levels show the food is hot.)
rationale: The machine stops when the food is done, so the user does not have to guess a time.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is practical and effective but not very radical.

title: Auto-Weigh Platter
new_elements: Weight-sensing platter (Load cell under the turntable reads food mass and sets time and power automatically.); Auto-select cooking program (Chooses time and power from the weight reading with no user input.)
rationale: The user places food and presses nothing, so there is no setting to learn.
judge_comment: A load cell is a simple, cheap substitute for the keypad and gives zero-input operation, though weight alone is a poor proxy for the right cooking program.

title: Tactile Bump Dial
new_elements: Raised-bump dial (A dial with one bump per setting so it can be used by feel alone.); Set by feel (Settings are chosen by touch, without looking.)
rationale: Touch works for everyone, including people in low light or with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: A simple, practical tactile dial that helps usability, though not radical and similar to existing dials.

title: Sunrise Clock Face
new_elements: Sun-arc timer (A curved arc of light that moves across the door as the food cooks.); Show time as an arc (The remaining time is shown as light moving along an arc.)
rationale: A moving arc is understood at a glance without reading minutes.
judge_comment: An intuitive at-a-glance time display that is easy to build with LEDs, though it is only a modest departure from existing progress bars.

title: Probe-Start Cook
new_elements: Insertion probe (A probe inserted into the food starts and stops cooking by its own reading.); Cook by probe (The probe decides when to heat and when to stop.)
rationale: Pushing a probe in is a clear physical action that sets everything up.
judge_comment: Probe-driven start and stop gives a clear one-action setup and is technically proven, though it needs a probe and cleaning.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto-Cook Plate
new_elements: Load-cell food plate (Turntable sits on a load cell that reads food mass and starts the cycle automatically.); Load-cell lookup-table cooking (Mass maps to a built-in time and power table, so no user settings are needed.)
rationale: The user places food and presses start, so there is nothing to set, read, or learn.
judge_comment: Load-cell weight sensing with automatic start is plausible and removes settings, though mass alone can't identify food type or the right power level.

title: Voice Command Without an App
new_elements: Offline wake-word chip (An onboard chip responds to a few spoken phrases such as 'warm soup' with no phone or app.); Embedded keyword spotting (A low-cost on-device speech model recognises a small fixed vocabulary.)
rationale: Speaking a natural phrase needs no manual, and it suits elderly users whose hands are unsteady.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is feasible and accessible, though users must discover the phrases and noisy kitchens can cause errors.

title: Popcorn-Style Acoustic Stop
new_elements: Acoustic sensor (A microphone listens for the crackle of popping or boiling and ends the cycle at the right moment.)
rationale: Listening for the food's own signal removes timing guesswork for anyone.
judge_comment: Microphone-based auto-stop removes timing decisions and is plausible, though it only suits popcorn or boiling foods and the sound-detection signal is unreliable for others.

title: Single Rotary Food-Colour Dial
new_elements: Colour-ring rotary dial (One dial with coloured zones: red for meat, green for vegetables, blue for drinks.)
rationale: Matching colours to food types replaces two dials with one intuitive choice.
judge_comment: Color-coded single dial is intuitive and simple to build, but categories are coarse and it still requires some food-type decision.

title: Self-Heating Meal Pod
new_elements: Sealed heating pod (A pre-packed meal contains its own heating element, triggered by one press.)
rationale: The meal carries its own heating, so the user does nothing but press once.
judge_comment: Self-heating packs already exist and a single press is as simple as it gets, though the idea replaces the microwave instead of improving it.

title: Tactile Braille-Style Dial
new_elements: Raised-bump dial (Dial positions are marked with raised bumps so they can be felt without looking.)
rationale: Users can set the dial by touch alone, which suits people with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: Tactile dial markings are simple, cheap and usable, but they are an incremental, well-known accessibility feature.

title: Ready-Meal Scan Cooking
new_elements: Camera food recogniser (A camera identifies the food on the plate and sets the cycle automatically.); On-device image classification (A small vision model classifies common foods without a network.)
rationale: Pointing at food is all that is needed, so the user never has to choose a setting.
judge_comment: A camera that recognises food and sets the cycle removes setting choice entirely, though it is already seen in some premium ovens and may misidentify foods.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: Spring-assisted door ajar (A spring nudges the door a few millimetres ajar at the end of cooking.)
rationale: The door itself signals completion, which needs no sound and no reading.
judge_comment: The door-ajar cue is intuitive and needs no reading or sound, but it only signals completion and may let heat escape.

title: Weigh-and-Go Plate
new_elements: Load-cell cooking plate (Strain-gauge plate under the turntable that reads the mass of food.); Auto-sets power and time from mass (Mass plus a food-type icon selects the entire program.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate is the only setting the user ever makes.
judge_comment: A load cell plus a food icon makes operation nearly one-step and is technically easy, but it is a known approach and the icon still has to be chosen.

title: Auto-Start on Door Close
new_elements: Door-close trigger (Reed switch that starts the last-used program when the door shuts.); Starts cooking on closing (Closing the door begins cooking with no start button.)
rationale: Closing the door is the same gesture as starting, so there is nothing new to learn.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive and easy to build with a reed switch, though accidental starts and empty-cavity runs are safety concerns.

title: Shape-Recognising Auto Program
new_elements: Overhead depth camera (Camera in the roof that identifies the food and its shape.); Picks the program from the image (Recognises the food and sets the correct power and time.)
rationale: The machine sees the food and needs no instructions from the user.
judge_comment: Camera-based food recognition removes all input and directly serves zero-learning-curve use, though reliable recognition and heating accuracy are challenging.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door Panel
new_elements: Pressure-sensing door skin (Full-face pressure sensor that opens the door when pressed anywhere.); Opens on any push (Pushing anywhere on the door releases the latch.)
rationale: There is no small button to hunt for, so opening the door is effortless.
judge_comment: Pressing anywhere on the door to open it is intuitive and needs no learning, and it replaces the button with a simpler mechanism, though accidental opening is a risk.

title: Glowing Ring Status
new_elements: LED status ring (Ring around the door that glows green, pulses, and then turns off.); Shows state by colour (One ring conveys ready, cooking, and done.)
rationale: One glowing ring replaces the lamp and every other indicator.
judge_comment: A single LED ring is cheap, simple, and clearly serves no-learning-curve operation, though it is not very radical.

title: Cook-by-Sticker
new_elements: Printed heat sticker (Sticker on food packaging that carries power and time as a code.); Reads packaging to cook (The oven reads the sticker and sets everything.)
rationale: The packaging sets the oven, so the user never needs to know what to set.
judge_comment: Packaging-encoded cooking removes all settings and is plausible via printed codes, though it needs packaging adoption and the 'heat sticker' is vague.

title: Single big button
new_elements: One-touch cook button (A single large button that starts a sensed default cook cycle.)
rationale: One press with one meaning removes every setting the user would otherwise need to learn.
judge_comment: One button is the simplest possible interface, but a default cycle may cook poorly, and the 'sensed' part is vague.

title: Weight-sensing auto-cook
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (The glass turntable weighs the food and sets duration automatically.)
rationale: Heavier food gets longer heating without the user needing to know any numbers.
judge_comment: A load cell is a concrete, plausible sensor, but weight alone does not determine the right time or power, so it only partly removes the need for user knowledge.

title: Smartphone-free QR pairing
new_elements: Printed QR recipe card (Scanning a card with the built-in camera loads the cooking program.)
rationale: Cooking instructions arrive as a single scan, with no settings to recall.
judge_comment: A built-in camera scanning printed cards is novel and concrete, but it adds a step and needs cards, so it isn't truly zero-learning.

title: Scent-based done signal
new_elements: Gas sensor (Detects the smell of toasting or browning and stops heating.)
rationale: Cooking stops at the right moment without any time input from the user.
judge_comment: Gas-sensing doneness removes time input entirely, which strongly serves the need, though reliability across foods is uncertain and the idea is not a clear substitution for a part.

title: Recipe-by-photo
new_elements: Food recognition camera (Placing food inside lets the oven identify it and set everything.)
rationale: The oven identifies the food itself, so the user does not have to name it.
judge_comment: Camera food recognition removes nearly all inputs and fits zero learning curve, though it needs robust recognition and similar products already exist.

title: Two-stage mini oven
new_elements: Start-or-stop lever (A lever with two positions that cooks on push and stops on pull.)
rationale: A lever with two obvious positions is more intuitive than any dial.
judge_comment: A start/stop lever is simple and cheap and clearly substitutes for the keypad, but it is not radical and offers little control over cooking.

title: Fridge-to-oven pod
new_elements: Self-timing pod (A pod with a built-in timer heats and signals when complete.)
rationale: The package carries the whole cook, so the oven needs only a place to sit.
judge_comment: A pod that carries its own cook instructions and timer substitutes the control panel and strongly cuts the learning curve, though a self-timing pod with heating and signaling is vague on mechanism.

title: Food-Scan Auto-Cook
new_elements: Barcode/QR food reader (Reads the package code and loads time and power automatically.); Auto-set cook program (Sets duration and power without any user input.)
rationale: The user scans the food and presses start, so no timer or power settings need to be learned.
judge_comment: Scan-and-start removes the need to learn timers and power levels, though it depends on a code database and not all foods carry usable codes.

title: Single Big Start Button
new_elements: Sensor-driven start pad (One large pad that starts a default cook when touched.)
rationale: One obvious action replaces a set of dials that every user must interpret.
judge_comment: A single start pad is very simple and easy to build, but it's an obvious idea and a default cook doesn't suit every food.

title: Sealed Single-Function Oven
new_elements: Single-purpose reheat (One fixed cycle that handles reheating only.)
rationale: Removing all choice removes all learning.
judge_comment: A single fixed reheat cycle eliminates learning, but it is a subtraction rather than a substitution and is not very radical.

title: Door Is the Only Switch
new_elements: Close door to start (Closing the door starts the default cook.)
rationale: Closing a door is an action everyone already performs.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive and replaces the start button, though accidental starts and empty runs are safety concerns.

title: Cook Bowl That Opens the Machine
new_elements: Tagged container (Container placed in the cavity triggers the door to open for loading.)
rationale: Loading the food is the trigger, so nothing else needs to be pressed.
judge_comment: Container-triggered door opening is a creative way to remove steps, though it needs tagged containers and says little about how cook settings are chosen.

title: Turntable Plate as Menu
new_elements: Picture menu plate (Plate has printed food pictures that tell the machine what to do when placed.)
rationale: Pictures are universally understood, so no learning is needed.
judge_comment: A printed plate that signals the cook program is intuitive and substitutes buttons, though the plate-to-machine recognition mechanism is vague and the plate limits flexibility.

title: Microwave Shouts Instructions
new_elements: Step-by-step voice guide (Device speaks each action needed, one at a time.)
rationale: Guidance is given in the moment, so no manual needs to be learned.
judge_comment: Voice guidance is very feasible and reduces learning, but it is a fairly common idea and does not substitute a part in a radical way.

title: Radio Button Cook
new_elements: Three-option radio (Only three choices exist: hot, warm, reheat.)
rationale: Three words are instantly understood and cannot be wrongly combined.
judge_comment: Three clear options minimize the learning curve and are very buildable, though not radical.

title: Kitchen Counter Is the Microwave
new_elements: Induction-style counter cavity (Heating zone is built into the counter surface and activated by placing food.)
rationale: There is no separate machine to learn; the counter itself responds to food.
judge_comment: A counter that heats food on placement is radical and removes the interface, but microwave energy and safety make it hard to realize.

title: Weigh-and-Go Tray
new_elements: Load-cell weight sensing (Strain gauge under the turntable estimates food mass and sets time automatically.)
rationale: Placing food on the tray is the only action needed, so no timer dial has to be learned.
judge_comment: Load-cell auto-timing is plausible and truly one-step, but weight alone poorly predicts the needed cook time and food type.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Gravity sand-flow timer (Fixed-size hourglass chamber; flipping it starts heating and the sand running out ends it.)
rationale: A visible hourglass needs no reading, and flipping it is a physical action that every user already understands.
judge_comment: A flip-to-start hourglass is whimsical and understandable, but a fixed duration can't suit varied foods and linking sand flow to the heater is awkward.

title: Pictogram Power Ladder
new_elements: Pictogram power strip (Five illustrated flame icons, each with a matching light that shows the chosen heat.)
rationale: Flames that get bigger show intensity with no words, which suits older users who avoid written labels.
judge_comment: Flame icons make power levels easier to read but still leave the user to choose settings, and the idea is incremental rather than radical.

title: Magnetic Glide Door
new_elements: Magnetic touch latch (A magnetic catch releases when the door is pulled firmly, with no button.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is the same action people use for any fridge, so no release button needs to be found.
judge_comment: A pull-to-open magnetic door is intuitive and easy to build, but it only affects opening the door and is not a radical change.

title: Bell-to-Buzz Haptic
new_elements: Haptic end-of-cook pad (A vibrating pad under the handle gives a felt pulse when cooking ends, with no bell.)
rationale: A felt pulse is noticed by users with hearing loss and is unmistakable in a noisy kitchen.
judge_comment: A haptic pulse aids accessibility and is feasible, but it does little to remove the learning curve of operating the oven.

title: Spoken Pictogram Cue
new_elements: Single-word voice prompts (A small speaker says Ready or Done in plain words, with no menus or voice commands.)
rationale: Speaking the state aloud is simpler than reading a display, and an older user can hear it from another room.
judge_comment: Spoken state words are easy to understand and cheap to build, though talking appliances are common and the idea does not substitute out a complex part.

title: Pre-Heat Pizza Button
new_elements: One-touch food-type heat (A large button per food type runs a tuned heat profile with no adjustment.)
rationale: A big button per food is the simplest possible way to choose, with nothing to adjust.
judge_comment: One-touch food buttons already exist on many microwaves, so they are very easy to use but not radical.

title: Zero-Button Shell
new_elements: Gesture-free oven (The oven starts from closing the door and stops when opened, with no buttons at all.)
rationale: Starting by closing the door and stopping by opening it removes every control the user must learn.
judge_comment: Starting on door close directly removes all learning, but there is no way to set time or power, and accidental starts (or running empty) are a safety risk.

title: Knobless Heat Plate
new_elements: Heat-zone touch plate (A single touch plate with pictures sets the whole oven state without any knobs.)
rationale: One picture-led plate replaces several controls, so there is only one place to look.
judge_comment: A single picture-based touch plate replacing the controls directly reduces the learning curve and is feasible, though the 'heat-zone' idea is vague.

title: Radar Metal Warning
new_elements: mmWave radar sensor (Millimetre-wave radar inside the cavity that detects metal.); Warns before arcing (Stops the cycle and shows a plain icon when metal is detected.)
rationale: The machine catches metal mistakes itself, so the user never has to remember a rule.
judge_comment: Automatic metal detection removes a rule users must remember, but radar inside a microwave cavity is technically difficult and unreliable.

title: Solid-State RF Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Gallium nitride amplifier that replaces the magnetron.); GaN power electronics (Semiconductor switching at microwave frequency.)
rationale: No magnetron means no warm-up, no high-voltage diode and instant start for the user.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a genuinely radical substitution that enables instant start and finer control, though its link to simple operation is indirect and cost is high.

title: Phased Array Stirring
new_elements: Phased RF emitter array (Several emitters that move the hot spots without any moving part.); Heats evenly without rotation (Removes the need to rotate food by hand or with a turntable.)
rationale: Users never need to think about turning food, because the field moves for them.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF arrays remove the need to turn food and cleanly substitute the turntable, directly reducing user effort.

title: Ambient Cook Lighting Mood
new_elements: Shows cooking state through colour (Changes the cavity glow from blue to green to amber as cooking progresses.)
rationale: The colour sequence tells the user the state at a glance, with no numbers to read.
judge_comment: Color-coded cooking state is understandable at a glance and replaces numeric display, though it mainly aids status rather than input.

title: Weigh-and-Go Plate
new_elements: Load-cell pressure plate (Starts a default cycle when a mug or plate is placed on it.)
rationale: Placing the food on the plate is the only action needed to start cooking.
judge_comment: Placing food to start is simple and feasible, but it risks unsafe or inappropriate default cooking (e.g., empty or metal items, varied foods).

title: Scan-the-Packet
new_elements: Packaging code reader (Reads the barcode or QR code on the food pack and loads its cooking program.)
rationale: The packet already contains the instructions, so the user only waves it at the oven.
judge_comment: Barcode-driven programs are plausible and already exist in some products, but they work only for packaged food and are not very radical.

title: Sound-Based Doneness
new_elements: Acoustic popping detection (Listens for the sound of popping or bubbling to judge when food is ready.)
rationale: The oven stops when the food is ready, so no one has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Acoustic doneness detection removes timing guesswork and is fairly novel, but it only works for foods that pop or bubble and microwave noise complicates sensing.

title: Door-Close Starts Cooking
new_elements: Auto-start on door close (Closing the door starts a default cycle.)
rationale: Closing the door is already a natural habit, so cooking starts without any extra step.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes steps and uses a natural habit, but accidental starts with no food or the wrong item are a safety risk.

title: Mug-Lid Microwave
new_elements: Mug-top heating lid (A lid that sits on a mug and heats only that drink.)
rationale: A single mug lid suits a student and needs no door, tray, or settings.
judge_comment: A heating lid is a radical simplification for one use case, and it removes the door, tray and settings, though heating only the drink raises power and safety questions.

title: Colour-zone time slider
new_elements: Colour-zone slider (Slider with green, amber and red zones for short, medium and long cooks.)
rationale: Colour zones replace precise numbers with obvious categories that work for any user.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and build, but it is a modest rethink of a time dial and the coarse zones may lack precision.

title: Infrared auto-stop on food temperature
new_elements: Infrared surface sensor (Stops heating when the food reaches a set warmth.); Infrared thermal sensing (Non-contact sensing of surface temperature.)
rationale: Stopping when food is warm means users never have to guess a time at all.
judge_comment: Auto-stop by food temperature removes guessing, but surface-only IR readings are unreliable and the idea is not very novel.

title: Gentle-to-strong slider
new_elements: Gentle-strong slider (One slider runs from Gentle to Strong with no numbers.)
