rationale: A simple direction-based control maps to intuition about heat without any scale to learn.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and simple to build, but it is a modest, fairly obvious replacement for the numeric power level.

title: How-hot thermostat icon dial
new_elements: Warmth icon dial (Dial shows a sun for warm to a flame for hot, mapping to duty cycle internally.)
rationale: Icons of warmth map to the intent of the user rather than the hidden technology.
judge_comment: The icons are intuitive and easy to build, but this is close to the slider idea and only a small change from existing controls.

title: Single hold-to-cook button
new_elements: Hold-to-cook button (Hold the button to cook and release to stop.)
rationale: A single intuitive gesture of holding to run and releasing to stop needs no instruction.
judge_comment: A hold-to-run button is intuitive and inherently safe, but holding it through a multi-minute cook is tiresome and gives no way to set time or power.

title: Picture-only control panel
new_elements: Pictogram control panel (All controls use large pictures with no text or numbers.)
rationale: Pictures need no reading or language, which suits older users and anyone new to the product.
judge_comment: Pictogram-only controls are easy to build and cut reading needs, but they are a familiar approach and not radical.

title: Package barcode auto-setup
new_elements: Package code reader (Scans a code printed on the food pack to set time and power.)
rationale: Scanning the food pack means the user does no setting at all.
judge_comment: Scanning the pack code removes all settings and is concrete, but it depends on a standard code and a camera or reader, and some packs carry no suitable code.

title: Radiant door-face guidance
new_elements: Raised door-face icon (Raised tactile icons on the door guide hand placement for opening and closing.)
rationale: Raised touch cues let users with low vision operate the door without reading any labels.
judge_comment: Raised tactile door icons are simple and help low-vision users, but they only cover door handling and do not address the learning curve of cooking settings.

title: Icon Tray Mats
new_elements: Picture mat (Printed mats with pictures of soup, pizza, or rice, placed under the dish.); Picture-based selection (Chooses the program by reading the picture under the dish.)
rationale: Recognising a picture needs no reading or learning.
judge_comment: Picture mats give an intuitive, no-reading selection, but the sensing method is vague and mats add an extra item to manage.

title: Hover-to-Adjust
new_elements: Hand-hover sensor (Infrared sensor above the door that reads a hand hovering up or down.); Gesture time adjust (Adds or removes time as the hand rises or drops.)
rationale: Raising a hand is a natural gesture, so no numbers or buttons need to be memorised.
judge_comment: Hover gesture is intuitive and novel for time setting, though IR precision and a lack of confirmation feedback could cause confusion.

title: Gentle Fast Slider
new_elements: Three-word slider (Slider labelled Gentle, Normal, and Fast with no numbers.); Plain-word power choice (Chooses heat using everyday words.)
rationale: Three words replace five numbers, which is far easier to understand.
judge_comment: Plain-word power choice cuts the learning needed, but it is a modest, fairly common simplification and not radical.

title: Tactile Three-Bump Dial
new_elements: Bump-stop dial (Dial with three clearly felt detents that can be used without looking.); Eyes-free setting (Sets power by feel alone.)
rationale: Three distinct bumps can be felt in the dark, so there are few choices to make.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible tactile dial, but detents are an incremental tweak rather than a radical substitution, and three power levels limit control.

title: Food-Scanning Camera Lid
new_elements: Food recognition camera (Camera that identifies the food on the plate and selects the cycle.); Visual food identification (Recognises the food and chooses the settings itself.)
rationale: The machine identifies the food, so the user never has to name a setting.
judge_comment: Camera recognition removes the need to choose a setting and fits the need strongly, but it is not cheaper or simpler, and accuracy and cost are concerns.

title: Autocomplete Heating Recipe
new_elements: Smart food sensor (Sensor that detects the mass and temperature of food and fills in the programme.); Predictive programme (Suggests the full cycle from sensor readings alone.)
rationale: The machine works out the whole cycle, so the user only needs to start it.
judge_comment: Sensing mass and temperature to auto-fill the cycle removes nearly all operation, though accurate sensing inside a microwave is hard and it isn't really a cheaper substitution.

title: Door Opens Itself at Done
new_elements: Spring-assisted door pop (At cycle end a spring lifts the door a few centimetres and the cavity light flashes.)
rationale: The door itself announces that the food is ready, so the user needs no sound or display to understand it.
judge_comment: The door pop is an intuitive and cheap done signal, but it covers only the end-of-cycle cue and not operation setup.

title: Ambient Interface on Food Photo
new_elements: Food-photo picker lid (The user taps a photograph of the food; the lid shows picture icons for each food type.)
rationale: Choosing by picture matches how people think about food and needs no reading.
judge_comment: Picking food by picture is very intuitive and removes reading, though the lid display and the mapping to cooking settings are only loosely described.

title: Child-Safe Tap Only
new_elements: Parent-tap lock (The oven starts only when an adult taps a wearable tag, so children cannot operate it.)
rationale: The family's safety needs are met without any locking menu to set up.
judge_comment: A wearable tag that acts as the child lock is feasible and removes menu setup, but it adds a step for adults and serves a narrow need.

title: Glove-Friendly Big Button
new_elements: Oversized glove-friendly button (A large, raised button can be pressed with an elbow or a gloved hand.)
rationale: A big, obvious control is used correctly on the first try by anyone.
judge_comment: A single large button is simple and accessible, but it is not radical and leaves open how cook time gets chosen.

title: Nano-Mesh Transparent Door
new_elements: Sub-wavelength nano-mesh film (Transparent conductive nano-pattern that blocks 2.45 GHz and passes visible light.); Clear microwave-tight door pane (Full-glass door with a nano-mesh film instead of perforated metal.)
rationale: A clear door lets anyone see the food at a glance, with no hunting for a window or a light.
judge_comment: A clear door helps users see the food, but it only marginally reduces the learning curve, and transparent mesh shielding is plausible yet hard to make.

title: Susceptor Crisp Plate
new_elements: Microwave susceptor plate (Metal-oxide coating heats up in the field and browns food from below.); Browning plate (Flat plate that replaces the glass turntable.)
rationale: One simple plate gives browning with no separate grill or setting to choose.
judge_comment: A susceptor plate gives browning with no extra settings, which modestly simplifies operation, and it is realistic since susceptors already exist.

title: Token-Magnet Power Setting
new_elements: Food-type magnet token (Magnetic tile placed on the door sets power and time, replacing the knob.)
rationale: Sticking a tile to the door is a physical act that cannot be done wrongly.
judge_comment: A magnetic tile on the door that sets power and time is intuitive and replaces the knob, though the tile-to-setting sensing and its interaction with door shielding and magnets are unclear.

title: Knock-to-Start
new_elements: Vibration knock detector (Accelerometer in the door reads a light tap as the start command.)
rationale: Tapping the door is a gesture everyone understands, even without reading any labels.
judge_comment: Knock-to-start is a simple gesture, but it needs a way to set time and power and could be triggered by accident, with only the start step simplified.

title: Aroma Done Signal
new_elements: Aroma release cartridge (Small cartridge releases a food-like scent when cooking ends.)
rationale: A smell tells the user the food is ready without any need to read or listen.
judge_comment: A scent cue for completion needs no reading or learning and is novel, but cartridge refills and unwanted odors make it less practical.

title: Light-Ring Power Indicator
new_elements: Colour-ring power indicator (Ring of light on the tray edge shows power as colour: green is gentle, red is full.)
rationale: Colour replaces numbers, so the power level is obvious without any learning.
judge_comment: Colour in place of numbers is intuitive and feasible, though it addresses only power level and not the rest of the operation.

title: Radar Food Scan
new_elements: Millimetre-wave food sensing (Low-power radar reads food state and sets cooking automatically.)
rationale: The machine senses when food is ready, so the user only places it and presses nothing.
judge_comment: Automatic cooking with no user input removes the learning curve entirely, but radar sensing of food doneness is unproven and the idea is vague on how it would work.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Food-icon dial (Single dial with raised icons for popcorn, leftovers, frozen meal and drink, replacing numbered minutes.)
rationale: Users pick a food picture instead of guessing minutes, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Icon dials are simple and effective, but they already exist on many microwaves and aren't radical.

title: Weighing Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Strain gauges under the turntable estimate mass and set cook time automatically.)
rationale: The machine sets its own time from what is placed on it, so the user never touches a timer.
judge_comment: Load-cell weighing for automatic timing is concrete and removes the timer, though mass alone is a poor proxy for food type and heating needs.

title: Close-to-Start Door
new_elements: Magnetic auto-start latch (Closing the door until the magnet clicks engages the magnetron without any button.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed, which matches what people already do with any cupboard.
judge_comment: Close-to-start is intuitive and radical, but it risks accidental starts when the oven is empty and raises safety concerns.

title: Single Tilt Dial
new_elements: Tilt-to-heat lever (A single lever tilted further means more heat and more time, like a thermostat.)
rationale: One lever controls both time and heat, so the controls become a single intuitive movement.
judge_comment: A single tilt lever merging time and heat is intuitive and fairly novel, though the time/power coupling limits control and the mechanism is vague.

title: Tactile Shape Knobs
new_elements: Shape-coded knobs (Each knob has a distinct shape and texture so it can be found by touch alone.)
rationale: Knobs that feel different can be used with the lights off or with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: Shape-coded knobs help accessibility and are simple to make, but they do little to remove the need to learn what the controls do.

title: Weight Scale Stop
new_elements: Mass-loss sensing (The turntable tracks food weight loss and stops heating once the target dryness is reached.)
rationale: Stopping on the right weight means the user never needs to judge how long to cook.
judge_comment: Weight-loss sensing on the turntable is a novel way to auto-stop, but a load cell in a microwave cavity and the unclear 'target dryness' make it hard to build.

title: Icon Labelled Door
new_elements: Door icon guide (A large printed icon on the door shows how to open, close and start the oven.)
rationale: Picture-only instructions on the door are readable at a glance and need no manual.
judge_comment: Directly targets no-learning-curve use and is easy to build, but icon labels are an obvious, incremental fix rather than a radical one.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Done
new_elements: Humidity-based doneness sensing (Detects steam rise and fall from the food to decide when cooking is finished.); Single START tile (One large tile that starts cooking; the machine picks the time itself.)
rationale: The user presses one tile and the machine decides the time, so no timer has to be learned.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensing auto cook with one start tile is already on sensor-cook microwaves, so it is highly relevant and feasible but not radical.

title: Continuous Solid-State Heat
new_elements: Solid-state RF amplifier (A GaN amplifier that delivers continuously variable power with no on/off cycling.); Single linear power slider (One slider that sets power continuously from low to high.)
rationale: One slider with no cycling steps removes the discrete power ladder users have to learn.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with a linear slider is real technology and simplifies power choice, but users still must decide on power and time.

title: Thermal-Glow Done Indicator
new_elements: Thermochromic turntable (A turntable coating that changes colour as food reaches serving temperature.); Thermochromic pigment coating (Pigment that changes colour at a set temperature without power.)
rationale: The plate changes colour when the food is ready, so the user needs no timing knowledge at all.
judge_comment: A color-changing plate gives an intuitive done cue, though it does not control cooking and thermochromic coatings face durability and safety concerns.

title: Spoken Status Voice
new_elements: Plain-speech speaker (Speaks short phrases such as Food is ready, or Open the door.); Announces state in plain words (Replaces display text and bells with spoken status.)
rationale: Spoken instructions tell the user what to do next, so no symbols need to be learned.
judge_comment: Spoken prompts directly reduce the need to learn symbols, but talking appliances already exist and it doesn't replace the controls themselves.

title: Projected Cavity Panel
new_elements: Turntable projector (A small projector under the turntable that shows step-by-step pictures on the turntable.); Shows instructions on the plate (Projects simple pictures onto the turntable to guide the user.)
rationale: Instructions appear where the food goes, so users read the guidance at the moment they need it.
judge_comment: Projecting pictorial guidance onto the turntable is intuitive and novel, but a projector in a microwave cavity faces heat, steam, and food-splatter problems.

title: Ambient Light Ring
new_elements: Ring light status band (A ring of light around the door that shows green for cooking and red for done.); Shows state by colour (Communicates running or finished through a universal colour code.)
rationale: A colour code everyone already knows from traffic lights shows status with no reading at all.
judge_comment: A simple colour status ring is easy and universally understood, but it is incremental and only covers status feedback.

title: Ask-Once Memory
new_elements: Learning reheat key (A key that stores the last setting; pressing it repeats the last cook.); Repeats last cook (Recalls the user's usual settings without asking for any.)
rationale: The machine remembers the last cook, so the user never repeats a setting they have already used.
judge_comment: A repeat-last-cook key is very feasible and easy to use, but similar features already exist on many microwaves and it does little for first-time cooks.

title: Coin-Slot Pre-Set
new_elements: Token-operated timer (A token slot; each token adds a fixed block of minutes.); Counts time in tokens (Sets time by counting tokens placed in the slot.)
rationale: One token equals one fixed block of time, so the user cannot pick a confusing value.
judge_comment: Token-per-time-block removes choice and is quirky, but needing tokens adds friction and a new thing to manage.

title: Stove-Style Flame Dial
new_elements: Flame-icon power ring (A ring of flame icons that shows low to high by how many flames are lit.); Shows power by visual intensity (Power shown as a glowing bar of flames, borrowed from gas hob design.)
rationale: Users already know more flames mean more heat from gas hobs, so the metaphor needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Familiar flame metaphor makes power obvious and is trivially buildable, though not very radical.

title: Position-Sets-Power Plate
new_elements: Zoned turntable (A turntable with a marked rim and centre zones; placing food in each zone sets its power.); Zone-weighted RF coupling (The cavity modulates power by the zone the food sits in.)
rationale: Putting food in a marked zone sets its power with no knob at all.
judge_comment: Radical zero-knob power setting by food position directly serves no-learning-curve, but microwave power cannot realistically be zoned this way and the cavity field is hard to control.

title: One-Dial Food Picker
new_elements: Food-picker dial (Single rotary dial with food pictograms; one turn selects time and power together.); Selects food preset (time and power in one action) (Maps one choice to a pre-tuned cooking profile.)
rationale: One picture-labelled dial replaces two abstract dials, so the user makes a single obvious choice with no manual to read.
judge_comment: Simple and highly feasible, but picture-based preset dials already exist, so it is not radical.

title: Weigh-and-Go Platter
new_elements: Load-cell platter (Strain-gauge plate under the turntable that reads food mass.); Estimates cook time from food weight (Converts measured mass into a time setting.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate and pressing start is the whole task, because the machine works out time from weight.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing is plausible and concrete, but weight alone doesn't determine the right time or power for different foods.

title: Full-Power-Only Heating
new_elements: Single full-power mode with time-only control (Power is fixed; only duration varies.)
rationale: Removing the power control leaves one variable, time, which everyone already understands.
judge_comment: Simple and effective for reducing learning, and it substitutes away power control, but it is hardly radical and many cheap microwaves already work this way.

title: Spoken 'Ready' Voice
new_elements: Micro-speaker with pre-recorded phrases (Says 'Ready' or 'Done' at cycle end.); Announces cycle status in plain speech (Works for users who cannot see the display.)
rationale: A spoken word replaces the ambiguous ding, so every user knows what has happened without interpreting a sound.
judge_comment: A spoken 'Ready' is clear and accessible but already exists in some appliances and adds a part rather than simplifying.

title: Thermochromic Doneness Label
new_elements: Thermochromic dish-sticker (Printed label that changes colour when the plate reaches serving temperature.); Thermochromic ink (Leuco-dye ink that changes colour at a set temperature.)
rationale: The plate changes colour to show that the food is ready, so the user reads one visible signal.
judge_comment: A visible doneness signal removes guesswork, but it adds a consumable label and doesn't change how the microwave is operated, so it only partly addresses the need.

title: Visual Countdown Ring
new_elements: Colour LED countdown ring (Ring around the cavity shrinks from green to red as time runs out.); Shows remaining time as colour (Progress shown without numbers.)
rationale: Colour progress needs no reading or arithmetic, so it is understood at a glance.
judge_comment: An intuitive color progress display is easy to build and understand, though it adds rather than substitutes and is not very radical.

title: Tactile Detent Knob
new_elements: Clicking detent knob (Knob with tactile clicks every 30 seconds for blind or older users.); Gives tactile feedback per step (Each click equals one fixed time step.)
rationale: Every click is felt, so a user can set the time by touch without looking.
judge_comment: A detent knob replaces buttons with a simple tactile control that needs no learning, but it is a familiar approach.

title: Turntable-Free Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Rotating metal mode stirrer (Spinning reflector spreads microwaves evenly through a fixed cavity.); Evens heating without a tray (Field distribution handled by the stirrer.)
rationale: No tray to remove, reseat, or clean means nothing to get wrong after loading.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves, and removing the tray modestly reduces user steps, though heating evenness may suffer.

title: E-Ink Control Panel
new_elements: E-ink picture panel (Bistable e-paper panel shows food icons and steps.); Electrophoretic e-paper (Low-power display that holds an image without power.)
rationale: Large picture icons on a panel are easier to follow than text labels.
judge_comment: Picture-based e-ink panel substitutes buttons and text and plausibly lowers the learning curve, though e-ink refresh and touch input are limitations.

title: Cartridge Recipe
new_elements: Recipe cartridge slot (Insert a shaped cartridge that sets all cooking parameters.); Physical preset (A physical object holds the recipe and needs no programming.)
rationale: Inserting a cartridge is simpler than setting any number.
judge_comment: A physical recipe cartridge removes number entry and is plausible, though it needs a cartridge ecosystem and it's less radical than it sounds.

title: Mirror Panel Assistant
new_elements: Reflective control surface (A mirror panel that shows one big 'Start' word over the user's reflection.); Smart reflective display (Shows text on a reflective surface when activated.)
rationale: A single large word on a familiar mirror is easier to read than any button layout.
judge_comment: A one-word 'Start' on a mirror is a striking idea and feasible with a smart mirror, but it doesn't address how to set time or power.

title: Spring-Pop Door
new_elements: Toaster-style spring latch (Door pops open a few millimetres when the lever is pressed down.); Press-to-release (Pressing down and letting go opens the door.)
rationale: The toaster lever is a motion everyone already knows, so no new gesture is needed.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever is a familiar gesture and easy to build, but it only covers door opening, not the cooking controls.

title: Thermal Icon Strip
new_elements: Heat-level icon strip (A strip of simple icons (sun, flame, snowflake) to choose power by feel.); Pictographic power (Power is chosen using pictures instead of numbers.)
rationale: Icons match intuitive ideas of hot and cold, which need no explanation.
judge_comment: Icon-based power selection is intuitive and easy to build, but it is a modest, fairly obvious change and a snowflake icon doesn't make sense for a microwave.

title: Edible Cook Indicator
new_elements: Food-stamp label (A small sticker on the food turns a clear colour when fully cooked.); Heat-activated ink (Ink that changes colour at a set temperature.)
rationale: The food reports its own readiness, so no lamp or inspection is needed.
judge_comment: A thermochromic food sticker removes the need to set or judge anything, but it only indicates doneness and does not control the cook, and it adds a consumable.

title: Reheat Memory Button
new_elements: Last-meal memory (Remembers the last cycle and repeats it with one press.); Repeat last cook (Repeats the previous settings on request.)
rationale: Households reheat the same things, so the machine remembers and removes the need to set anything.
judge_comment: Easy to use and fully feasible, but 'repeat last' buttons already exist, so it is not radical, and it does not help the first use.

title: Pizza Slice Dial
new_elements: Portion slice selector (Pick a slice shape to set heating for one, two or a whole pizza.); Portion-based heating (The machine heats for the amount selected.)
rationale: Choosing an amount of food matches how people think about meals, not time.
judge_comment: Portion-based selection fits how people think and removes time entry, though it does not clearly substitute a cheaper part and food variation limits accuracy.

title: Stove-Style Dial Ring
new_elements: Hob-style control ring (A ring control copies the stove burner dial people already know.); Familiar-dial control (Turning a dial sets heat as on a hob.)
rationale: Users already understand a hob dial, so the existing skill transfers directly.
judge_comment: Familiar hob-style dial transfers existing skill and is easy to build, but dials on microwaves are already common and not radical.

title: Cook-by-Weight Scale Tray
new_elements: Integrated scale tray (The turntable weighs food and selects heating automatically.); Automatic load sensing (Weight is measured and used to choose the cycle.)
rationale: Placing food on the tray is the entire set-up, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto selection removes settings, but weight alone poorly identifies food type and heating needs, so results may be unreliable.

title: Ask-Once Setup Voice
new_elements: Single spoken food name (Say the food name once and the machine chooses the cycle.); Speech intent recognition (Understands a single spoken food name.)
rationale: Speaking the name of the meal requires no vocabulary or manual.
judge_comment: Saying the food name to pick the cycle directly removes the need to learn controls and is feasible with current speech recognition, though voice control on appliances is not new and the cooking result depends on food quantity.

title: Three-Word Power
new_elements: Gentle/Normal/Fast slider (A three-position slider with plain-word labels replaces the five-step knob.)
rationale: Three plain-language choices are far easier to understand than five unlabeled numeric steps.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible, but an incremental relabeling of power levels that still leaves a decision for the user.

title: Automatic Power by Food Type
new_elements: Food-category power map (The microwave infers the correct power from a single food-category tap, with no power setting at all.)
rationale: Choosing a food type removes the need to understand power at all.
judge_comment: Food-category buttons are common, though they do remove the need to understand power.

title: Time-Implies-Power
new_elements: Duration-derived power (Setting a longer time automatically lowers power; the user only chooses how long.)
rationale: One variable instead of two removes the power decision from the user entirely.
judge_comment: Collapsing two variables into one is a clever simplification, though the implied power may not suit all foods.

title: Outside Status Glow
new_elements: Ambient status halo (A soft glow around the top edge shows cooking, done, or idle with simple colors.)
rationale: A single glow visible from across the room tells the user the state without any numbers.
judge_comment: A status light is simple and easy to read, but it is common and not a very radical substitution.

title: Magnetic Self-Opening Door
new_elements: Magnetic spring latch (Magnets hold the door shut and push it open a few millimetres when power is cut.)
rationale: The door pops open by itself at the end, so the user never has to work out how to release it.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch that pops the door open is plausible and mildly helpful, but it only simplifies the door and not the settings.

title: Sealed Bag Cooker
new_elements: Pre-sealed cooking pouch (A single-use heat-safe pouch holds the food and needs no cleaning.)
rationale: The user drops in a pouch and presses one button, with no dishes or cleaning to learn.
judge_comment: A pouch with a single button truly reduces decisions and learning, and pouch meals can plausibly encode cooking settings.

title: Acoustic Boil Watch
new_elements: Acoustic bubble listener (Listens for the first boiling sounds and cuts power before eruption.); Prevents eruptive boiling automatically (Stops heating when boiling becomes unsafe.)
rationale: The machine guards against eruptions itself, so the user never has to watch the cup.
judge_comment: Acoustic boil detection removes the need to watch or learn timing, though reliably detecting superheated water without bubbles is hard, and it only partly addresses operation overall.

title: Dorm-Room Plug-In Cube
new_elements: Plug-in cooking cube (A small cube microwave that runs on a standard socket and has one control.)
rationale: A single-person device with one control suits students who have no time to learn a machine.
judge_comment: A single-control compact microwave is very simple and feasible, but it already exists and isn't radical.

title: Grandmother Mode Tap Plate
new_elements: Large tactile tap plate (A big flat plate with a single large tap area and a raised pattern for easy grip.)
rationale: A big plate that a hand can find without looking is simple for everyone, including new users.
judge_comment: A large tactile single-tap plate is intuitive and easy to build, though it is a moderate departure from the usual buttons.

title: Container Speaks
new_elements: NFC tag on food container (The container's tag sends its heating instructions to the oven when it is placed inside.)
rationale: The packaging does the thinking, so the user never has to set anything.
judge_comment: An NFC tag on the container gives zero-input operation, but it requires packaging ecosystem adoption and the tag must be kept clear of the microwave field.

title: Magnetic Nudge Door
new_elements: Magnetic push-to-open latch (A magnet holds the door and releases it with a light push.)
rationale: Pushing the door itself replaces the lever mechanism, so no button or mechanism needs explaining.
judge_comment: Push-to-open doors already exist and the change only affects opening, so it does little for the learning curve of operating the cook cycle.

title: Two-Icon Panel
new_elements: Hot and cold icon panel (The panel offers only a warm icon and a reheat icon, with no numbers.)
rationale: Two icons are the simplest possible control layout.
judge_comment: Very simple to use, but two icons are a modest, fairly obvious reduction and give little control over time or power.

title: Chef-Less Auto Recipe
new_elements: Automatic recipe matching (The oven recognises the food type from the cavity camera and picks the program.)
rationale: The machine chooses every setting, so the user only inserts the food.
judge_comment: Camera-based recognition removes all decisions, but it is costly and unreliable, and it is not a simple substitution.

title: Pressure Plate Start
new_elements: Pressure-sensing floor pad (A pad under the tray starts cooking when the food sits on it.)
rationale: Placing food on the tray is the only action, with no buttons at all.
judge_comment: Placing the food as the only action is radical and intuitive, but there is no way to set the cooking and it risks accidental starts, with no safety check that the door is closed.

title: Hand Warmer Mode
new_elements: Single warm setting (The oven warms all food to a safe serving temperature with no other options.)
rationale: A single outcome means the user can never choose wrongly.
judge_comment: A single-outcome oven removes choice and learning, though it limits usefulness and the sensing needed for a safe temperature is not described.

title: Plain-Word Voice Done
new_elements: Speaker with plain speech (Says 'Food is hot' or 'Ready' in a short spoken phrase.); Spoken completion (Announces the end of cooking in plain language.)
rationale: A spoken sentence needs no decoding, unlike a bell that might be mistaken for the smoke alarm.
judge_comment: Plain speech is very easy to understand and cheap, but talking appliances are already common and it only covers completion.

title: Drawer Instead of Door
new_elements: Sliding cavity drawer (The whole cavity slides out like a drawer, so food loads at counter height.); Pull-out loading (Food is placed on a tray that pulls out toward the user.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer is an everyday motion, so the user never has to find a door latch.
judge_comment: Drawer loading uses a familiar motion and exists in some built-in models, though it is more complex and costly than a door and doesn't address controls.

title: Single Lever Power
new_elements: Slider with food words (A slider labelled 'gentle' at one end and 'fast' at the other.); Intent slider (Sets how hard the food is cooked with one movement along a line.)
rationale: A slider with plain words replaces a numbered power scale with no need to learn what each step means.
judge_comment: A simple word-labelled slider is easy and intuitive but is an incremental change, and it still leaves time to be set.

title: Auto-Start on Close
new_elements: Door-closed sensor (Detects the door closing and starts a default heat cycle.); Start by closing (Closing the door is the start command.)
rationale: Closing a door is the most natural gesture, so no start control is needed.
judge_comment: Starting by closing the door is very simple and technically easy, but a default cycle risks unwanted heating and fits only some uses.

title: Cook-Anything Button
new_elements: Sensor-driven heat button (One button that uses humidity and temperature sensing to pick power and time.); Adaptive sensing (Measures food state during the cycle and adjusts itself.)
rationale: The machine decides everything, so the user only has to press one button.
judge_comment: One button with auto-sensing removes nearly all learning, though sensor cooking is already on the market and accuracy varies.

title: Shelf-Sensing Auto Setup
new_elements: Container recognizer (Camera or sensor under the turntable that identifies the container and food.); Object recognition (Identifies items placed in the cavity.)
rationale: The machine sees what is in it and sets itself, so the user has nothing to decide.
judge_comment: Camera-based recognition that sets cooking automatically directly removes decisions; it's been tried (cameras in ovens) but is still hard to do reliably.

title: Tall-Button Heat Lever
new_elements: Push-pull heat lever (One lever that pushes to heat and pulls to open the door.); Two-motion control (Push and pull are the only actions.)
rationale: Push and pull are the only motions anyone has to learn, and both are already familiar.
judge_comment: A single push-pull lever is very simple, but it doesn't address how to set time or power.

title: Temperature Spike Stick
new_elements: Food probe stick (A probe pushed into food that tells the machine when the centre is hot.); Core-temperature stop (Stops cooking when the centre reaches a safe temperature.)
rationale: The machine stops when the food is safe, so nobody has to guess times.
judge_comment: A probe removes time guessing but adds a step of inserting and cleaning a probe, and microwave-safe probes are tricky.

title: Mat Start Pad
new_elements: Floor-style start mat (A mat in front of the machine that starts cooking when stepped on.); Foot-start (Cooking starts with a foot press.)
rationale: A mat can be used with full hands, which removes the need for a button.
judge_comment: Foot-start mat is novel and helps full hands, but it only replaces the start button and leaves time and power unaddressed, with some safety concerns about accidental starts.

title: Tap-Rhythm Cook
new_elements: Tap pad (A pad where the number of taps sets the power level.); Count-to-power (Taps are counted to choose the power.)
rationale: Counting taps is a skill everyone already has.
judge_comment: Tap counting is simple and cheap, but users must remember the mapping from taps to power, so there is still some learning.

title: Kettle-Style Lid Click
new_elements: Click-to-heat handle (A handle that clicks down to heat, like a kettle, and springs up when done.); Spring-up done (The handle pops up to signal the end.)
rationale: A kettle-style handle is already understood by almost everyone.
judge_comment: Familiar kettle metaphor makes operation intuitive and the mechanism is plausible, but it is unclear how cook time or power is set, and it is a modest substitution.

title: Pre-Set Pantry Cards
new_elements: Pantry card stack (Printed cards for common foods, each with a picture and a single button to press.); Card-led cooking (The card is placed on the machine to set the cook.)
rationale: Placing a card that shows the food sets the machine with no reading or learning.
judge_comment: Picture cards remove reading and learning and are easy to implement with a reader, though cards can be lost and the range of foods is limited.

title: Ask-the-Food Reheat
new_elements: Food-type scanner (Camera that identifies the food type from its appearance.); Food recognition (Recognises common foods from images.)
rationale: The machine looks at the food and does the setting, so the user answers no questions.
judge_comment: Camera recognition would remove all operation steps, but accuracy, cost and the lack of any cheaper or simpler substitution make it weaker on feasibility.

title: Tray Icon Magnet Lock
new_elements: Magnetic plate ID (Each plate has a magnetic code that sets the oven when placed on the turntable.)
rationale: Placing a plate is the only step and the plate decides the settings.
judge_comment: Plate-coded settings remove all input, but it needs special plates and cannot cover arbitrary food or cookware.

title: Magnetic Breakaway Door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch (Strong magnetic catch that releases on a light push and cannot jam.)
rationale: A magnet with no moving hooks fails less and is easier to operate than a spring lever.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch is simple, cheap and feasible, but it is an incremental change with little novelty.

title: Auto-Reheat Only Mode
new_elements: Single-setting reheat (One automatic mode adjusts power and time for any food.)
rationale: Removing all power choices means there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Directly removes choices so there is nothing to learn, but single-button microwaves already exist and sensor-based accuracy is the challenge.

title: Dial-Free Rotary Ring
new_elements: Single rotary ring (One ring turns for food category and a click confirms; no timer or power knob.)
rationale: A single control with one action removes the need to understand several dials.
judge_comment: A single rotary ring is simple and feasible, but it is a modest simplification and not very radical; it also needs durations to be inferred from the food category.

title: Self-Locking Cable Dock
new_elements: Magnetic power connector (Connector snaps into place magnetically and disconnects safely on a pull.)
rationale: Plugging in cannot be done wrong, and pulling the cable cuts power instantly.
judge_comment: A magnetic breakaway connector makes plugging in foolproof and is safe, though it only touches setup, not cooking operation.

title: Ambient Scent Done Signal
new_elements: Scent emitter (Oven releases a faint food-like scent when cooking is complete.)
rationale: A smell signal is noticed by people who are not looking at the oven.
judge_comment: Scent cue is quirky and easy to implement, helps notice completion without learning, but doesn't address operation of controls and replaces nothing cheaper.

title: Single-Button Auto Cook
new_elements: Humidity sensor array (Reads vapour from food and decides when cooking is done); Auto-selects time and power (Removes the need for any user setting)
rationale: One button and no settings means a first-time user cannot get it wrong.
judge_comment: Strongly serves zero-learning-curve operation, but humidity-sensor auto-cook already exists in many microwaves, so it is not very radical.

title: Food Icon Drum Replaces Timer Knob
new_elements: Pictogram drum (Rotating drum showing food icons such as rice, pizza and soup)
rationale: Users pick what they are cooking instead of guessing minutes.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and simple to build, but it is an incremental take on preset buttons and gives only coarse control.

title: Weight Plate Sets Everything
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Turntable that weighs the food and sets power and time from mass)
rationale: Placing food on the plate is the only step the user takes.
judge_comment: A load-cell turntable removes all input steps, but mass alone does not identify the food type and the load cell adds cost and complexity to the rotating mount.

title: Door Springs Open at Finish
new_elements: Spring door opener (Door pops open a few centimetres when cooking finishes)
rationale: The physical state of the machine itself signals that the meal is done.
judge_comment: A spring-loaded door that pops open at finish is an intuitive, cheap, existing-style mechanism, and it signals completion with no learning; it does not help with setup.

title: Packet Barcode Scan
new_elements: Barcode window scanner (Reads the packet barcode through the door window)
rationale: Pressing start on a packet already set up for the oven needs no decisions.
judge_comment: Scanning a barcode makes operation near-zero effort, but it depends on packaging adoption and the scanner replaces the dial only for supported foods.

title: Hold-to-Run Heat
new_elements: Heat only while held (Magnetron runs only while the user holds a button)
rationale: The machine only heats while the user is paying attention, so no timer is needed.
judge_comment: Hold-to-run is intuitive and safe and needs no timer, though it is tiring for long cooks and not radical.

title: Dual-Mode Turntable Replacement
new_elements: Mode stirrer fan (Rotating metal fan that spreads microwaves evenly across the cavity)
rationale: Food heats evenly with no plate to place and no motor to check.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are a real, common substitute for turntables, making it simpler to use with nothing to place, though not radical.

title: Fixed Plate Multi-Feed
new_elements: Multi-port waveguide feed (Several feed points spread energy evenly so the plate can stay still)
rationale: A fixed plate is easier to clean and cannot jam.
judge_comment: Multi-port feeding to replace the turntable is a real substitution that removes a part, but even heating is technically tricky and the benefit is mostly cleaning rather than operation.

title: Printed Placement Grid Tray
new_elements: Icon placement tray (Ceramic tray with printed zones showing where to put each food)
rationale: The printed zones show where food goes, so no instructions are needed.
judge_comment: The printed zones guide users intuitively and are easy to build, but they are mundane and only loosely tied to the operation itself.

title: Hot Plate Reveal Lamp
new_elements: E-ink status label (Low-power label showing the current state in words)
rationale: A plain word such as Cooking or Done explains the state without a light or manual.
judge_comment: Plain-word status on a low-power e-ink label clarifies state without learning, and is feasible, though the label's name is mismatched.

title: Food-Sensing Auto-Cook
new_elements: Infrared food-state sensing (Thermal and humidity sensors read when food reaches serving temperature and stop automatically.); Cook until done without setting time (The user never chooses a duration; the machine decides when to stop.)
rationale: Removing the duration dial means there is no time to calculate, so anyone can operate it on first use.
judge_comment: Directly eliminates the time-setting step, though IR and humidity sensing of food doneness is only partly reliable and already exists in sensor-cook modes.

title: Cook Button Is the Door Itself
new_elements: Door-close auto-start (Closing the door with food inside starts the program immediately.)
rationale: Closing a door is already a habit, so the machine starts with no extra step.
judge_comment: Door-close auto-start removes a step and is easy to build, but it needs a way to determine time or program, and it risks accidental starts.

title: Icon Dishes Instead of Keypad
new_elements: Picture-plate selector (Large photos of common dishes on a dial; the user taps the picture of their meal.)
rationale: Recognizing a picture of the meal is faster than reading any label.
judge_comment: A picture dial for dishes is clear and feasible but resembles existing preset buttons, so it is only modestly novel.

title: Projected Control on Counter
new_elements: Counter-top light projection (Simple projected icons appear on the countertop beside the machine.)
rationale: The controls appear where the user already looks, avoiding a distant panel.
judge_comment: Projected icons put controls where users look, but the projector and touch sensing are unspecified, and it adds complexity rather than substituting a simpler part.

title: Microwave With No Settings at All
new_elements: Default-only cooking (The machine has one smart program that adapts to any food placed inside.)
rationale: With no settings to choose, there is no possibility of confusion.
judge_comment: Removing all settings directly eliminates the learning curve, though a single program that adapts to any food needs sensing that the idea doesn't describe.

title: Clock Face Becomes Progress Ring
new_elements: Circular progress ring (A ring of light fills up as cooking progresses, showing how close the food is to done.)
rationale: A filling ring is a self-explanatory display that needs no number reading.
judge_comment: A progress ring is easy to build and understand, but it is a familiar interface pattern and not radical.

title: Stick-On Recipe Cards
new_elements: Magnetic food cards (Cards placed on the microwave door select the program when touched to the panel.)
rationale: Physical cards mean the user only needs to pick a picture, not understand any function.
judge_comment: Tap-a-card selection replaces the keypad with a picture and needs no learning, though it adds cards to manage and the substitution is only loosely defined.

title: Door Cannot Be Opened Wrongly
new_elements: Automatic pause on opening (Opening the door pauses cooking and resumes when closed, with no stop button.)
rationale: Users can open the door at any time without needing to know how to stop cooking.
judge_comment: Pause on door open is already standard in microwaves, so it adds little, though it does help with stopping.

title: Microwave in a Tray Cover
new_elements: Lidded serving bowl (The bowl the food comes in is the only cooking vessel and fits the cavity.)
rationale: Cooking and serving in one vessel removes the need to transfer food or choose containers.
judge_comment: A single purpose-built vessel removes container choices and could pair with a code or preset, but it ties users to proprietary bowls.

title: Microwave Speaks Your Language Via Icons
new_elements: Universal pictogram display (Icons only, with no text, that are understood by any user worldwide.)
rationale: Pictograms need no reading skill or translation, so anyone can operate it.
judge_comment: Icon-only display directly removes reading and translation barriers, but pictogram interfaces are already common and not very radical.

title: Microwave Built From Food Packaging
new_elements: Disposable heating sleeve (A cheap sleeve around the food that generates the heating pattern itself.)
rationale: The packaging does the work, so the user just places the food and presses start.
judge_comment: A disposable sleeve that sets the heating pattern is radical and removes the need for settings, but a passive sleeve with this function is technically doubtful.

title: Thermochromic Package Sensing
new_elements: Thermochromic food label (Label on the food turns colour when the food reaches safe serving temperature.)
rationale: The package signals done-ness by colour, so the user needs no instructions or sensors.
judge_comment: A color-changing label gives intuitive done-ness feedback, but it doesn't control the oven and needs packaging adoption.

title: Two-Button Cook Or Stop
new_elements: Cook and stop keys (Only a large green and red key remain, with no other controls.)
rationale: Two self-explanatory keys cover the entire experience with no possibility of confusion.
judge_comment: Very simple and feasible, but lacks control over time/power and isn't very radical.

title: Food Recipe Cartridge
new_elements: Recipe cartridge slot (Insert a cartridge with the food's settings printed as a code and the oven does the rest.)
rationale: Inserting a cartridge is more obvious than programming, so students never need a manual.
judge_comment: Cartridge is a novel, concrete interface, though it adds a consumable and extra steps versus simply pressing start.

title: Tap-to-add-30-seconds button
new_elements: Single tap-counter button (Each press adds 30 seconds, and a long press starts cooking.)
rationale: Counting taps needs no reading or arithmetic, and it removes the timer's imprecision for short durations.
judge_comment: Simple and cheap, but users still must judge the time, and the tap-counter is already common.

title: Load-cell weight-loss stop
new_elements: Turntable load cell (Strain gauge under the turntable measures mass loss from evaporation and stops when the target is reached.)
rationale: The machine stops by itself based on what happens to the food, so the user never has to estimate minutes.
judge_comment: Weight-loss sensing is novel and plausible, but the target mass loss is unclear without knowing the food, and the user still has to specify a target.

title: NFC food-packet programming
new_elements: NFC food-packet tags (Ready meals carry tags that send cooking time and power settings when touched to the panel.)
rationale: Users tap the packet to the machine and never choose a setting themselves.
judge_comment: Tapping the packet to the panel removes setting selection for ready meals, though it needs tags on packaging and does not cover other food.

title: Cavity camera on the front screen
new_elements: Cavity camera and screen (A camera inside shows a live picture of the food on a small screen on the front.)
rationale: Users check food by looking at a screen they already trust, not by bending to peer through a door.
judge_comment: A camera and screen are feasible and concrete, but they add complexity and cost, and they help monitoring more than operation.

title: Proximity auto-open door
new_elements: Proximity sensor door opener (An infrared sensor opens the door when a hand is brought close to the handle.)
rationale: The door opens without any button to find or press, which suits users with weak grip or poor sight.
judge_comment: Removes the need to find a button and helps accessibility, but it adds cost and can trigger accidentally, and it does not address the rest of the operation.

title: Self-stirring antenna replaces turntable
new_elements: Rotating mode stirrer (A moving metal vane spreads microwaves so food heats evenly with no turntable to fit.)
rationale: Users no longer need to place the glass plate correctly or wash it, so there is one less step.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves, so it is feasible but not novel, and it only mildly simplifies use by removing the plate.

title: NFC tap plate with one button
new_elements: NFC tap pad (A pad on the top reads a tagged plate or packet and starts the right programme.)
rationale: Tapping a plate is the only interaction needed, which means there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Tapping a tagged item to auto-start is near zero-learning and the NFC hardware is cheap, but it depends on tagged packets and plates.

title: Reheat-only appliance
new_elements: Single reheat function (The machine has one reheat mode and no separate cooking modes.)
rationale: Removing every mode except reheat means there is nothing to choose.
judge_comment: It removes choices entirely and so cuts the learning curve, but it is a feature removal rather than a radical substitution and limits utility.

title: Single Picture Dial
new_elements: Picture dial with 4 food icons (One rotating dial showing pictures (soup, frozen meal, drink, reheat) that sets time and power together.)
rationale: Users choose a picture of what they are cooking instead of deciding on minutes and power levels.
judge_comment: Easy to use and very buildable, but preset-icon dials already exist, so it is a modest substitution.

title: Glowing Cooking-Status Wall
new_elements: Colour-shifting status wall (Cavity walls shift colour from cool blue to warm amber as the food heats.)
rationale: Colour gives status at a glance, so no reading of numbers or dials is needed.
judge_comment: Colour status is intuitive and needs no learning, but coloured walls that track food temperature are hard to build and it only shows status without simplifying controls.

title: Haptic Handle Ding
new_elements: Handle vibration pulse motor (A small vibration motor in the door handle buzzes three times at the end of cooking.)
rationale: A felt pulse signals completion to users who cannot see the screen or hear a bell.
judge_comment: Easy to build and useful for accessibility, but it only replaces the beep and barely reduces the learning needed to operate.

title: Door Shell Touch-to-Open
new_elements: Full-door touch panel (The whole door face opens on a light push, with no button or latch to find.)
rationale: Pushing anywhere on the door opens it, so the user never has to search for a button.
judge_comment: Removes the need to find the open button, but a touch-sensitive door panel is vague and risks accidental opening.

title: Phone Tap Setup
new_elements: NFC tap-to-cook tag (Tap the food package on the unit and it reads cooking settings from the label.)
rationale: Settings come from the food package, so the user never enters numbers.
judge_comment: Reading settings from the package removes number entry entirely, but it depends on packaging adoption, and the name 'Phone Tap' does not match the description.

title: Butter Melt Pocket
new_elements: Melt-only tray insert (A shallow insert with a fixed low-power melt program for butter and chocolate.)
rationale: A single insert with one fixed job removes every setting for the task.
judge_comment: A fixed-program insert is simple and easy to build, but it covers only a narrow task and the insert would need to be recognized by the oven.

title: Recipe Card Cooking Mat
new_elements: Printed recipe mat (A flat mat placed under the dish shows its own pictured instructions and colour strips.)
rationale: The mat carries the instructions with the food, so the machine needs no instructions of its own.
judge_comment: Moving instructions onto a mat is a creative substitution, but the machine still has to read the mat (via colour strips or sensing) to act, and the mechanism is unclear.

title: Reheat Pizza Button
new_elements: Dish-named reheat keys (Keys are labelled with dish names such as pizza, rice and coffee, each with its own preset.)
rationale: Named dish keys replace unknown numbers with words people already use.
judge_comment: Dish-named keys are intuitive but already common on microwaves, and are not radical.

title: Single Ring Status Light
new_elements: Three-colour LED ring (Green means ready to go, amber means cooking, red means finished.)
rationale: Three colours are the only states, so the machine's status is understood without reading anything.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible status indication, but it's an incremental feature and doesn't address how to operate the oven.

title: Photo Menu Touchscreen
new_elements: Picture-tile display (Large photo tiles show foods such as popcorn, soup and leftovers.)
rationale: Users tap the picture of what they are cooking, so no settings need to be understood.
judge_comment: Picture tiles make operation intuitive, but this is an obvious, widely seen approach and it adds a costly screen rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Temperature Probe Stick
new_elements: Disposable probe tip (A plug-in probe stuck into food that stops cooking at the target temperature.)
rationale: Users only need to stick the probe in and the machine finishes the job correctly.
judge_comment: A probe gives reliable results, but inserting and handling a probe is an extra step that adds learning rather than removing it.

title: Dome Cloche Cooker
new_elements: Microwave dome cloche (A domed lid that sits on any plate on the counter and heats only what is inside.)
rationale: The appliance becomes a lid, so there is no box, door or panel to learn.
judge_comment: A cloche replaces the whole box in a radical way, but shielding, energy delivery and safety make it technically hard.

title: Snap-On Preset Caps
new_elements: Preset cap cartridges (Snap-on cartridges that set the whole cycle for popcorn, potatoes or soup.)
rationale: Snapping in a cartridge is a physical action, so the settings never have to be understood.
judge_comment: Physical cartridges replace the keypad logic and remove the need to understand settings, though extra parts add cost and loss risk.

title: Colour-Coded Food Tiles
new_elements: Colour tile set (Coloured tiles, one per food type, placed on the door to set the program.)
rationale: Matching colours is simpler than reading five power levels.
judge_comment: Colour matching is intuitive and easy to build, but it still needs tiles and a mapping from colour to food, so some learning remains.

title: Single Dial Stop Cook
new_elements: One-turn dial (One dial with one direction: turn to start, turn back to stop, and it cooks until done.)
rationale: A single direction of turn has nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single dial that starts and stops is very simple to use, but it needs automatic sensing to know when the food is done and is only moderately novel.

title: Sealed Cook Pouch
new_elements: Microwave cook pouch (Sealed bag that vents itself at the right moment, placed in a box oven with no controls.)
rationale: The pouch handles venting and timing, so the user only needs to put it in.
judge_comment: A pouch that vents itself plus a control-free oven is radical and simple, though timing in the pouch is unclear and it needs special pouches.

title: Cook Ring Sticker
new_elements: Peel-off cook sticker (Sticker placed on the food, read by the oven camera to set the cycle.)
rationale: Putting a sticker on the food hands all decisions to the machine.
judge_comment: A sticker read by a camera that sets the cycle automatically removes user decisions and is plausible, though it adds a consumable and a camera, and it doesn't clearly substitute a cheaper part.

title: Read-the-Packet Cooking
new_elements: Packet barcode/NFC reader (A reader under the cavity floor scans the ready-meal packet and loads its cooking program.)
rationale: The food packaging tells the machine what to do, so the user never sets anything.
judge_comment: Zero input for ready meals, but depends on packaging adoption and does not cover non-packaged food.

title: Voice Says What You Want
new_elements: On-device speech recognition (Short local voice commands such as 'warm my coffee' map to presets without cloud access.)
rationale: Speaking a plain request needs no manual, and it works for users who cannot read small labels.
judge_comment: Natural, no-manual interaction that is feasible with on-device recognition, though noise and accents are an issue and voice microwaves exist.

title: Close-to-Start Door
new_elements: Door-closure sensing auto-start (Latching the door automatically starts the last-used or default program, with no start button.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action a user already knows, so it doubles as the start command.
judge_comment: Very simple and cheap, but auto-starting a default program could be unsafe or undesired, e.g. when empty.

title: Infrared Doneness Eye
new_elements: Infrared thermopile food sensing (A thermopile in the roof reads the food surface temperature and stops when it is hot enough.)
rationale: The machine decides when food is done, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: A thermopile for automatic doneness removes time guessing and is concrete, but surface-only IR sensing is limited for microwave heating and is not very new.

title: Popcorn Pop-Counter
new_elements: Acoustic pop detection (A microphone counts popping sounds and stops the cycle when the pops slow down.)
rationale: Popcorn needs no settings, because the machine listens and stops at the right moment.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection is already used in some microwaves and is feasible, but it only solves a single use case.

title: Fixed Tray Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Fixed ceramic tray with mode stirrer (A stationary tray uses a rotating metal stirrer in the waveguide to even the field.)
rationale: Users never need to think about how to place a dish, because the field spreads evenly on its own.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers with fixed trays are common in existing microwaves; it removes a placement worry but is not radical.

title: Single Feel Power Slider
new_elements: Three-zone power slider (One slider runs from Gentle to Fast, with three marked zones and no numbers.)
rationale: Three plain words are enough for any user to choose a power level.
judge_comment: A three-word slider simplifies the interface directly and is easy to build, but it is an incremental UI change.

title: Hold-to-Heat Button
new_elements: Press-and-hold heat button (Holding the single button heats the food and releasing it stops, like a kettle switch.)
rationale: Holding a button is a familiar action that gives the user direct, visible control with no settings.
judge_comment: A hold-to-heat button is instantly understood and needs no settings, though it is tiring for long cook times and can't run unattended.

title: Two-Word Command Panel
new_elements: Plain-language word buttons (Buttons read Warm, Cook, Thaw, and Melt in large print with icons.)
rationale: Plain action words need no manual, and large text helps elderly users read the panel quickly.
judge_comment: Plain word buttons are very easy to use and simple to build, but the idea is incremental and not radical.

title: Automatic Cook-Mode Learning
new_elements: Usage-learning cook presets (The machine learns the household's usual settings and offers them as the default.)
rationale: The appliance adapts to each household, so the user rarely has to set anything at all.
judge_comment: Learned defaults can reduce the number of settings a user has to make, but this is not really a substitution and it is only modestly radical.

title: Food Icon Dial
new_elements: Picture dial with food icons (Single dial showing soup, rice, pizza, leftovers, each pre-setting time and power.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of the food removes the need to understand minutes, percentages or power levels.
judge_comment: A simple and highly feasible icon dial that is intuitive, but it is an incremental and fairly common preset approach.

title: Hourglass Starter
new_elements: Flip-to-start sand hourglass (Flipping the hourglass starts heating; sand running out ends it.)
rationale: Flipping a visible sand timer is an action anyone already understands, so no numbers or settings are needed.
judge_comment: A flip-to-start hourglass is an intuitive and playful substitute for a timer, but it is imprecise, needs mechanical sensing, and offers only fixed durations.

title: Heat Level as Colour Bar
new_elements: Touch colour bar (Tap anywhere on a bar from cool blue to red hot; the position sets power.)
rationale: Colours map intuitively to heat, so the user does not need to read a numbered power scale.
judge_comment: A touch colour bar maps heat to intuitive colour and replaces numeric power levels, and it is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Auto Power by Feel
new_elements: Adaptive duty-cycle controller (Chooses the on/off ratio automatically from the food's heat response.)
rationale: Letting the machine pick the power means the user never sees or touches a power setting.
judge_comment: Removing the power setting entirely fits zero learning curve, though sensing food heat response without a sensor is technically hard and it doesn't clearly substitute a part.

title: Bell Becomes Door Pop
new_elements: Spring-assisted door pop (When cooking ends, the door springs open a few centimetres to signal completion.)
rationale: The door itself announces that the food is ready, so no bell or number is needed to understand the machine's state.
judge_comment: A door popping open is a clear and simple completion signal, replacing the bell, though it does not simplify starting or setting the cook.

title: Magnet Door Latch
new_elements: Neodymium magnetic latch (Magnet holds the door shut and releases with a firm pull, no levers needed.)
rationale: A magnetic catch has no button or lever to learn, so the door simply closes and opens by feel.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch is simple and cheap and removes the release button, but magnets near a microwave and the door safety interlock need care.

title: Lift-Up Lid Oven
new_elements: Gas-spring lift lid (Top-opening lid lifts with a gas spring, so the user simply lifts it like a box.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is an everyday action, and the gas spring means an elderly user needs almost no force.
judge_comment: A top-opening lid with a gas spring is an intuitive action and more radical, but it is awkward for spills and for reaching hot food, and the microwave-safe seal is harder.

title: Remove the Turntable
new_elements: Built-in mode stirrer (Field stirrer evens out heat so the food sits still on a flat tray.)
rationale: With no turntable to lift out and reposition, cleaning and loading involve fewer steps.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are established tech, and removing the turntable does simplify loading and cleaning, which gives a moderate fit with the need.

title: Card Cook
new_elements: Picture card slot (Insert a wallet-sized card with a food picture and the machine cooks it.)
rationale: A printed card with a picture is simple, cheap and makes choosing a recipe a physical, visual act.
judge_comment: A picture card replaces the keypad with an intuitive physical action, though the user must hold the right cards.

title: Printed Recipe Dial Cover
new_elements: Recipe cover with cut-outs (Clear cover over the dial shows only a few large pictures for the common dishes.)
rationale: Showing only a handful of large, obvious choices removes clutter for users who find small labels hard to read.
judge_comment: A cheap overlay with large pictures is a real simplification and an easy swap, but it is not radical.

title: Snapping Fingers Starts It
new_elements: Clap-to-start microphone (Two claps or a snap start cooking; a silence after the bell stops it.)
rationale: A clap is an action anyone can make, so it removes both the timer and the door button from the learning curve.
judge_comment: Clap-to-start is intuitive and removes controls, though false triggers and unclear cook duration/power limit it; the stop mechanism is vague.

title: Oven Speaks Your Language
new_elements: Spoken prompt speaker (Speaks short plain prompts like 'Put food in, press start' in the user's language.)
rationale: Spoken instructions in the user's own language remove the need to read a manual or any on-panel text.
judge_comment: Spoken prompts in the user's language remove the need to read text, but voice guidance is not new, and it adds a component rather than substituting a cheaper or simpler one.

title: Retro Cooker With Only a Bell
new_elements: Single sprung timer lever (One lever wound by hand; cooking runs for a set fixed turn of the lever.)
rationale: A single lever with a fixed turn is the simplest possible timer, removing any choice of minutes.
judge_comment: A single wind-up lever with a fixed cook time is very simple and a true substitution of the keypad, but a fixed time limits what it can cook.

title: Rotating Antenna Replaces Turntable
new_elements: Rotating RF mode stirrer (Spins the field inside a fixed cavity.)
rationale: Food heats evenly without being placed on a turning plate, so no alignment is needed.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves, so this is feasible but not new, and it only slightly reduces the thinking users must do.

title: Voice Food Name Command
new_elements: Local speech recognizer (Accepts simple food names offline.)
rationale: Users say the food name, which needs no manual or menu knowledge.
judge_comment: Offline voice commands by food name are plausible and need no learning, but they are already common in appliances and the concept is only moderately concrete.

title: Barcode Auto-Program
new_elements: Packaging code reader (Reads a code printed on the food package.)
rationale: Scanning the package sets the program, so the user does not choose settings.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning for cooking programs is feasible and already exists in some products; it only works for packaged food.

title: NFC Tap-to-Cook Plate
new_elements: NFC food tag (Tag on a plate or packet sets the cooking profile.)
rationale: Touching the food to the oven gives it the instructions it needs.
judge_comment: NFC tags give a simple tap-to-cook interaction and are cheap and feasible, but they require tagged plates or packets.

title: Printed Pictogram Floor
new_elements: Pictogram glass turntable (Turntable printed with food icons and placement marks.)
rationale: Visual placement marks show where food goes without reading a manual.
judge_comment: Printed icons on the turntable give intuitive placement guidance and are cheap and feasible, but they address only part of operation.

title: Glass-Free Screen Door
new_elements: Door touchscreen (Shows a live camera image of the cavity.)
rationale: A live picture replaces the window, so users see the food without any settings.
judge_comment: A camera-fed door screen replaces the window and could enable intuitive visual control, though the stated rationale is weak and it adds cost and complexity, and shielding is an issue.

title: Weighing Tray Auto-Timer
new_elements: Load-cell tray (A weighing tray measures the food and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: The oven decides how long to cook from the weight of the food, so the user does not have to.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic timing is a strong zero-input idea, but weight alone is a poor guide to cooking time, and the load cell has to work inside a microwave cavity.

title: Stirrer-Fan Turntable Removal
new_elements: Rotating waveguide stirrer (A moving metal stirrer spreads the microwaves so the food heats evenly without a turntable.)
rationale: With no turntable to load, the user only places food in the oven, and that is all there is to do.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are standard in many ovens and removing the turntable slightly simplifies loading, but the gain is minor and the idea is not radical.

title: Frozen-Meal Drive-Through Hatch
new_elements: Single-action hatch (A hatch in the side lets a meal slide in and out, with a single cycle that runs automatically.)
rationale: A student can put a meal in and take it out with no decisions in between.
judge_comment: A single automatic cycle with a pass-through hatch removes decisions, which strongly serves the need, though it needs automatic meal detection and shielding.

title: Stick-On Heat Label
new_elements: Thermochromic reheat sticker (A label on the plate changes colour when the food is hot enough.)
rationale: The plate reports its own state, so users read a colour instead of reading a timer.
judge_comment: A thermochromic indicator replaces timer reading with a simple colour cue, though it does not simplify starting the oven and is limited in heat accuracy.

title: Egg-Timer Ring Dial
new_elements: Ring-timer dial (A ring of coloured segments shows time left, with one turn to add time.)
rationale: Colour segments are read instantly and one turn adds time, with no numbers to learn.
judge_comment: Egg-timer style dial is intuitive and cheap, but mechanical timer dials already exist on microwaves, so it isn't radical.

title: Stackable Pod Oven
new_elements: Pod cooking chamber (Each pod is a sealed meal chamber that the oven heats, with no settings.)
rationale: The meal chamber defines the cooking so the oven has nothing for the user to set.
judge_comment: Sealed meal pods remove all settings, but they require a pod ecosystem and the heating mechanism is vague.

title: Glowing Ring Status
new_elements: Colour-ring status light (A ring of light changes from red to green to show whether the oven is heating.)
rationale: Red means wait and green means ready, a signal that needs no manual.
judge_comment: A color status ring is easy to build and intuitive, though it is a common pattern and only covers feedback, not input.

title: Memory Repeat Button
new_elements: Remember last cook (Stores the last successful cook and repeats it on one press.)
rationale: Most users reheat the same things, so the machine learns them and the user never sets anything.
judge_comment: Practical and easy to use, but it isn't a substitution or radical, and it fails on the first use of any new food.

title: Counter Projection
new_elements: Counter projector (Projects the cooking status and buttons onto the counter in front of the machine.)
rationale: Controls appear where the user is already looking, with no panel to study.
judge_comment: Projected controls put the interface where the user is looking, but glare, cost, and the need for touch sensing make them less practical.

title: Pop-Sound Doneness
new_elements: Acoustic doneness detect (Listens for popping, bubbling, or silence to decide when food is done.)
rationale: The machine judges doneness by sound, so the user doesn't need to time anything.
judge_comment: Acoustic doneness sensing removes timing entirely and popcorn-style detection is proven, but generalizing to other foods is hard and the idea doesn't say how cooking starts.

title: Pet-Like Reactions
new_elements: Expressive face display (A small face on the door that smiles when food is ready and frowns if the door is open.)
rationale: A face is understood without any manual, so status is clear to anyone.
judge_comment: A face display is easy to build and understood by anyone, but it only communicates status and doesn't simplify operating the controls.

title: Weight-scale auto power
new_elements: Load-cell turntable scale (Weighs the food and picks the power level from mass and density.)
rationale: Power is chosen by the machine from the weight placed on the turntable, so the user has nothing to set.
judge_comment: A load-cell scale that picks power automatically removes settings, but weight alone is a weak proxy for the food type and the heating needed.

title: Auto-eject door at end
new_elements: Spring-loaded door eject (Door pops open a few centimetres when cooking finishes.)
rationale: The machine opens itself, so the user never has to remember to press a release.
judge_comment: A spring eject at the end is simple and plausible, and it reduces one step, but it does not address how to start or set cooking.

title: Sliding drawer cavity
new_elements: Sliding drawer front with RF seal (A drawer that slides out on rails, with the RF seal at the sliding gap.)
rationale: A pull-out drawer is understood by anyone and works with no swing or latch to learn.
judge_comment: A drawer is highly intuitive, and a radical substitute for a swing door, but the RF seal at the sliding gap is hard to engineer.

title: Lift-up lid like a laptop
new_elements: Top-hinged lid with gas strut (Lid lifts straight up on a gas strut, with the window facing the user.)
rationale: Lifting an obvious lid needs no instruction, and it stays open without a hand.
judge_comment: A lid that lifts up is intuitive and stays open hands-free, which helps ease of use, and a gas strut is a feasible, concrete part.

title: Cavity mode-stirrer fan
new_elements: Rotating metal mode-stirrer (A small metal stirrer in the cavity scatters the field, replacing the turntable.)
rationale: A flat, empty plate that needs no loading or alignment is simpler to use.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves and a flat plate does slightly ease use, though it is not a radical idea.

title: Bubble-breaker rod for milk
new_elements: Dielectric nucleation rod (Small ceramic rod placed in the cup that prevents superheated liquid from erupting.)
rationale: The user drops in a rod and heats safely with no settings or fear of boiling over.
judge_comment: A ceramic nucleation rod plausibly prevents superheating and removes a safety worry, though it is an extra item the user has to remember and it covers only liquids.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Turntable load-cell weight sensor (Strain gauges under the glass tray estimate food mass and select time and power automatically.)
rationale: The user places food on the tray and presses one button, with no need to know times or power levels.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto settings cut the need for user input, though mass alone doesn't identify the food type and load cells in a microwave add cost and have to cope with the environment.

title: Food-Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Pictogram selector ring (A ring with icons (milk, bread, frozen, popcorn) replaces numeric power steps.)
rationale: Users choose by recognising the food rather than translating a power number into a result.
judge_comment: Pictogram selection is intuitive and easy to build, but it is already common on appliances.

title: Voice-Named Cooking
new_elements: Far-field voice microphone array (Recognises plain requests such as warm my milk and sets the cycle.)
rationale: Users state what they want in their own words, so no panel layout has to be learned.
judge_comment: Voice control directly removes the need to learn a panel and is plausible, but voice-controlled microwaves already exist.

title: Hip-Bump Open
new_elements: Proximity-triggered latch release (Capacitive sensing unlatches the door when a hand or hip approaches the door face.)
rationale: Users with full hands can open the door without finding a small button.
judge_comment: Proximity door opening is easy and convenient but only addresses opening, not the core operation of setting the cooking cycle.

title: Hourglass Progress Window
new_elements: Electrochromic glass progress band (A band on the door glass darkens from one side to the other as cooking progresses.)
rationale: Progress is shown as a fill level, which everyone understands without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A visual fill-level progress band is intuitive feedback, but it helps with monitoring rather than the operation itself, and electrochromic glass in a microwave door is awkward.

title: Spoken Ready Message
new_elements: Small speech synthesiser (Says The food is ready when cooking finishes.)
rationale: The machine tells the user in plain words what has happened, so no code of beeps has to be learned.
judge_comment: A spoken message is easy to understand and highly feasible, but talking appliances already exist and the idea isn't radical.

title: Stirring Field, No Turntable
new_elements: Rotating mode-stirrer fan (A metal paddle inside the cavity stirs the field so food heats evenly wherever it sits.)
rationale: Users no longer need to centre a dish or know that it must rotate, so placement is never a question.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already standard in many microwaves, so this is feasible but not new, and it only removes the placement concern.

title: Lift-Lid Cavity
new_elements: Gas-strut lift-up lid (The whole top opens like a rice-cooker lid and holds itself open with a gas strut.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is a gesture everyone already knows, so no door mechanism needs explaining.
