judge_comment: A top-opening lid with a gas strut is a familiar gesture and is concrete, but it raises RF-seal, spill and usability problems for a cavity that is hard to see into.

title: Wave-to-Start Air Gesture
new_elements: Infrared gesture recogniser (A wave of the hand in front of the door starts or stops the cycle.)
rationale: A wave is a universal gesture, so there is no panel to find and no operation to memorise.
judge_comment: A wave to start is intuitive and plausible with cheap IR sensors, but stopping and starting without choosing time or power leaves the real operation unresolved and risks false triggers.

title: Thermal Doneness Coin
new_elements: Passive thermochromic doneness coin (A disposable coin placed on food changes colour when the food is hot enough.)
rationale: A plain colour change says the food is ready, so the user needs no timer knowledge.
judge_comment: A thermochromic coin is a creative, simple doneness cue, but it does not replace the controls and can't signal heating state well in a microwave.

title: Slot-Feed Cooking
new_elements: Drop-in slot feed tray (Food slides in through a slot like a toaster and is cooked on a conveyor.)
rationale: Putting food in a slot needs no door, tray or placement decisions, which matches a toaster's familiarity.
judge_comment: A toaster-like slot with a conveyor is radical and familiar to use, but containment of microwaves, liquids and varied foods is hard.

title: Fridge-Style Auto-Start
new_elements: Door-open auto-light and auto-stop (Opening the door stops cooking; closing it resumes cooking from where it stopped.)
rationale: Opening and closing behave as the user expects from a fridge, so no pause or resume button is needed.
judge_comment: Pause-on-open and resume-on-close already exist in most microwaves, so it is easy to build but not novel; it does remove the need for resume steps.

title: Tray-Counted Cooking
new_elements: Tap-to-count ring light (A ring around the tray lights up in steps to show remaining time.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown as lit segments that need no reading or setting.
judge_comment: A ring light showing remaining time is intuitive and easy to build, though it covers only the display and not input.

title: Ask-the-Cook Companion
new_elements: On-device conversational guide (A small speaker helps users pick a setting by answering simple questions about their food.)
rationale: The machine guides the user through each choice in plain language, which removes the need to learn settings.
judge_comment: A conversational guide removes the need to learn settings and is technically plausible, though voice assistants in appliances already exist and noisy kitchens can hurt reliability.

title: Hunger-Shaped Dial With Food Pictograms
new_elements: Pictogram ring with four detents (Ring showing a bowl, a plate, a bread slice, and an ice cube.); Selects a food preset by picture (Each picture maps to a tested power and time.)
rationale: Pictures replace numbers and duty-cycle labels, so the user chooses by what they are eating.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is cheap, simple and easy to build, but it is incremental and offers only coarse choices.

title: Camera Doneness Watcher
new_elements: Ceiling camera with infrared lens (Watches food through a cavity-safe lens and sees browning or steam.); Computer-vision doneness model (Classifies food state from images.)
rationale: The machine watches the food so the user never needs to guess the time.
judge_comment: Removes the need to set time entirely, but a camera in a microwave cavity is hard to build and is not a cheaper substitute.

title: Fill-To-Set Water Cup
new_elements: Measuring cup input tray (Fill cup to a line; the line sets the cooking program.); Sets power and time from fill volume (Volume in the cup is mapped to a cook recipe.)
rationale: Filling a container to a line is a familiar kitchen action that replaces a technical power setting.
judge_comment: Fill-line-to-program is intuitive, but volume is a poor proxy for many foods and the mapping is limited.

title: Dial-Less Gesture Field
new_elements: Short-range radar gesture sensor (Detects a hand wave and a palm hold from the front face.); mmWave gesture recognition (Recognises a small set of hand gestures.)
rationale: A wave starts cooking and a palm stops it, so there is no physical control to find or misread.
judge_comment: A radar gesture sensor is plausible and concrete, but wave-to-start gives no way to set time or power, and gestures themselves must be learned.

title: Ring-Around-Door Dial
new_elements: Rotary ring around the door frame (A large ring that the user turns clockwise to add time.)
rationale: A big ring is easy to grip and turn, and the rotation direction matches the familiar clock sense.
judge_comment: A big door-ring dial is intuitive and cheap to build, and it is a moderately fresh take on the control.

title: Three Words, Not Numbers
new_elements: Three-word power selector (Embossed words Gentle, Normal, Hot replace the five-step numeric cam)
rationale: Plain words are understood immediately, so the user never has to work out what power level 3 means.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap substitution, but a minor tweak that still requires choices and is not radical.

title: Push-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Magnetic push-to-open latch (Light press on any part of the door releases it with a spring and magnet)
rationale: Users never have to find a specific button, so the door just opens wherever they push.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build, but it only helps with opening the door, which is a small part of operating the microwave.

title: Stirrer Instead of Spin
new_elements: Metal mode-stirrer fan (Rotating metal vane inside the waveguide mixes the field so the food can stay still)
rationale: The food never moves, so there is no tray to misplace or align.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves and remove the turntable, which simplifies use modestly but is not radical.

title: Tap-to-Melt Butter Tray
new_elements: Single-press soften mode (Pressing the butter icon softens butter for cake baking with no setting)
rationale: A dedicated icon for softening butter removes the guesswork that baking tasks normally need.
judge_comment: A one-press butter-soften preset is simple and workable, but it's a preset button rather than a radical substitution.

title: Fused Fascia Single Molding
new_elements: Single-shot injection-molded fascia (One molded part forms the whole control panel with embossed controls)
rationale: A simple, sealed panel has no gaps to clean and no extra parts for the user to worry about.
judge_comment: A sealed molded panel with embossed controls is simple and easy to clean, but it is an incremental substitution with modest effect on learning curve.

title: Weigh-to-Power Mat
new_elements: Load-cell cooking mat (A flat plate under the turntable that weighs the food and sets time and power from its mass.)
rationale: Placing food on the mat is the only action needed, because the machine works out the rest from weight.
judge_comment: Weight-based automation removes all inputs, but weight alone poorly predicts the cooking needs of different foods, and a load cell under a rotating turntable is difficult to build.

title: Tap-Glass to Open
new_elements: Vibration tap detection (An accelerometer in the door detects two taps on the glass and releases the latch.)
rationale: Tapping the glass is an instinctive gesture that needs no searching for a button.
judge_comment: Tapping glass to open is intuitive and specific, but a double-tap is a gesture to learn and could be set off by accident.

title: Sliding Block Counter
new_elements: Stackable time blocks (Each block is one minute; the user places blocks on a tray and they drop off as time passes.)
rationale: Counting physical blocks is concrete and needs no reading of numbers.
judge_comment: Tangible minute blocks that drop off as time passes are intuitive and novel, though the mechanism is clunky and limits power control.

title: Packaging Reads Settings
new_elements: Packet code reader (The microwave reads a code printed on ready-meal packs and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: The food packaging carries the settings, so the user only places the pack and presses start.
judge_comment: Reading codes from packaging is plausible and cuts steps (similar products exist), but it only works for coded ready meals.

title: Tap-to-Cook Tray
new_elements: NFC cooking tray (A tray with a chip that tells the microwave the food's settings when placed inside.)
rationale: Placing the tray is the only action, so no settings need to be chosen.
judge_comment: An NFC tray is feasible and needs one action, but it requires special trays tied to specific foods, which limits its use.

title: Single Start Pad
new_elements: One large start pad (A single pad that starts a cycle chosen automatically from what the camera sees on the turntable.)
rationale: One pad is the entire interface, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single pad is the simplest possible interface, but it relies on camera recognition being reliable and it has no override.

title: Heat Gauge Slider
new_elements: Thermometer slider (A vertical slider with a red-to-blue gauge that fills up to show the heat level.)
rationale: A gauge filling up is read as intensity with no numbers.
judge_comment: A numberless gauge slider is intuitive and replaces the numeric keypad, though a heat level alone leaves time unaddressed.

title: Glow-Ring Countdown
new_elements: Shrinking light ring (A glowing ring around the plate that shrinks as cooking goes on and vanishes at the end.)
rationale: A ring that visibly shrinks shows progress from across the room.
judge_comment: A shrinking light ring is an intuitive progress display that replaces the digits, but it shows only progress and not input.

title: Stationary Cavity Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Mode stirrer fan (A rotating metal vane spreads microwaves so the turntable is not needed.)
rationale: Removing the glass plate means nothing can be misplaced or lifted off its track.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, so this is feasible but not novel, and it only modestly reduces the operating burden.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (The cavity is a drawer that slides out toward the user with the food on a flat tray.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer out brings the food to the user without reaching into a hot cavity.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist and are intuitive to use, but the drawer does not remove the need for controls, so it helps the learning curve only slightly.

title: Bounce-Back Tab Door
new_elements: Spring tab release (A tab at the door edge that springs the door open a few centimetres when pressed.)
rationale: A door that opens a little on its own is a clear cue that it has released.
judge_comment: A spring-release door is simple and familiar, and the cue that it has released is helpful, though it is incremental.

title: Knock-to-Open Door
new_elements: Acoustic knock sensor (A microphone detects a knock on the door and releases the latch.)
rationale: A knock is a natural gesture that needs no button location.
judge_comment: Knocking to open is intuitive and needs no learning, but false triggers from noise and added cost are drawbacks.

title: Weigh-and-Go Tray
new_elements: Load-cell turntable sensor (The turntable measures mass and sets cook time from the weight alone.)
rationale: Mass is the only input needed, so the user never estimates minutes.
judge_comment: Load-cell weighing is a simple, feasible substitute for time entry, but weight alone poorly determines cook time across food types.

title: Spoken Status Oven
new_elements: Voice speaker (Speaks plain sentences such as Your soup is hot and Stop, it is ready.)
rationale: Clear spoken status removes the need to interpret a bell or a timer.
judge_comment: Spoken status is easy to build and helps understanding, but talking appliances already exist and it adds a part rather than substituting a simpler one.

title: Lean-to-Open Door
new_elements: Pressure-sensing door panel (Pushing the door anywhere opens it, with no button to find.)
rationale: Leaning on the door is a natural motion, so there is no button to locate.
judge_comment: Pushing the door open removes the need to find a button and is plausible, though accidental opening and safety interlocks need handling.

title: Stirring Antenna Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Mode stirrer (A rotating metal vane spreads microwaves evenly without any tray to place.)
rationale: With no turntable to fit, users place food anywhere and it heats evenly.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist and do remove the tray, which helps simplicity somewhat but is not radical.

title: Tap-to-Start Cup Coaster
new_elements: Infrared cup coaster (Placing a cup on the coaster heats it until the target temperature is reached.)
rationale: A single drop-and-go coaster asks no decisions from the user.
judge_comment: Drop-and-go heating coaster is very simple, but it only suits liquids in cups and 'infrared' heating of a cup's contents is questionable, so it replaces rather than serves the microwave's full role.

title: Fill-Line Mug Cook
new_elements: Fill-line mug sensor (Placing a mug with a fill line sets the cook time based on the liquid level.)
rationale: Pouring to a mark is a skill everyone already has, so no time guessing is needed.
judge_comment: Using a fill line to set time uses an intuitive action, though the sensor mechanism is vague and it is limited to liquids in special mugs.

title: Sliding Heat Ribbon
new_elements: Continuous heat slider (A slider from cold to hot with no numbered steps, showing a color gradient.)
rationale: A slider from cold to hot needs no numbers and maps naturally to intensity.
judge_comment: A continuous slider replaces numeric power/time entry intuitively and serves no-learning-curve operation, though it is a modest substitution.

title: Food-Weight Memory Plate
new_elements: Labelled food pads (Plates with printed food icons pair with the oven to set default cycles.)
rationale: Icons on a plate replace settings, so the user just matches picture to food.
judge_comment: Icon plates that pair with the oven replace settings with picture matching, directly reducing learning, though requires special dishware.

title: Printed Recipe Tray
new_elements: Printed cook-card slot (Insert a card printed with food and quantity to set the program.)
rationale: A paper card requires no setup and works with any kitchen.
judge_comment: A card slot that sets the program is simple to use and plausible, though it needs a card system and reader, and it loosely fits the substitute operator.

title: Food Token Dial
new_elements: Interchangeable food tokens (Shaped plastic tokens with pictures of food (soup, rice, bread) are slotted into a receptacle that sets the program.)
rationale: Matching a picture to a token is more intuitive than reading numbers on a dial.
judge_comment: Pictorial tokens are intuitive, but loose parts get lost and there is still a selection step to learn.

title: One-Power Pulse
new_elements: Adaptive pulse controller (A fixed power level is pulsed automatically by food type, so the user never picks a power.)
rationale: Removing the power choice altogether means there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Removing the power decision altogether is strongly aligned with no-learning-curve, though it needs food recognition or user input to pulse appropriately.

title: Solid-State GaN Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (A 2.45 GHz gallium-nitride amplifier replaces the magnetron and the high-voltage stack.)
rationale: Low-voltage operation removes the lethal-charge risk and the magnetron wear that drive user worry.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is concrete and radical, but it is mainly a safety and reliability change and barely affects ease of operation; cost is still high.

title: Glowing Edge Band
new_elements: Electroluminescent door-rim band (A glowing band around the door rim shows the cooking state in colour.)
rationale: A coloured rim is readable from across the kitchen and needs no reading.
judge_comment: A color-coded status rim is glanceable and needs no reading, which directly supports zero learning curve, though it is not really a substitution of a cheaper part.

title: Tap-to-Cook Tray
new_elements: Recessed NFC tray plate (A recess in the glass plate reads a single disk that tells the unit how long to cook.)
rationale: Placing a disk on the plate is the only action, so no settings are needed.
judge_comment: Placing a disk is simple and needs no settings, but the user must own and choose the right disk.

title: One-Button Infrared Cook
new_elements: Infrared surface sensor (Watches food surface temperature and ends cooking when it reaches the target.); Cook-until-done (Runs until the food is ready without a time setting.)
rationale: A single button with no numbers means nothing needs to be understood.
judge_comment: A single button with an IR sensor that cooks until done is simple, but IR reads only surface temperature and is unreliable for uneven heating.

title: Aroma-Stop Sensor
new_elements: Volatile gas sensor (Detects the rise in steam aroma and stops heating at the right moment.); Stop on smell (Ends cooking when the food is ready, judged by its smell.)
rationale: Users never need to guess a time because the machine uses the same cue they do.
judge_comment: Stopping on aroma is an intuitive and fairly novel substitute for a timer, but gas sensing in a microwave cavity is hard to make reliable.

title: Single Plain-Word Panel
new_elements: One-word display (Shows only the words READY or COOKING, with one large button.); Show only one word (All state is reduced to one word in plain language.)
rationale: A single word removes any sense of a control panel to learn.
judge_comment: A one-button, one-word interface is very easy to use and simple to build, but it is not radical and offers little cooking control.

title: Stone-Warmer Plate
new_elements: Heated ceramic plate (Cooks food by heat conduction from a warm plate that is switched on by setting food on it.); Heat by placing (Cooking starts when food is placed on the plate.)
rationale: Placing food on a plate is the only action required.
judge_comment: Placing food to start cooking removes all learning, but conduction heating from a plate is not microwave cooking and would be slow and uneven.

title: Hot Sticker Pictograms
new_elements: Pictogram sticker reader (Uses stickers showing a picture of the dish to start the matching program.); Start by picture (Placing a dish picture on the door starts its program.)
rationale: Pictures of dishes replace numbers and are understood at any age or language.
judge_comment: Picture stickers that start programs are intuitive and language-free, and RFID or camera reading is plausible, though the stickers add handling.

title: Auto-Release Door Catch
new_elements: Passive door latch (A magnetic latch that releases when the door is pulled, with no button.); Open by pull (The door opens by pulling its handle.)
rationale: Pulling a handle is the same as opening any cupboard, so there is nothing new to learn.
judge_comment: A pull-open magnetic latch is very easy and feasible, but it only covers door opening and is not new.

title: Cube Heater Bowl
new_elements: Heated cube bowl (A bowl that is itself the heater, so the whole machine is just the bowl.); Cook in the bowl (Food is cooked in the bowl the user already uses.)
rationale: Using the bowl you already have leaves nothing new to learn.
judge_comment: Radical, with no new interface to learn, but a heated bowl isn't a microwave and the user's own bowl can't be the heater, so it's technically murky.

title: Hot-Food Fidget Dial
new_elements: Spin-to-pick dial (A dial that spins freely and clicks through the dishes as it is turned.); Pick dish by spinning (A spin selects the dish, which is then confirmed by pressing.)
rationale: Spinning is a playful motion that is easy to repeat until the right dish appears.
judge_comment: A clicking dish-selection dial with press-to-confirm is simple and easy to build, but it resembles existing rotary controls and is barely radical.

title: Chime-Free Clapper
new_elements: Clap-start sensor (Starts cooking with a clap and stops with a second clap.); Start and stop by clap (A clap controls the machine.)
rationale: Clapping is a universal action that works without finding or reading any control.
judge_comment: Clap start/stop is simple and intuitive, but it is prone to false triggers and does not set cook time or power, so it only partly replaces the controls.

title: Snap-Fit Icon Keys
new_elements: Three-icon key set (Three physical keys with icons for reheat, cook and defrost.); Use icon keys (The user presses the icon matching the job.)
rationale: Three icons remove any need to understand power levels or settings.
judge_comment: Simple and effective for no learning curve, but a modest, fairly obvious substitution of dials with icon keys.

title: Dinner-Bell Melody
new_elements: Melody announcer (Plays a short tune that rises in tempo as the food nears completion.); Announce by melody (Progress is announced through a tune.)
rationale: A tune that speeds up needs no reading and is easy to notice from another room.
judge_comment: A tempo-rising tune is easy to build and understand, but it only announces progress and does not simplify the main operation of setting the microwave.

title: Pictogram Dial Replacing Numbers
new_elements: Food-picture dial (One dial whose positions show pictures of soup, bread, leftovers and popcorn instead of numbers.)
rationale: Users choose by recognising the food rather than interpreting minutes and power percentages.
judge_comment: A picture dial is simple and cheap and easy to learn, but it is an incremental, familiar approach rather than a radical one.

title: Tap-the-Picture Touchscreen
new_elements: Large-icon touch panel (A panel with four large photos of common foods that starts the cycle on tap.)
rationale: A single tap on a recognisable photo gives an immediate result with no menus to navigate.
judge_comment: Highly intuitive and easy to build, but picture-based touch panels already exist and four foods limit flexibility and power/time control.

title: Proximity Door Opener
new_elements: Capacitive proximity door latch (The door unlatches when a hand approaches, with a spring pushing it slightly open.)
rationale: The door responds to an approaching hand, so the user never has to find the release point.
judge_comment: A capacitive latch with a spring-assist is concrete and workable, but it only fixes door opening, not operation, and risks accidental opening.

title: Thermocouple Probe Finish
new_elements: Heat-sensing probe (A probe is inserted into the food and stops cooking at a set temperature.)
rationale: Stopping on temperature means the user never has to judge done-ness.
judge_comment: Probe-based cooking already exists in ovens and some microwaves, so it is plausible but not novel, and users still must insert a probe and set a temperature.

title: Fixed Power, Smart Pulse Rhythm
new_elements: Adaptive pulse controller (The firmware picks an on/off rhythm for each food type, so the user never sees a power setting.)
rationale: Hiding power selection in firmware removes the need to choose any level.
judge_comment: Hiding power levels in firmware simplifies use, but without food sensing the firmware cannot know the food type, so how it chooses a rhythm is unclear.

title: Two-State Gentle or Full Switch
new_elements: Gentle/Full slider (A slider with only two positions, Gentle and Full, mapped to fixed duty cycles.)
rationale: Two options are easier to understand than five, with no meaningless middle steps.
judge_comment: A two-position slider is very simple and buildable but is an incremental reduction of options rather than a radical idea.

title: Smiley Face Power Control
new_elements: Expression power dial (The power dial shows a smile for gentle heating and a grin for strong heating.)
rationale: Facial expressions carry meaning across languages and literacy levels.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and build, but facial icons for power levels are somewhat ambiguous and not radical.

title: Drop-Down Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (The cavity slides out like a drawer, with food placed on a tray.)
rationale: Drawers are familiar objects, so the user loads food the way they open a kitchen drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar mechanism and a genuinely different form, though it brings microwave sealing and mechanical complexity challenges.

title: Microwave-Free Food Tray
new_elements: Microwave-absorbing susceptor film (A film in the food tray absorbs microwaves and heats food directly.)
rationale: Packaging does the heating work, so the machine's controls can be fewer.
judge_comment: Susceptor film is a real, proven technology that is already widely used, so it is plausible but not new, and it only slightly simplifies controls.

title: Light-Pulse Done Indicator
new_elements: Pulsing done light (The cavity light pulses slowly when food is ready and stays still while cooking.)
rationale: A pulsing light is an obvious signal that needs no reading of numbers or sounds.
judge_comment: A pulsing light is cheap and easy to build and gives a clear done signal, but it only covers one small part of operation and is not radical.

title: Lid-Open Auto-Pause
new_elements: Door-open auto-pause sensor (Opening the door pauses cooking and resumes it when the door closes, with no restart needed.)
rationale: Opening the door is intuitive and safe, so users never have to remember to restart.
judge_comment: Microwaves already pause when the door opens, and auto-resume is a small convenience that is easy to build, with some safety concerns.

title: One-Dial Context Cooking
new_elements: Single context-aware dial (One detented dial whose position is interpreted by a small MCU as a food category, replacing separate timer and power knobs.)
rationale: A single dial with food-category presets removes the need to understand two independent numeric controls.
judge_comment: Simple and buildable, but the dial still needs some learning for categories and is an incremental simplification rather than radical.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable weighing (Strain gauges under the turntable estimate food mass and set time automatically.)
rationale: Users place food and press start, so no timer setting is needed.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time is truly zero-setting, though mass alone poorly predicts cook time and the load cell adds cost and heat/RF challenges.

title: Spoken One-Word Cooking
new_elements: Offline keyword recognition (A tiny on-device speech model recognises a few words such as warm, defrost and ready.)
rationale: Speaking a single word needs no reading, which suits elderly and visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Single-word voice control is accessible and feasible offline, though noise and discoverability of the vocabulary limit it.

title: Door Ring Progress Light
new_elements: Colour LED door ring (A ring of LEDs around the door that fills as cooking progresses and turns green when done.)
rationale: A progress ring shows status at a glance without the user needing to interpret anything.
judge_comment: A clear and feasible status display, but it covers only progress and not operation, and similar indicators already exist.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Push-to-open magnetic latch (A magnetic latch that opens when the door is pressed anywhere along its edge.)
rationale: Pressing the door opens it, so no one needs to search for a release button.
judge_comment: Push-to-open latches are proven and intuitive, replacing the button simply, but it is more incremental than radical.

title: Magnetic Snap Hinge
new_elements: Magnetic detent hinge (Magnets hold the door open or shut at set angles with no spring.)
rationale: The door holds where you leave it, so it never drifts or slams.
judge_comment: A magnetic detent door is simple, plausible and gives intuitive door behaviour, so it is the idea most related to ease of use, though the gain is small.

title: Pre-Portioned Meal Pods
new_elements: Sealed meal pod (A sealed single-serve pod with a built-in cook program, placed in a small cavity.)
rationale: A single pod removes portioning and programming, which suits students who just want to eat.
judge_comment: Pods with built-in cook programs remove programming entirely and strongly serve zero-learning use, though they need a pod ecosystem and substitute a whole usage model.

title: Power Level by Picture
new_elements: Picture-tile selector (Three large tiles showing an egg, a bowl of soup, and a loaf of bread.); Maps food picture to power curve (Each tile loads a fixed power profile.)
rationale: The five-step knob becomes three pictures, so the choice is obvious.
judge_comment: Picture tiles make power choice intuitive and are cheap to build, but the idea is incremental and not radical.

title: Pogo-Pin Magnetic Dock
new_elements: Magnetic pogo-pin base (Magnetically aligned base that couples to the oven and cuts power when lifted.); Self-aligning power connection (The oven clicks onto its base and never needs a plug.)
rationale: Placing the oven on its base is the only connection step, with no plug to fumble.
judge_comment: A magnetic dock with auto power cut-off is plausible and removes plug fumbling, though it only touches one small part of operation.

title: Popcorn Pop-Stop
new_elements: Pop-rate microphone (Microphone that counts the pop rate and stops when it slows.); Stops when popping slows (Automatically ends the popcorn cycle without a timer.)
rationale: The popcorn tells the machine when to stop, so the user never guesses.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection is proven and simple, but it applies to one food only and exists in some products.

title: Dial-Free Preset Dish
new_elements: Dish-shaped button (Single large button shaped like a plate.); One press cooks the dish (Pressing the plate runs the stored recipe.)
rationale: One big button means no choices at all, which is the simplest interface possible.
judge_comment: One-press operation has no learning curve, but a single stored recipe limits usefulness and it isn't very radical.

title: Thermal Shutter Door
new_elements: Shape-memory alloy shutter (Metal shutter that closes over the vent when the cavity overheats.); Self-closing vent (Vent that shuts itself without a thermostat.)
rationale: The vent protects itself, so the user never needs to watch for overheating.
judge_comment: Clever passive safety mechanism with a named material, but it has little bearing on ease of operation.

title: Autonomous Power Ramp
new_elements: Ramps power by food temperature (Power rises and falls as the food heats.); Adaptive power controller (Controller that adjusts the power curve itself.)
rationale: The machine chooses the power itself, so the user never sets a level.
judge_comment: Removes the need to choose power levels, directly serving no-learning-curve, though sensing food temperature inside a microwave is hard and the mechanism is vague.

title: Timer Replaced by Doneness Icon
new_elements: Doneness slider (Slider from raw to done that sets the end point.); Sets end point by doneness (The user slides the food from raw to done.)
rationale: Users choose how done they want the food instead of how many minutes to cook it.
judge_comment: Replacing the timer with a doneness slider removes the need to know cooking times, which is a strong fit for the need, but sensing doneness reliably is hard.

title: Auto-Power Mode
new_elements: Adaptive duty cycle (Chooses power level from food moisture and mass without user input.)
rationale: Removing the choice of power level removes the most confusing setting.
judge_comment: Removing the power setting simplifies use, but sensing moisture and mass reliably is hard and the mechanism is vague.

title: Target Temperature Dial
new_elements: Infrared food thermometer (Reads the surface temperature of food.); Heats food to a target temperature (Dial sets a temperature, not a power.)
rationale: Setting a temperature like an oven is easier to grasp than a power percentage.
judge_comment: An IR-sensed temperature dial is intuitive and substitutes power with a familiar concept, though surface-only readings limit accuracy.

title: Voice-only cooking
new_elements: Microphone and speech recogniser (User says 'reheat coffee' and the oven sets time and power itself.)
rationale: Replaces dials with a plain spoken request, so no controls need to be learned.
judge_comment: Voice control removes the need to learn dials, but it is already on the market and does not substitute a cheaper or simpler part, and it can fail in noisy kitchens.

title: Glowing floor path
new_elements: Light-strip status ring (A low-power LED ring around the base shows progress in colour.)
rationale: Colour states such as green for ready are read at a glance, with no manual to decode.
judge_comment: An LED status ring is easy to build and read at a glance, but colour meanings still need learning and it doesn't simplify input.

title: Sound-based status
new_elements: Spoken status voice (The oven announces 'almost done' and 'stir now' in plain words.)
rationale: Feedback comes through speech, so the user does not need to read a display.
judge_comment: Spoken prompts are simple and cheap to implement and help guidance, but voice feedback is common and doesn't change how the oven is operated.

title: Door that opens on its own
new_elements: Spring-loaded door (Door pops open when the cycle ends, with a gentle click.)
rationale: The machine signals completion by opening itself, which removes a step.
judge_comment: Spring-loaded auto-open is simple and cheap and gives a clear done signal, but it covers only one step and is already common.

title: Cooking by colour
new_elements: Colour-coded tray (Each tray colour matches a preset power level printed on the oven.)
rationale: Matching colours replace reading numbers and percentages.
judge_comment: Colour-matched trays remove number reading, though tray detection and mapping need a sensing mechanism that isn't described.

title: Ever-locked safety
new_elements: Auto-lock magnetic latch (Door locks itself while running and unlocks when safe, with no user action.)
rationale: Safety happens automatically, so the user cannot make a mistake with it.
judge_comment: Automatic door locking is easy to build and removes a safety step, but microwaves already have interlocks and it barely eases operation.

title: Pre-portioned chamber
new_elements: Shaped cavity insert (Cavity shape guides food into the right spot with no positioning.)
rationale: The shape of the cavity does the placing, so there is no guesswork.
judge_comment: A shaped insert removes placement guesswork and is feasible, but it limits the range of food containers and does not address power or time settings.

title: Cook by touching the food
new_elements: Capacitive food sensor (The user touches the food package and the oven reads its properties.)
rationale: Touching the food is the only action needed, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Touch-to-cook is a very simple interaction, but a capacitive sensor can't reliably read food properties or cooking instructions through packaging.

title: Voice-Free Gesture Wave
new_elements: Infrared proximity sensing (Detects a hand wave near the door to open it.)
rationale: Waving at the door is a natural action that needs no finding of a button.
judge_comment: Wave-to-open is feasible with IR sensors and mildly useful, but it only covers opening and can trigger accidentally; the 'voice-free' label adds nothing.

title: Door That Opens Itself
new_elements: Spring-loaded self-opening door (Door pops open when the cook ends and a finished state is reached.)
rationale: The machine performs the opening step, so the user never has to work out how the door works.
judge_comment: A self-opening door is easy to make with a spring latch and saves one step, but it doesn't address how the cook is set up.

title: Food Speaks Its Status
new_elements: Spoken progress updates (Device announces what it is doing in plain language.)
rationale: Spoken status removes the need to read a dial or display to know what happens next.
judge_comment: Spoken updates help users follow progress but don't remove the need to set the cook, and they add a speaker rather than substituting a part.

title: Hand-Shaped Cavity Shelf
new_elements: Self-centering plate (Plate locks into place so food cannot be loaded wrongly.)
rationale: The shape forces the correct placement, so no instructions are needed.
judge_comment: A self-centering plate prevents misplacement, but placement is a minor part of the learning curve and the title's hand-shaped cavity is unclear.

title: Snap-On Cook Modules
new_elements: Clip-in magnetron cartridge (Cartridges pre-set power for one job, such as popcorn or soup.)
rationale: Choosing a cartridge is a simpler act than adjusting power.
judge_comment: Concrete and a real substitution of the power control, but swappable magnetron cartridges are costly and impractical, and the user still has to pick the right cartridge.

title: Microwave as a Drawer
new_elements: Sliding drawer door (Pull the drawer and it opens with no button.)
rationale: A drawer is opened by a universal gesture everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A drawer is plausible, as such microwaves already exist, and it replaces the door latch and button with a familiar gesture, but it only simplifies opening, not cooking.

title: Cook Schedule Is Your Routine
new_elements: Learns daily habit (Device learns times the user usually cooks and offers them.)
rationale: The machine does the setting, so the user only confirms.
judge_comment: Learning habits lowers the setup burden and is technically plausible, but it is not a substitution of parts and the mechanism is thin.

title: Fridge Magnet Remote
new_elements: Magnetic one-button key (A magnet on the fridge starts the last cook.)
rationale: Tapping a fridge magnet is the simplest possible cook command.
judge_comment: A magnet-triggered repeat cook is simple and feasible, but it only covers the 'last cook' case and has little to do with substitution of parts.

title: Stick-On Power Label
new_elements: NFC food sticker (Stick on food to program cook settings with a phone tap.)
rationale: Setting the cook happens on the food, not on the appliance.
judge_comment: NFC stickers are plausible, but requiring a phone and stickers adds steps and works against zero learning.

title: Cook Button Is the Food Itself
new_elements: Touch-to-cook food tray (Touching the food on the tray starts a cook suited to it.)
rationale: The action happens where the user already points, with no separate control.
judge_comment: Touching food to start a cook is radical and removes controls, but detecting the food type and safely triggering it is hard and the mechanism is underspecified.

title: Bell Becomes a Tap
new_elements: Tap-to-finish plate (Device prompts the user with a touch pulse until they tap to stop.)
rationale: Ending the cook is a single tap, which is the simplest possible action.
judge_comment: Replacing the bell with a tap-to-stop plate is simple and feasible, but it only simplifies the end of the cook, not how the user sets it up.

title: Cooking Fuse Cord
new_elements: Burn-down fuse cord (A coloured cord burns or dissolves over a set time and trips the cut-off when it breaks.)
rationale: A cord with coloured zones is intuitive to read, and it stops cooking without any mechanical timing.
judge_comment: A burn-down fuse cord is a wild idea, but it is consumable, hard to make safe inside a microwave, and still requires the user to choose a time.

title: Inverter Continuous Heat
new_elements: Variable-frequency magnetron drive (Inverter drive gives continuous power control, replacing on/off cycling.)
rationale: Continuous power needs no power dial, because one heat setting gives the right result.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist, and while they improve results, the user still has to pick time and power, so the gain for a no-learning-curve goal is modest.

title: Defrost-Only Mode
new_elements: Single-step defrost by weight (Defrost runs automatically from load-cell weight, with no user choice of power.)
rationale: Most users only defrost or reheat, so one automatic defrost mode covers the common case with no settings.
judge_comment: Automatic defrost by weight is workable and simple, but it covers only one use case and does not replace a general interface.

title: Push-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Push-to-open door catch (Pressing anywhere on the door face releases a spring catch and the door swings open.)
rationale: Users need not find a small button, because the whole door face is the control.
judge_comment: Easy to use and very feasible, but it only simplifies door opening and is an incremental change that already exists on some appliances.

title: Motion-Approach Opener
new_elements: Proximity sensing (An infrared sensor unlatches the door when a hand or plate approaches within a few centimetres.)
rationale: The door responds to the approach of the user, so there is no button or latch to locate.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening is plausible, but accidental triggers are a risk and it leaves the rest of the operation (setting time and power) untouched.

title: Auto-Eject Door
new_elements: Spring-assist door eject (A spring pushes the door partly open when cooking ends and the lock releases.)
rationale: The door opens by itself when the food is done, so the user never has to work out how to get it out.
judge_comment: A simple spring eject is cheap and workable, but it only addresses the end of the cycle and is not very radical.

title: Drawer-Front Oven
new_elements: Sliding drawer front (The whole front slides out like a drawer on runners with a fixed handle.)
rationale: A drawer is an everyday motion, so the user pulls it out as they would a kitchen drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer motion is familiar and intuitive and the concept is distinctive, though sealing and radiation containment in a sliding front add engineering difficulty.

title: Cavity Flash Cue
new_elements: Cavity light flash (The interior lamp flashes three times when cooking ends and then stays on.)
rationale: Reusing the existing lamp as the end signal needs no new part and is seen from across the room.
judge_comment: Feasible and a true substitution of the lamp for a beeper, but it only covers the end signal and is hardly radical.

title: Voice Says Yes
new_elements: Yes-or-no voice dialogue (The oven asks Warm or Cook and the user answers yes or no.)
rationale: A yes-or-no question is the simplest possible interaction for a user who has never used a microwave.
judge_comment: A yes/no dialogue is very low-barrier, but it needs speech recognition and gives only coarse control over cooking.

title: Food-Shaped Oven
new_elements: Single-purpose reheat box (A fixed-programme oven that only reheats one pre-packed meal type.)
rationale: With one job and no controls, there is nothing to learn at all.
judge_comment: A fixed-programme single-meal oven would need no learning, but it is very limiting and the substitution is vague.

title: Glass Turntable Vanish
new_elements: Static ceramic plate (A fixed plate with a built-in stirring field replaces the turntable.)
rationale: No turntable means nothing to fit, clean, or reposition, so the user has one fewer step.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable saves a cleaning and fitting step, but it only slightly reduces the learning needed.

title: Snap-On Door Handle
new_elements: Magnetic handle grip (A large handle snaps on with magnets and opens the door when pulled.)
rationale: A large, obvious grip is found at once and gives an older user a firm hold to open the door.
judge_comment: A large magnetic handle is feasible and easy to find, but it is an incremental change that only helps with opening the door.

title: Dome Lid Microwave
new_elements: Top-loading dome oven (The oven opens from the top like a lid, so food is placed from above.)
rationale: A lid that lifts like a bread bin is a familiar motion and keeps the food visible from above.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid is a familiar motion and fairly novel, but the link to simple operation is moderate and it raises safety and shielding concerns.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door Release
new_elements: Capacitive touch sensing (Detects a hand on the door face without any moving button.); Opens door on any touch (Releases the latch when the user touches the door panel.)
rationale: No one has to find a small button, because any part of the door opens it.
judge_comment: Makes opening easy, but accidental opening is a risk and it addresses only a small part of operation.

title: Self-Opening Door on Completion
new_elements: Spring-assisted door hinge (Hinge with a spring that pushes the door open at the end of a cycle.); Presents finished food (Opens the door so the food is ready to take out.)
rationale: The machine signals completion by itself opening, which needs no reading or interpretation.
judge_comment: A spring-open door is easy to build and gives an intuitive completion signal, but it does not help with setup or starting.

title: Interior Progress Projection
new_elements: Interior light projector (Micro projector that shows a progress ring on the turntable.); Shows remaining time visually (Displays how much cooking time is left as a shrinking ring.)
rationale: A shrinking ring needs no reading of digits and works for any age or language.
judge_comment: A projected progress ring is intuitive and unusual, but it only shows status and does nothing to simplify input; it is also hard to see on food and the turntable.

title: Door Window as OLED Countdown
new_elements: Transparent OLED door panel (See-through OLED layer bonded to the door glass.); Displays large countdown (Shows a big, simple countdown on the door window.)
rationale: A large single number on the door is the only display a user needs.
judge_comment: A transparent OLED on the door gives a clear, big countdown, but it is costly, hard to make heat- and RF-tolerant, and not really a simplification.

title: Automatic Pulse Defrost
new_elements: Automatically pulses frozen food (Detects frozen food and cycles power without a defrost setting.)
rationale: Defrost happens automatically, so the user never needs to find a defrost setting.
judge_comment: Directly removes a confusing setting, but detecting frozen food and automating pulsing is vaguely specified and not truly a substitution of a part.

title: Magnetic Self-Closing Latch
new_elements: Magnetic latch (Magnet pair that holds the door closed without springs or levers.)
rationale: A door that closes itself and stays shut needs no effort or attention.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch is simple and plausible and slightly eases door use, but it is incremental and not radical.

title: Sliding Drawer Door
new_elements: Sliding drawer front (Front panel that slides sideways on rails.)
rationale: A drawer is already understood by everyone, so it needs no learning.
judge_comment: A familiar drawer metaphor is intuitive, though sealing microwave leakage on a sliding front is a challenge.

title: Edible Cooking Tray
new_elements: Edible starch tray (Disposable tray made of edible starch that replaces the glass plate.)
rationale: There is no plate to load, wash or put back, so the cycle is just place and go.
judge_comment: Removes the plate handling step and is a fun substitute, though a disposable tray adds cost and does not simplify controls.

title: Tap-Rhythm Timer
new_elements: Sets time by tapping door (Each tap adds one second, so short times are easy to enter.)
rationale: Tapping is an intuitive physical gesture, which replaces the imprecise dial for short times.
judge_comment: Tapping the door to add seconds is an intuitive gesture, but it is tedious for longer times and adds little for a user who has never used a microwave.

title: Sound-Free Start Feedback
new_elements: Confirms start with light pulse (A single soft light pulse confirms that cooking has begun.)
rationale: A pulse of light is a plain, universal confirmation that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A light pulse confirming start gives clear feedback at low cost, but it is incremental and does not simplify the controls.

title: Shared Smart Speaker Interface
new_elements: Smart speaker link (Speaker-based control that accepts simple requests.)
rationale: A student asks in plain words and never needs the appliance manual.
judge_comment: Voice control removes the need to learn the interface, but it is vague and adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Ceramic Stacking Tray
new_elements: Stackable ceramic tray (Tray shape that clicks onto the platform in only one way.)
rationale: The tray can only fit one way, so there is no wrong placement to learn.
judge_comment: A keyed tray that fits only one way is mistake-proof and concrete, but it is a modest improvement that doesn't touch the main controls.

title: Auto-Sense Dome
new_elements: Infrared food-state sensor array (Reads surface temperature and moisture to pick time and power automatically.); Infrared food-state sensing (Maps heat and moisture of the food to a cooking profile.)
rationale: The user never sets a time or power, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Fully automatic cooking removes all operation, but IR sensing of moisture and food state through a closed microwave is technically hard, and the two listed elements are redundant.

title: Snap-In Recipe Cartridge
new_elements: Keyed recipe cartridge (A plug-in cartridge that encodes power and time for one dish.)
rationale: Inserting a cartridge replaces every dial with a single physical action.
judge_comment: Cartridges are simple to use but add a cost and a purchase burden and limit flexibility, and they add parts rather than substituting cheaper ones.

title: Field-Steered Stirring
new_elements: Dual-source field steering (Two phase-shifted sources move hot spots around without any moving part.)
rationale: Even heating happens automatically, so the user never needs to turn or rotate the food.
judge_comment: Replaces the turntable with phase-shifted sources so no turning is needed, but it only loosely addresses operating simplicity and is costly and complex.

title: Press-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Full-face pressure panel (A broad front panel that releases the door when pressed anywhere on it.)
rationale: The user cannot miss the release, so no one has to search for a small button.
judge_comment: A broad press panel is easy to use and plausible, but it only simplifies door opening and is not very radical.

title: Magnetic Bump Latch
new_elements: Magnetic detent latch (Magnets hold the door closed and release it on a light push.)
rationale: A door that bumps open and shuts with a magnet needs no mechanism to learn.
judge_comment: Magnetic latches are plausible and simple to use, but they are common and raise safety interlock concerns.

title: Ring-Light Progress
new_elements: Colour ring around the door (Changes colour from red to green as the food finishes.)
rationale: A colour ring needs no reading, so the user knows the status at a glance.
judge_comment: Colour status needs no reading and is easy to implement, but it adds a part rather than substituting one and is a familiar concept.

title: Spoken Done
new_elements: Voice speaker (Says a short phrase such as Ready when cooking ends.)
rationale: A spoken message replaces the bell and needs no reading or interpretation.
judge_comment: Easy to build and clear, but it only improves the end-of-cook signal, not the operation itself, and talking appliances are common.

title: Solid-State GaN Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Generates microwave power at low voltage with no high-voltage supply.)
rationale: Removing the high voltage removes the lethal-charge hazard that makes the oven feel dangerous.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and a genuine substitution, but removing the high voltage does little for a no-learning-curve user interface, and it is costly.

title: Self-Limiting Vessel
new_elements: Water-jacket cooking vessel (Water inside caps the food at boiling point, so it cannot overheat.)
rationale: The vessel controls temperature by itself, so the user cannot make a mistake.
judge_comment: A self-limiting vessel does remove user error in temperature and timing, though a water jacket is limited to boiling-type heating and is awkward to use.

title: Boil-Safe Glass Rod
new_elements: Nucleation glass rod (A rod placed in the cup that gives bubbles a place to form.)
rationale: Bubbles form gently around the rod, so the user never faces an eruption.
judge_comment: A boil-prevention rod is plausible and somewhat helpful for safety, but it adds an accessory and does little for operation simplicity or learning curve.

title: Camera Metal Refusal
new_elements: Metal-detecting camera (Refuses to start and shows a simple icon when metal is in the cavity.)
rationale: The oven will not start unsafely, so the user does not need to know the rule.
judge_comment: Camera-based metal refusal with an icon removes the need to know the rule, and it is plausible though imperfect at detecting metal, and it is not a true substitution of parts.

title: Built-In Susceptor Browner
new_elements: Susceptor tray (A tray that heats up to brown and crisp food without a separate setting.)
rationale: Crisp food appears automatically, so the user needs no special mode.
judge_comment: Susceptor trays already exist and remove a mode, but they only help for crisping and add little to overall learning-free operation.

title: Hot-Plate Start Gesture
new_elements: Hand-wave sensor (Starts or stops cooking when the user waves a hand over the top.)
rationale: A wave is a gesture everyone already knows, so no controls need to be learned.
judge_comment: A wave to start or stop is intuitive and simple, but it gives no control over time or power and risks accidental triggers, and it only partly substitutes the controls.

title: Shape-Detecting Preset
new_elements: Container shape reader (Detects the container shape and picks a suitable power and time.)
rationale: The oven matches the container itself, so the user never needs to guess.
judge_comment: Auto-selecting settings from the container removes decisions, but shape alone says little about food, so it is technically doubtful.

title: Hover-open door
new_elements: Proximity-sensing door opener (Door swings open when a hand approaches, with no button to find.)
rationale: Opening the door becomes a natural reflex with no button or handle to learn.
judge_comment: Proximity-sensing opening is easy to build, but it risks accidental opening and only addresses one small interaction rather than operation overall.

title: Auto-eject door on finish
new_elements: Spring-eject door (Door pops ajar when cooking ends so users never forget to open it.)
rationale: The machine itself announces completion, so the user needs no step to end the cycle.
judge_comment: A spring-eject door is simple and cheap, and the finish cue is helpful, but it is common on existing microwaves and does not address setting up cooking.

title: Tap-anywhere door
new_elements: Full-face pressure panel (Pressing anywhere on the door face releases the latch.)
rationale: Users cannot miss a target the size of the whole door, which helps older users with poor aim.
judge_comment: A full-face pressure release removes aiming difficulty, though accidental opening during use or cleaning must be prevented by interlocks.

title: Green-glow safe-to-open edge
new_elements: Door-edge status light (Edge glows green when the magnetron is off and the door is safe to open.)
rationale: A single colour signal tells the user when it is safe to act, with no manual to read.
judge_comment: A simple status light is easy to build and understand, but it adds a part instead of substituting one, and it is only a minor aid to operation.

title: Progress-ring light instead of numbers
new_elements: Light-ring time display (A light ring around the base fills or empties as time passes.)
rationale: Watching a ring empty needs no reading or numeracy, so anyone can tell how long is left.
judge_comment: An intuitive light-ring timer replaces numeric displays and is easy to build, though it only simplifies reading time, not setting it.

title: Rolling-ball timer track
new_elements: Gravity-ball timer (Ball rolls down a track, and the ball's landing ends the cook.)
rationale: A visible ball falling is a physical timer that needs no numbers and no setting.
judge_comment: A visible ball timer is playful and number-free, but the ball's duration is hard to set, so the mechanism is vague and less intuitive.

title: Solid-state continuous power
new_elements: Solid-state RF amplifier (Semiconductor amplifier that varies power continuously without a magnetron.)
rationale: Smooth power means the dial responds predictably, with no cycling to puzzle over.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and radical, but it is costly and its benefit to ease of operation is indirect.

title: Power shown as ring colour
new_elements: Ring colour power display (Ring colour changes from blue for gentle to red for strong.)
rationale: Colour communicates power intensity at a glance, with no labels to read.
judge_comment: Colour is an intuitive display, but it only shows the power level and does not simplify how the user sets it.

title: Mass-scaled automatic power
new_elements: Load-adaptive power control (Power is set from the food mass and type.)
rationale: The machine chooses the power itself, so the user has no decision to make.
judge_comment: It removes the decision entirely, which serves the need well, but sensing mass and food type reliably is hard and the mechanism is left vague.

title: Thermochromic cavity liner
new_elements: Thermochromic liner (Liner changes colour as the cavity gets hot, showing heat state.)
rationale: Colour reveals heat state directly, so users read the food's status without interpreting a display.
judge_comment: Heat-state colour feedback is intuitive and needs no reading, but cavity temperature in a microwave doesn't reflect food heat, so it could mislead.

title: Tagged-food auto-programming
new_elements: Passive RF food tags (Tags on food packaging tell the oven the correct settings.)
rationale: Tags provide food-state information so the user never has to program anything.
judge_comment: Passive RF tags enable zero-input cooking, but they need industry-wide adoption of tagged packaging, and passive tags can't truly sense food state.

title: Gas-Sensing Popcorn Brain
new_elements: VOC gas sensor (Detects the aroma of popping corn or reheating bread and adjusts heating.); Aroma-driven heat control (Matches heat level to what the food smells like.)
rationale: The food tells the machine its own settings, so the user does not need to know any power levels.
judge_comment: VOC sensing for popcorn exists and is somewhat novel, but it covers few foods and the user may not understand how it behaves.

title: Hot Button Only
new_elements: Single HOT button (One large button that runs a sensible default heat cycle.); One-press heating (Heats food with one press, using a default cycle.)
rationale: A single obvious button removes every decision from the interface.
judge_comment: A single button is highly relevant and easy to build, but it is an obvious idea and a default cycle will not suit every food.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door-close sensor (Magnetic switch that starts heating as soon as the door shuts.); Start on close (Begins the cycle when the door closes.)
rationale: Closing the door is a natural motion, so starting the machine requires no extra step.
judge_comment: Auto-start on close removes a step and is simple, but it's a known concept and raises safety issues with accidental starts and unset time or power.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Flush pressure door (Door with no handle or button; a push anywhere on its face opens it.); Open by pushing (Opens on any push, with no need to find a control.)
rationale: No one has to look for a button, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A handleless push-to-open door is easy to use and plausible, but it only covers opening and leaves the cooking controls untouched.

title: Voice of One Word
new_elements: Wake-word microphone (Microphone that listens for a single command such as Heat.); Single spoken command (Runs a default cycle on one spoken word.)
rationale: Speaking one word needs no menus, so there is no interface to learn.
judge_comment: A single-word voice command is easy to use and feasible, but it is fairly obvious and offers little control.

title: Smart Mug Coaster Remote
new_elements: NFC coaster remote (A coaster that the user taps on the microwave to start a cycle.); Tap-to-heat (Starts a cycle when the coaster is tapped.)
rationale: A tap on a familiar object replaces every control on the machine.
judge_comment: NFC tap is easy and feasible, but a single coaster cannot specify time or power, and it adds a loose item to lose.

title: Ear-Based Doneness
new_elements: Sizzle microphone (Microphone that listens for changes in the sound of cooking food.); Sound-triggered stop (Stops heating when the food's sound changes.)
rationale: The machine listens for doneness, so no one needs to watch or judge the food.
judge_comment: Removes the need to set anything, but acoustic doneness detection is unreliable across foods and a noisy microwave.

title: Ambient Countdown Projection
new_elements: Counter projector (Projects a simple countdown ring onto the counter in front of the machine.); Projected status (Shows time left where the user is already looking.)
rationale: Status appears where the user is already looking, so no display needs to be read.
judge_comment: Projected countdown is novel and put status where the user looks, but it adds a part rather than simplifying operation and may wash out in bright light.

title: Solid-State No Warm-Up
new_elements: Solid-state RF amplifier (Amplifier that starts instantly and needs no warm-up cycle.); Instant heating (Heats immediately when started, with no waiting.)
rationale: Instant response means the user never waits or wonders whether it is working.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and gives instant feedback, but it is costlier rather than simpler and only indirectly reduces learning.

title: Auto-Pause on Reach
new_elements: Reach sensor (Sensor that pauses heating when a hand approaches the cavity.); Automatic pause (Pauses the cycle without any button press.)
rationale: Reaching in automatically pauses the machine, so there is no stop button to remember.
judge_comment: Removes the need for a stop button, but microwaves already pause when the door opens, and the reach sensor adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Two-Button Heat Pet
new_elements: Cute character face (Simple face that smiles when food is hot and blinks when it needs attention.); Emotional status (Shows status through a friendly face.)
rationale: A face needs no explanation, so the machine's state is understood instantly.
judge_comment: A two-button design with a friendly face is easy to build and communicates status intuitively, though it mainly helps with feedback and less with setting heating parameters.

title: Light-Only Done Signal
new_elements: Ambient glow strip (A soft colour gradient on the top edge fades from blue to warm white as cooking ends.)
rationale: A colour change is understood without any instruction and never needs a sound setting.
judge_comment: A light-based done cue is easy to understand and trivial to build, but it is incremental and does not simplify operation itself.

title: Solid-State GaN Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state 2.45 GHz amplifier (Transistor RF source with instant start, no cathode wear, and continuously variable output.); Gallium nitride RF power amplifier (Wide-bandgap transistors produce 2.45 GHz RF without a vacuum tube.)
rationale: Instant start and no warm-up mean the oven responds exactly when the user touches it.
judge_comment: A GaN solid-state RF source is a real and radical substitution for the magnetron, but it is expensive, and instant start only slightly helps ease of use.

title: Continuous Power Without Cycling
new_elements: Continuous RF level control (Amplifier output is adjusted smoothly, removing the need for on/off cam cycling.)
rationale: Power is set by one smooth heat level with no cycling to understand.
judge_comment: Inverter-style continuous power is real and removes cycling, but it does little to simplify what the user actually operates.

title: Shape-Coded Knobs
new_elements: Shape-coded control set (Each function has a distinct physical shape so it can be found by touch alone.)
rationale: Shape tells the user the control's job, so no labels need reading.
judge_comment: Tactile shape coding aids discoverability, but it is an incremental idea and users still have to learn what each shape means.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door Release
new_elements: Capacitive door touch zone (A tap anywhere on the door face opens it, with no button to find.)
rationale: Users cannot miss a door that opens when they touch almost any part of it.
judge_comment: A capacitive touch zone on the door is feasible and removes the need to find a button, but accidental opening and the safety interlock need care.

title: Walk-Up Door Opener
new_elements: Proximity door sensor (Door opens when a hand approaches at the right distance, and the interlock still confirms.)
rationale: Users with limited dexterity can open the door without pressing anything.
judge_comment: A proximity sensor that opens the door is feasible and good for accessibility, but it risks false triggers and does not simplify the rest of operation.

title: Self-Centering Tray
new_elements: Self-centering turntable ring (The tray snaps into a ridged ring, so it cannot be fitted wrongly.)
rationale: The tray can only sit one way, so there is no assembly error to make.
judge_comment: Keyed tray fitting prevents setup errors, but it is a minor tweak that is rarely a real learning barrier.

title: Hot-Plate Breakfast Mode
new_elements: One-touch warm drink (A single press warms a drink to a set safe temperature, with boil prevention built in.)
rationale: One press gives a safe warm drink, so the user never has to judge time or boiling.
judge_comment: One-press drink warming is simple to use and technically easy with a sensor, but it is close to existing beverage presets.

title: Glanceable Status Ring
new_elements: Progress light ring (A circular light fills as cooking progresses, readable from across the room.)
rationale: A filling ring shows progress at a glance, so no time needs to be read.
judge_comment: Easy to build and readable at a glance, but it only shows status, so it does little for operating the microwave without learning.

title: Thaw Is Automatic
new_elements: Automatic defrost by weight (Mass sensing picks a defrost program and ends it at a safe temperature without any choice from the user.)
rationale: Defrosting happens without any choice, so the user never has to know how to thaw.
judge_comment: Removing the defrost decision is valuable, but reliable mass sensing and safe-temperature detection inside a microwave are hard.

title: Solid-State GaN Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Gallium nitride transistors generate 2.45 GHz at low voltage with no cathode or HV.); Solid-state RF module (Replaces magnetron and HV chain.)
rationale: Without a lethal HV supply or an ageing magnetron, the appliance can be left alone safely for years.
judge_comment: GaN solid-state RF is a real substitution that is technically plausible, but it mainly improves safety and lifespan rather than reducing the learning curve.

title: Camera Peek Cavity View
new_elements: Cavity camera with auto-display (Small camera shows the food on a built-in display when cooking.)
rationale: The food is shown on a screen without opening the door or bending to look inside.
judge_comment: A camera view helps the user monitor food without guessing, but it adds cost, steam and RF challenges, and does not simplify controls.

title: Push-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Door touch-plate (Pressing any part of the door face releases the latch, so there is no small button to find.)
rationale: A large target that works from anywhere on the door is easy to find for users with poor eyesight or dexterity.
judge_comment: A whole-door release is accessible and easy to build, but it only addresses opening, not the operation.

title: Hand-Wave Release
new_elements: Infrared proximity opener (A hand held near the handle triggers the latch release.)
rationale: Reaching toward the door is an intuitive gesture, so no press has to be learned.
judge_comment: Touchless opening is intuitive, but it only covers the door and risks accidental triggers; infrared proximity is cheap and proven.

title: Tap-Twice Knock Opening
new_elements: Knock-sensing accelerometer (A door accelerometer recognises two taps on the glass and releases the latch.)
rationale: Knocking on a door is a universal gesture that requires no instruction.
judge_comment: Knocking to open is a charming gesture, but it is not that discoverable and could misfire from bumps or vibration.

title: Sliding Pocket Door
new_elements: Side-sliding door (The door slides sideways into the wall of the casing, so no hinge or swing arc is needed.)
rationale: A sliding door behaves like a cabinet or fridge door that people already understand.
judge_comment: A sliding door is familiar and removes the swing arc, but sealing against microwave leakage is hard and the benefit for learnability is modest.

title: Drop-Down Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (The whole cavity slides out like a toaster drawer to load food, then slides back in to cook.)
rationale: Loading food in a drawer is simpler than reaching into an opening, which helps users with limited reach.
judge_comment: A drawer is very intuitive and accessible, but shielding, a moving cavity and the turntable make it technically difficult.

title: Done Chime Turntable
new_elements: Slow-spin finish signal (The turntable spins slowly to show cooking has ended instead of ringing a bell.)
rationale: A moving turntable is a visible and silent signal that does not depend on hearing.
judge_comment: Using the turntable as a silent done signal is simple and removes a part (the bell), though a slow spin may be ambiguous with normal cooking.

title: Haptic Done Pulse
new_elements: Handle vibration motor (A small vibration in the handle signals the end of cooking.)
rationale: Users with hearing loss still get a clear end-of-cook signal they can feel in their hand.
judge_comment: A handle vibration is feasible and intuitive, but it adds a part rather than substituting a cheaper one and the handle is not touched while cooking.

title: Dish-Tagged Power
new_elements: RFID-tagged dish sensing (A chip in the dish or meal tray sets the power level when placed inside.)
rationale: The power is set by the food, so the user never chooses a power level at all.
judge_comment: Removes power selection entirely, but it depends on tagged dishes and does not set the time.

title: Preset Heat Ramp
new_elements: Smooth inverter magnetron drive (An inverter supply gives continuous power, so the duty-cycle cam is no longer needed.)
rationale: Continuous power removes the on-off clicking, which makes the heat behave as expected.
judge_comment: An inverter drive is a real, named component, but it addresses heating behaviour rather than ease of operation, and inverters already exist.

title: Universal Power Brick
new_elements: Auto-voltage input (A wide-range input supply accepts 100 to 240 V at 50 or 60 Hz, so one model works everywhere.)
rationale: One model for every mains supply means users never need to check which version they have.
judge_comment: Universal input is feasible and concrete, but it matters little to the operating learning curve since it only affects purchase and setup.

title: Auto Door Cooking Start
new_elements: Presence-start timer (Placing food inside and closing the door starts cooking with a time set from the food type.)
rationale: Loading and closing the door is the only step, so starting happens on its own.
judge_comment: Close-door-to-start is very simple, but setting time from food type needs identification and risks heating empty or wrong items.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable weighing (The glass turntable sits on load cells that estimate food mass and set the time.); Weight-sensing turntable (A turntable that doubles as a scale and the timer input.)
rationale: Putting food on the plate is the only setup step, so timing becomes a side effect of loading.
judge_comment: A load-cell turntable removes timing input, but weight alone is a poor proxy for cook time and the load cells must survive heat and rotation.

title: Three-Bowl Power Language
new_elements: Texture bowls (Three colour-coded bowls labelled soft, medium and crispy, each matched to a power level.); Bowl-detect RF tuning (The cavity detects which bowl is loaded and tunes the magnetron output.)
rationale: Choosing a bowl by what the food should become replaces dial positions that mean nothing to new users.
judge_comment: Bowl-detected power is an inventive mapping, but it forces users to own special bowls and the bowl-to-texture link is somewhat abstract.

title: Haptic Handle Ping
new_elements: Vibrating door handle (A door handle that buzzes in the hand when cooking ends.); Haptic actuator (A small vibration motor placed in the handle.)
rationale: A buzz in the hand reaches users who are deaf, hard of hearing or distracted by a bell.
judge_comment: Haptic alert helps accessibility but does little to remove the learning curve of operating the microwave.

title: Rolling Shutter Front
new_elements: Roll-up shutter front (A flexible slatted shutter that rolls up and stays up at the top of the unit.); Spring-counterbalanced roller (A roller with a spring that holds the shutter open at any height.)
rationale: The shutter rolls up and stays up, so there is no door to hold, prop or catch.
judge_comment: A roll-up shutter is novel, but microwave RF containment with a slatted flexible front is very difficult and it also hurts cleanability and safety.

title: Sensor-Free Wave Open
new_elements: Hover-to-open sensor (An infrared sensor that opens the door when a hand is held near the front.); Passive infrared presence detection (Detects a hand within a short range without contact.)
rationale: Waving a hand at the door is the whole interaction, so there is no mechanism or button to learn.
judge_comment: Hand-wave opening is intuitive, but it needs a motorized door, risks accidental triggers, and the title contradicts itself (sensor-free yet uses an IR sensor).

title: Tap-to-Cook Glass
new_elements: Tap-on glass panel (The door window works as a touch panel; tapping it once starts cooking.); Capacitive touch through conductive coating (A transparent conductive film that senses touch through glass.)
rationale: Tapping the glass the user is already looking through removes the need to find and turn a knob.
judge_comment: Tapping the door glass to start is intuitive, but the conductive film must stay compatible with microwave shielding and a single tap offers no way to set time or power.

title: Plug-In Timer Puck
new_elements: Plug-in timer puck (A removable puck that stores a cook time and clips to the outside of the door.); Carries stored timing (Stores and transfers a timing preset from one cook to the next.)
rationale: A preset puck the user simply clicks in means they never set the same time twice.
judge_comment: A clip-on preset puck is simple and buildable, but the user still has to choose and manage pucks, so the learning burden is only partly removed.

title: Gravity Plate Clock
new_elements: Tilt-to-time plate (Tilting the turntable plate a set angle for one minute of cooking, like a sundial.); Inclinometer timing (A simple tilt sensor that converts angle into time.)
rationale: Tilting a plate to a mark is a physical gesture that needs no numbers.
judge_comment: Wildly novel, but tilting a plate with food on it is impractical and unintuitive, so it works against ease of use.

title: Dish-Lid Cooking Mode
new_elements: Self-venting lid (A lid that vents steam when a set pressure is reached, so there is no vent to set.); Passive pressure relief (A spring valve that lets steam out at a fixed pressure.)
rationale: The lid vents by itself, so the user never has to decide when or how to open it.
judge_comment: Self-venting lids exist already and remove one decision, but they don't address the core controls.

title: Audio-Cued Reheat
new_elements: Tap-to-sound cue (A sound that plays once when the user taps the panel, saying how long the cook will take.); Confirms time by sound (Plays back the set time so the user can check it without looking.)
rationale: Hearing the time spoken back confirms the setting without needing to read it.
judge_comment: Easy to build and helpful for confirming settings, but it is incremental and only adds feedback to an existing interface.

title: Grandma's Single Recipe Card
new_elements: Printed cook card (A card on the door with one picture per food and what to do next, printed on a flip panel.); Replaces the manual (Gives everything needed to operate the unit on one page.)
rationale: One printed card that covers everything removes the need to read a manual.
judge_comment: A printed card replaces the manual cheaply and simply, but it is a low-novelty approach and does not simplify the controls themselves.

title: Voice-Free Smart Cap
new_elements: Fridge-magnet control (A magnetic control unit the user puts on the fridge; placing it near the microwave loads the last program.); Magnetic proximity pairing (Short-range magnetic sensing that pairs a control unit with the microwave.)
rationale: A magnet on the fridge with the programs already set makes operating the microwave simple from anywhere.
judge_comment: A fridge magnet that loads a preset is a novel idea, but magnetic pairing is vague and the magnet adds an extra device and complexity.

title: Plasma Glow Cavity Light
new_elements: Neon-argon glow tube (Gas tube inside the cavity that glows when RF energy is present.); RF-excited gas discharge (Microwave field ionises low-pressure gas.)
rationale: The glow shows that cooking is on without a separate bulb, so there is no lamp to forget or replace.
judge_comment: A clever substitution of the lamp with a gas glow tube, but it mainly indicates that RF is on and does little for ease of operation.

title: GaN Solid-State Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Gallium-nitride transistor amplifier at 2.45 GHz running from low-voltage DC.); Gallium-nitride RF transistor (Solid-state microwave power device.)
rationale: Removing the kilovolt transformer and magnetron removes the lethal-voltage hazard, so the appliance is safer for everyone in the family.
