new_elements: Photocatalytic cavity coating (Titanium-dioxide coating breaks down splashes under the light from a heating cycle)
rationale: Spills disappear without scrubbing, so cleaning requires no learned routine.
judge_comment: Photocatalytic self-cleaning removes a chore, but TiO2 needs UV light rather than heating-cycle light, so feasibility is weak and it is only tangential to operation.

title: Chopstick Thermometer Probe
new_elements: Disposable food probe (Probe inserted into food sends a temperature reading to the controller)
rationale: The probe tells the appliance when the food is safe, so the user never has to guess.
judge_comment: A probe that tells the oven when food is done removes guesswork, but wireless readings inside a microwave field are difficult and the probe is an extra item to handle.

title: Recipe Card Scanner
new_elements: Phone-camera recipe capture (Phone camera reads a printed recipe card and sends settings to the oven)
rationale: Users point their phone at a recipe and the machine does the rest, so no settings need to be read or typed.
judge_comment: Scanning a recipe card removes manual entry, but it needs a phone app and pairing and recipe cards rarely carry microwave settings, which adds a learning burden.

title: Hands-Free Voice Cook
new_elements: Wake-word speech recognition (Speaking heat for two minutes starts a cooking program with simple phrases)
rationale: Speaking a plain request is more natural than any knob, and it lets people walk away while cooking.
judge_comment: Voice control is natural and needs no learning, but it's a common idea and it is not a cheaper substitution.

title: Three Emoji Buttons
new_elements: Three pictogram buttons (Large buttons marked with a flame, a pot and a snowflake for cook, simmer and defrost.)
rationale: Three symbols replace a five-step numeric knob, so the power choice is obvious without any manual.
judge_comment: Pictogram buttons are easy to understand but still leave the user to guess the duration, and the icons are ambiguous.

title: Magnetic Self-Latch Door
new_elements: Magnetic self-latching catch (A magnet closes and holds the door when it is pushed shut, and releases when pulled firmly.)
rationale: The door latches itself on closing, so the user never has to think about the latch.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch is cheap and simple, but it is common in other appliances, and microwave safety interlocks complicate it.

title: Habit-Learning Preset
new_elements: Usage pattern learner (The machine remembers what is cooked most often and presets it when the door opens.)
rationale: The most common setting is already chosen, so regular use takes no thought.
judge_comment: Auto-presetting the most common setting cuts effort for habitual users, but it is a vague learning algorithm and does not substitute any part.

title: Continuous Smooth Power
new_elements: Inverter magnetron supply (A solid-state supply that runs the magnetron at any continuous power without cycling.)
rationale: Smooth power removes the on-off pulsing that confuses users, so food heats evenly.
judge_comment: Inverter supplies already exist in commercial microwaves and mainly improve cooking quality, not the learning curve.

title: Ambient Smell Preheat
new_elements: Smell-based heat matching (The microwave reads food smell to pick the right heat level automatically.)
rationale: Choosing power by sensing the food removes the need to make any setting.
judge_comment: Automatic smell-based heat selection would remove the need for any settings and is radical, but reliable food identification by smell is implausible and the mechanism is vague.

title: Three-Word Mood Power
new_elements: Soft, Normal, Done selection (The five power steps collapse into three plain-language choices.)
rationale: Three words are easier to remember than five numbered steps.
judge_comment: Collapsing power levels to three words simplifies slightly, but time entry remains and the idea is modest and unambitious.

title: Scent Done Signal
new_elements: Aroma emitter (Releases a mild popcorn or bread scent when cooking finishes.)
rationale: A smell is an instinctive signal that needs no reading or learning.
judge_comment: A scent signal is unusual and intuitive, but smell is unreliable and may be unpleasant, and it addresses only the completion cue.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (The cavity slides out like a drawer, showing the food on a flat tray.)
rationale: A drawer matches how people already open kitchen storage, so it needs no learning.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar motion and exists in some built-in models, but sealing against microwave leakage and the mechanism cost are challenges.

title: Knock-to-Open Door
new_elements: Acoustic knock sensor (A single knock on the door face releases the latch.)
rationale: Knocking on a door is a universal gesture that anyone understands.
judge_comment: Knocking is intuitive, but accidental knocks, a nonstandard door-opening habit, and the lack of any cooking-control simplification limit its value; it substitutes the handle or button, which is not the main learning hurdle.

title: Stop-When-Opened Timer
new_elements: Pause on door open (Opening the door pauses cooking, and closing it resumes.)
rationale: Users can check food without worrying about the timer or safety.
judge_comment: Already standard on nearly every microwave, so it is feasible and mildly helpful but barely new.

title: Steam-Stop Glass
new_elements: Condensation sensor on door glass (Stops cooking when steam condenses on the door window.)
rationale: Steam is a visible sign of done, so the oven needs no time to set.
judge_comment: It removes time-setting entirely, which is highly relevant, but condensation is unreliable across foods and containers, so it often won't work.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Visible hourglass chamber (A transparent chamber of fine grains empties at the rate of the cook cycle.)
rationale: Watching sand fall shows remaining time at a glance without reading a dial.
judge_comment: A visible hourglass is intuitive, but it adds mechanical complexity, and it substitutes the display without removing the need to set a time.

title: Pebble Start
new_elements: Single pressure-sensitive pebble (One smooth, sealed touch pad on the fascia that starts cooking with a press and stops with another.)
rationale: One pebble with one behaviour removes the choice of which control to use.
judge_comment: A single touch pad is easy to understand but does not say how time or power are set, so the simplicity is partial.

title: Sand Timer Display
new_elements: Visible sand-fall timer column (A transparent column of fine granules drains at a steady rate, so remaining time can be read at a glance.)
rationale: A physical level that visibly empties needs no reading and no number literacy.
judge_comment: Intuitive visual timer is easy to read, but it only addresses time display and is a familiar hourglass metaphor; it also adds a mechanical element and the user still must set the time.

title: Ambient Glow Chime
new_elements: Soft colour-change ambient ring (A ring of soft light on the base changes colour to show the cooking state, paired with a gentle chime.)
rationale: A glow plus a single soft tone works for all ages and hearing levels.
judge_comment: A light ring plus chime is easy to build and clearly communicates state, but it is an incremental idea that doesn't simplify control.

title: Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Rotating mode stirrer (A metal fan in the waveguide mixes the field so the food does not have to move.)
rationale: No turntable means nothing to align, no roller ring to clean and no wobble.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are proven and do replace the turntable, but they are already common in commercial units and users barely notice the change.

title: Photo Recognition Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera food recognition (A small camera in the roof recognises the food and sets the cooking program.)
rationale: The camera sees the food, so the user does not have to describe it.
judge_comment: Camera recognition is zero-effort in principle, but accuracy and steam or splatter on the lens are a concern.

title: Wipe-Clean Fascia
new_elements: Flush capacitive glass fascia (A flat glass front with printed icons and no gaps for grease.)
rationale: A flat front with big icons has no crevices to clean and nothing to misread.
judge_comment: Flat capacitive glass with big icons is plausible and aids clarity, though already common on appliances and not radical.

title: Voice-Free Spoken Cue
new_elements: Recorded spoken status (A short spoken word, such as 'Ready', plays at the end of cooking.)
rationale: A spoken word needs no learning and is clear to people with visual impairment.
judge_comment: A spoken 'Ready' cue is intuitive and accessible, but it only covers the end-of-cook feedback and not operation itself; the 'voice-free' name is also contradictory.

title: Pictogram Recipe Cards
new_elements: Picture-only recipe card (A card with pictures alone shows the three steps for common foods.)
rationale: Pictures teach the process at a glance, so the user can start without reading.
judge_comment: Picture-only cards help novices start without reading, but they are an add-on and not a radical change to the operation itself.

title: Dome Lid Replaces Door
new_elements: Clear magnetic dome lid (A lid that lifts off like a bowl cover and seals the heat zone when placed.); Open and close by lifting (The lid opens with a lift and no button.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is an action every user already knows how to do.
judge_comment: A lift-off lid is intuitive, but it creates microwave leakage and safety issues, and it only addresses opening and closing, not the settings.

title: Self-Opening Door
new_elements: Spring-loaded door latch (Pops the door open slightly when cooking finishes.); Announce completion by opening (The door itself signals that the food is ready.)
rationale: The door opening is an obvious signal that needs no reading or hearing.
judge_comment: It is simple and feasible, and some microwaves already do it, but it only signals completion and does not simplify operation.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Sand-fill timer column (A clear column whose sand level falls as the food cooks.); Show remaining time visually (The remaining cooking time is seen as a falling level.)
rationale: A falling level needs no reading of numbers and works like an hourglass people already understand.
judge_comment: A sand timer shows time intuitively, but it adds mechanical complexity and does nothing to simplify setting the time.

title: Thermochromic Food Sticker
new_elements: Heat-reactive sticker (A sticker on the food changes colour when the food is hot all the way through.); Check doneness on the food (Doneness is judged on the food, not on the machine.)
rationale: The user only has to look at the food, which is the thing they already care about.
judge_comment: A doneness sticker is a clever way to check food, but it adds a consumable and does not replace the controls.

title: Phone Tap Pairing
new_elements: NFC tap pad (A phone tapped on the lid sends the cooking profile to the oven.); Configure by tapping (The machine is configured with one tap of a phone.)
rationale: A single tap replaces all settings, so there is nothing to learn on the machine.
judge_comment: NFC tap setup is technically easy, but it depends on a phone and app, which adds a learning step and is not really a substitute.

title: Wave-to-Start Gesture
new_elements: Hand-motion sensor (Starts cooking when a hand is waved in front of the door.); Start by gesture (Cooking begins with a wave, with no button to find.)
rationale: A wave is a natural gesture that needs no search for a control.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start removes the button but gives no way to set time or power, and accidental triggering is a risk.

title: Popcorn-Sound Stop
new_elements: Acoustic popping sensor (Listens for the pop rate and stops when the popping slows.); Stop on sound (Cooking ends when the audible cue changes.)
rationale: The food itself announces when it is done, so the user only has to listen.
judge_comment: Acoustic popping detection already exists on some microwaves and helps only with popcorn.

title: Light-Projected Doneness
new_elements: Floor projector (Projects a progress bar of light onto the turntable.); Show progress on the food (A light bar on the food surface shows how much time is left.)
rationale: The status is shown exactly where the user looks, so no separate display needs reading.
judge_comment: Projecting progress onto the food is intuitive, but the projector has to survive the heat and steam and it doesn't simplify input.

title: Shape-Coded Knob Stack
new_elements: Shape-keyed dial (Each power level is a different shape a user matches to a shape on the food box.); Match shapes (The user matches a symbol rather than reading a number.)
rationale: Matching shapes is a very low-effort task that needs no literacy.
judge_comment: Shape matching replaces numbers simply, but it needs matching symbols on food packaging, and it is still a dial with a mapping to learn.

title: Spring-Slider Power
new_elements: Spring slider (A slider that springs back to the middle and sets power by its position.); Set power by slider (Power is changed with one movement.)
rationale: A slider is simpler to use than a five-step knob that needs counting.
judge_comment: A spring-return slider is simple and feasible, but it is an incremental swap of a knob and not radical.

title: Egg-Shaped Smart Pebble
new_elements: Dish-shaped control puck (A puck placed on the food that reads its heat and runs the cook.); Control by placing a puck (A puck on the food acts as the entire control panel.)
rationale: A puck in the food needs no knobs and no reading to start cooking.
judge_comment: A puck on the food as the whole control is a bold, no-learning concept, but sensing food heat from the puck inside a microwave is hard and the mechanism is vague.

title: Phosphor Glow Interior
new_elements: Glow-in-dark liner (A photoluminescent interior that stays lit for a while after cooking.); Light the cavity passively (The interior is visible without power.)
rationale: The cavity can be seen without any switch or wiring.
judge_comment: Feasible and concrete, but it contributes little to simple operation, and the glow fades quickly so it is of limited use.

title: Ask-the-Kitchen Card
new_elements: Recipe card scanner (A plain card with a photo is scanned to choose cooking.); Cook from a card (A printed recipe card sets the machine.)
rationale: A card is a familiar object that needs no manual to read.
judge_comment: Scanning a card to set cooking is feasible, but it adds cards to manage and is only moderately simpler than a button.

title: Flat Kitchen Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out drawer (The cooking chamber is a drawer that slides out to load food.); Load by sliding (Food is loaded by sliding the drawer, as with a dishwasher.)
rationale: Sliding a drawer is a motion everyone already knows from kitchen appliances.
judge_comment: A familiar drawer motion is intuitive, and drawer microwaves exist, but it only simplifies loading and not cook settings.

title: Frosted Glass Preset Panel
new_elements: Touch-glass panel (A flat glass surface where the only active area lights up when needed.); Show controls only when needed (The panel is blank until the user needs it.)
rationale: Hiding controls until needed reduces visible complexity to zero.
judge_comment: Hidden controls are easy to build, but a blank panel could confuse users and does not truly cut the learning curve.

title: Eat-Now Pizza Stone
new_elements: Single-food preset plate (A plate that is pre-set for one food type by its surface pattern.); Choose food by plate (The food type is set by which plate is used.)
rationale: Choosing a plate needs no setting, since the plate already knows the food.
judge_comment: A plate that encodes the food type removes settings, but it needs a plate-recognition mechanism and limits flexibility, so users would need a plate for each food.

title: Cord-Pull Start
new_elements: Pull-cord starter (A cord that is pulled once to start a cook and pulled again to stop.); Start by pull cord (A single pull controls the whole cook.)
rationale: A pull cord is a familiar mechanism, like a lawnmower starter, that requires no reading.
judge_comment: A pull cord is a wild and familiar single-action control, though it is unclear how it sets duration and is mechanically odd for a microwave.

title: Barcode Card Slot
new_elements: Printed instruction card slot (The user slides in a card printed with a barcode for the food, and the machine cooks to match.)
rationale: Sliding in a card is a physical action that needs no reading or knob-turning.
judge_comment: A card slot is feasible but adds a step and loose cards to manage, and it is no simpler than a button.

title: Wave-to-Start Gesture
new_elements: Infrared gesture sensor (A sensor on the front detects a wave or hand motion and opens or starts the unit.); Passive infrared motion detection (Low-power IR sensing is cheap and needs no contact.)
rationale: A natural hand wave is intuitive and removes any need to find or press a button.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start is feasible, but it doesn't say how time or power get set, and accidental triggers are a risk.

title: Ambient Colour Ring Status Light
new_elements: Colour ring light (A ring around the cavity glows green while cooking and turns to a steady colour when done.)
rationale: Colour states mean something everywhere, so no numbers or reading are needed to know the status.
judge_comment: A color status ring is simple and easy to build and understand, but it only conveys status, not operation, and is a fairly common idea.

title: Progress Bar Replacing Countdown
new_elements: Filling progress strip (A horizontal strip on the door fills with colour as cooking progresses.)
rationale: A visible fill shows progress without needing to read numbers or handle the timer's imprecision.
judge_comment: A progress strip is intuitive and cheap, but it only replaces the countdown display and is not very radical.

title: Retractable Sliding Door Panel
new_elements: Sliding glass panel (A door panel slides sideways on a rail instead of swinging on hinges.)
rationale: A door that slides needs no clearance and no decision about which way to swing.
judge_comment: A sliding door removes the swing-direction question and clearance issue, but the sealing and safety challenges are significant and it only modestly helps ease of use.

title: Magnetic Self-Closing Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch (A magnet pulls the door shut and holds it closed with no latch to press.)
rationale: The door closes on its own, so the user never needs to check it or operate a latch.
judge_comment: Magnetic catches are already common and feasible, but it only simplifies door closing, a minor part of operation, and it is not radical.

title: Rotating Drum Door
new_elements: Rotating drum cavity (A drum rotates to bring the opening to the front, so no separate door is needed.)
rationale: A rotating drum is a single movement, which avoids hinges, latches and interlocks.
judge_comment: A rotating drum that replaces the door is radical and does simplify the opening action, but sealing microwave leakage and keeping the interlock safe are hard problems, and the effect on ease of use is not clear.

title: Fully Automatic Open-Close Cycle
new_elements: Motorised door actuator (A small motor opens the door at the end of cooking and closes it when the food is placed.)
rationale: The door opens and closes by itself, so the user never has to work the mechanism.
judge_comment: A motorised door removes a manual step but adds cost, and a door that closes itself raises pinch-safety concerns.

title: Single Preset for Every Food
new_elements: One-touch universal preset (A single button runs a universal preset that adapts time and power to the food inside.)
rationale: One button for every food removes all decisions and any need for a manual.
judge_comment: One button with no decisions fits zero learning curve, but adapting to the food needs sensors that the idea does not specify.

title: Plug-and-Play Smart Plate Ring
new_elements: Power-sensing plate ring (A ring placed under the bowl reads what it contains and sets power to match.)
rationale: Placing the dish on the ring is the only action, and the power follows automatically.
judge_comment: A ring that reads the dish contents is a bold idea, but sensing food type from underneath is technically doubtful and vaguely specified.

title: Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Recipe card slot (A slot on the fascia that accepts a printed card whose pattern sets time and power.)
rationale: Inserting a card that looks like a kids' game card gives instant results with zero settings.
judge_comment: Card insertion is intuitive and cheap to build, but requires owning cards and is a clunky replacement for a dial.

title: Scent Done Cue
new_elements: Aroma cartridge (A small cartridge releases a warm bread or cinnamon scent when cooking ends.)
rationale: A smell cue tells the user food is ready without any setting or interpretation.
judge_comment: A scent cue is highly novel but needs consumable cartridges, can be confused with food odors, and does little for operating the microwave.

title: Wristband Done Buzz
new_elements: Bluetooth wristband (A wearable that vibrates when the appliance finishes, paired once by the family.)
rationale: Vibration reaches users who are deaf or who walk away, with no setup beyond one pairing.
judge_comment: A wristband is workable and helps deaf users, but it adds pairing and a device, which cuts against a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Foot-Kick Door Release
new_elements: Floor kick plate (A low plate at the base that opens the door when kicked, for users with full hands.)
rationale: A kick plate works with full hands and needs no aim or learning.
judge_comment: Hands-free kick release is easy to understand but is a niche convenience, risks accidental opening, and does not address the core operation of settings.

title: Solid-State Cooking Engine
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Transistor amplifiers at 2.45 GHz replace the magnetron, transformer and HV chain.)
rationale: Removing the lethal high-voltage chain removes the fear of electric shock for families.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is very concrete and real technology, but it targets safety fear and cost rather than learning-free operation, though it enables precise control.

title: Mode Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Rotating mode stirrer (A metal fan blade in the cavity roof spreads microwaves without moving the food.)
rationale: With nothing to load or align, the user just places food on a flat floor.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common in commercial and some domestic ovens, and they do remove the turntable alignment concern, so it's practical but not radical.

title: Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Sand-flow timer column (Transparent column of fine granules that empties over the cook cycle.); Shows remaining cook time visually (Sand level reads progress without any numbers.)
rationale: Time is shown as a falling pile of sand that anyone can read at a glance.
judge_comment: A sand column is a simple and readable display, but it only shows time and does not remove the need to set it.

title: Solid-State RF Heater
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Gallium nitride transistors generate 2.45 GHz without a magnetron or HV supply.); Solid-state RF module (Low-voltage amplifier block replacing the magnetron stack.)
rationale: Without lethal high voltage, the machine needs no warnings and no fear.
judge_comment: A GaN solid-state RF source is a real, novel substitution for the magnetron, but it is expensive and does little for ease of operation.

title: Hands-Free Acoustic Doneness
new_elements: Acoustic boil sensor (Microphone that tracks the bubble noise of liquid and popcorn pops.); Reduces power at boil onset (Cuts power when bubbling starts, which prevents eruptive boiling.)
rationale: The machine listens for the food and needs no knowledge of how to cook it.
judge_comment: Acoustic sensing of boiling is clever and removes the need for cooking knowledge, but a microphone in a noisy kitchen is unreliable and doesn't handle starting.

title: Fridge-Style Drawer Oven
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Shallow drawer that slides out on rails to load food.); Loads food by sliding a drawer (Sliding out is more natural than swinging a door.)
rationale: A drawer behaves like a fridge drawer, which every user already understands.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar interaction and exists in some commercial models, but RF sealing is harder and it doesn't simplify controls.

title: Infrared Doneness Reader
new_elements: Thermopile food reader (Infrared sensor that reads the surface temperature of food.); Stops at serving temperature (Ends cooking when the food reaches a safe temperature.)
rationale: The machine stops when the food is hot, which makes it impossible to get wrong.
judge_comment: IR temperature-based stopping is workable and removes time guessing, but it reads only surface temperature and similar sensors already exist.

title: Gravity-Close Door
new_elements: Counterweight hinge (Weighted hinge that swings the door shut from any open angle.); Closes the door on its own (Door shuts when released and locks with a click.)
rationale: The door closes itself, so the user never has to find a latch.
judge_comment: A counterweight self-closing hinge is simple and feasible, and it removes a small step, but it is only mildly radical.

title: Turntable Replaced by Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Rotating mode stirrer (Metal fan that stirs the RF field to even heating.); Evens heating without a turntable (Fan stirs the field so food needs no spinning plate.)
rationale: No turntable means no plate to remove, wash, and refit.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, and removing the turntable helps cleaning but does little for operating simplicity.

title: Voice Says Done
new_elements: Voice assistant speaker (Speaker that reads out food status in simple sentences.); Announces state in plain speech (The oven says 'Your soup is ready.')
rationale: Plain speech tells the user what to do next, which removes any need to read a manual.
judge_comment: Easy to build and helps understanding, but it only announces status and doesn't simplify operation much; also a common idea.

title: Single-Button Reset Tile
new_elements: Reset tile (Large tile that resets every setting to the safe default.); Restores safe defaults (One tap returns the oven to the basic setting.)
rationale: A single reset means no mistake can ever leave the oven in a confusing state.
judge_comment: A reset tile helps recovery from errors, but it adds a control rather than substituting a part, and it is a fairly obvious idea.

title: Sound-Cued Cook Start
new_elements: Clap-activated start microphone (Microphone that starts cooking on a clap.); Starts from a sound cue (A clap or a spoken word begins the cook.)
rationale: A clap is a gesture everyone already knows, so starting takes no thought.
judge_comment: A clap start is simple and cheap, but it risks false triggers and only starts the cook without setting time or power, so it is only a partial answer to the need.

title: Transparent body
new_elements: Electrochromic window (A door panel that clears when cooking begins, so food is always visible.)
rationale: The user never has to open the door or find a light switch to check the food.
judge_comment: An electrochromic door is eye-catching and feasible, but it addresses visibility rather than operation simplicity, and the microwave shielding mesh makes it harder.

title: Zero-button door
new_elements: Hover-open sensor (Door opens when the user waves a hand near the handle area.)
rationale: Opening the door works the way people expect, without a hidden button to find.
judge_comment: Proximity-sensor door opening is plausible and easy to grasp, but it only addresses opening and a hand wave isn't obviously more intuitive than a handle.

title: Hands-free gesture control
new_elements: Gesture camera (Thumbs up starts cooking, and a flat palm stops it.)
rationale: Gestures are universal, so nobody needs to learn the controls.
judge_comment: Gesture control removes buttons, but the gestures aren't truly universal, and setting time or power is not addressed.

title: Projected controls
new_elements: Floor projection keypad (A large projected keypad appears on the counter when the user approaches.)
rationale: Controls appear only when needed, which keeps the panel clear.
judge_comment: A projected keypad is eye-catching but adds complexity and still presents a full keypad, which doesn't ease operation.

title: Magnet-snap cooking
new_elements: Snap-on heating pods (Pre-set heating pods snap to the base and cook on contact.)
rationale: Snapping a pod in is simpler than arranging a plate.
judge_comment: Snap-on heating pods are an interesting substitution for the cavity and plate, but self-heating pods aren't really microwave cooking and the mechanism is unclear.

title: Colour-coded safe mode
new_elements: Visual door-state indicator (The door edge glows red while hot and green when safe to open.)
rationale: The user knows when it is safe without reading any warning.
judge_comment: A door glow indicator is easy to build and understand, but it addresses safety feedback rather than the operation learning curve.

title: Microwave that listens for silence
new_elements: Acoustic sensor (Detects boiling or popping and reduces power automatically.)
rationale: Overheating is prevented without the user needing to monitor the food.
judge_comment: Acoustic sensing of boiling and popping can automate power adjustments, but it is only partially reliable and doesn't remove the need to set up the cook.

title: Plate-drop cooking
new_elements: Drop-in cook sleeve (A disposable sleeve drops in and the oven runs its built-in profile.)
rationale: Dropping in the sleeve is simpler than loading and setting a dish.
judge_comment: Disposable sleeve triggering an automatic profile removes settings, but how the oven reads the sleeve is unspecified and it overlaps with the cartridge idea.

title: Printed cook chart on the door
new_elements: Pictorial door panel (The door shows pictures of foods and matching cook buttons.)
rationale: Pictures explain the options better than numbers or words.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build, but pictorial preset buttons are already common and not radical, though it does substitute pictures for numbers.

title: Dual-purpose stop button
new_elements: Universal stop bar (A wide bar across the front stops cooking and opens the door.)
rationale: One wide bar is easy to hit and remember compared with a small button.
judge_comment: A large stop bar is simple and feasible, but it only addresses one control and is a minor change.

title: Bell Replaced by Done Glow
new_elements: Ambient edge light ring (Soft colour change around the cavity signals completion.)
rationale: A colour cue is understood instantly without knowing what a timer bell means.
judge_comment: A light ring is a simple, plausible replacement for the bell, but it only addresses the completion signal and not operation.

title: Cook Times Painted Into Plates
new_elements: Printed heat-map cue (Icons printed on the food tray show the right setting by pictogram.)
rationale: Pictograms replace numbers, which everyone can read at a glance.
judge_comment: Pictograms on the tray replace numbers, but the tray cannot communicate settings to the oven unless it is linked to the controls, so the mechanism is unclear.

title: Hug to Heat
new_elements: Proximity heat pad (Placing a hand on the pad starts reheating.)
rationale: A physical gesture with a natural meaning starts the heating.
judge_comment: Hand-on-pad start is intuitive but vague about how it knows time or power, and accidental triggers and safety are a concern.

title: Pour-and-Go Cavity
new_elements: Liquid-fill basin (Pour food into a basin that the machine reads by weight.)
rationale: Weight sensing removes the need to specify portion or time.
judge_comment: Weight-sensing basin removes settings in principle, but weight alone can't determine heating time, and pouring food into a basin is messy and impractical.

title: Light Fades In With Your Hand
new_elements: Motion-triggered glow (Light turns on only when the door is near.)
rationale: The light appears when needed, so the user has nothing to switch.
judge_comment: A motion-triggered light is easy to build but is a minor convenience that barely affects operation learning.

title: Rotating Cabinet Front
new_elements: Single rotary dial (One dial with one icon for start, stop and power.)
rationale: One control with one meaning is the smallest learning burden possible.
judge_comment: A single dial is simple and feasible, but it is a mild reduction of existing mechanical microwaves and one control for start, stop and power is ambiguous.

title: Wearable Cook Band
new_elements: Proximity wristband (A band on the wrist opens the door when near.)
rationale: Opening the door needs no action at all.
judge_comment: A proximity wristband that opens the door is novel but adds hardware and an item to wear, and opening a door is already simple.

title: Cook Stops When You Walk Away
new_elements: Presence-aware cook (Cook pauses when the user leaves the room.)
rationale: Users never need to manage the cook while they are away.
judge_comment: Presence-aware pausing is plausible and spares the user some management, but it is a safety feature more than a simplification and mostly adds parts.

title: Family Remote Cook
new_elements: Preset per person (Each family member has a preset cook selected by a photo tile.)
rationale: Each user chooses by face or picture rather than by settings.
judge_comment: Photo-tile presets are easy to use and plausible, but they need setup and aren't a real substitution of parts.

title: Gravity Door Lock
new_elements: Magnetic self-latch (Door closes and latches by pressure alone, with no catch to find.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only physical step, which everyone can perform.
judge_comment: A magnetic self-latch is plausible and removes a minor friction, but door latching is not the main learning barrier, and microwave safety interlocks still need mechanical engagement.

title: Reheat by Hand Sweep
new_elements: Motion sweep control (Sweeping a hand across the front raises or lowers power.)
rationale: A sweep is a natural gesture that needs no labels.
judge_comment: A hand-sweep power control is a novel, label-free gesture, but it is not clearly discoverable, it is imprecise, and it is not cheaper or simpler than a dial.

title: Bimetal Done-Strip
new_elements: Bimetal temperature strip (A strip on the cavity wall bends when the cavity reaches cooking heat and trips the cut-off.)
rationale: Heat tells the machine when to stop, so precise timing is no longer a question the user has to answer.
judge_comment: A bimetal strip is a cheap substitute for a timer, but cavity air temperature is a poor indicator of food readiness and the strip's behavior varies with the load.

title: Foot-Pedal Release
new_elements: Floor pedal release (A low pedal at the cabinet base releases the door latch by pressing with the foot.)
rationale: Hands are often full, and a foot pedal lets an older user open the door without fine finger movement.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is unusual and practical for full hands, but it is not an intuitive control and it moves away from a no-learning-curve interface.

title: Vertical Lift Door
new_elements: Counterweight lift door (The door slides up like a garage door on a counterweight and stays open at the top.)
rationale: A door that rises and stays up needs no hinge decision and cannot swing into the user.
judge_comment: Lift door removes swing and stays open, modestly aiding ease of use, but a counterweight adds cost and doesn't address operating controls much.

title: Camera Big-Screen Door
new_elements: Door-mounted camera screen (A small camera inside the cavity streams to a large screen on the door with big text.)
rationale: A large live image lets an older user see the food without bending down or squinting through a mesh.
judge_comment: Large camera screen helps older users see food, but adds cost and complexity, which runs against the simple operation goal.

title: Periscope Viewer
new_elements: Top-mounted mirror periscope (A mirror at the top of the door reflects the cavity into a small viewing lens on the front.)
rationale: A viewing lens at eye level lets users check the food without stooping, and it needs no light.
judge_comment: A periscope is a concrete idea, but a dark cavity gives poor visibility without a light, and it does little for ease of operation.

title: Stove-Top Cover Panel
new_elements: Sealed-touch panel (A flat glass touch panel with raised dots replaces all knobs and switches.)
rationale: A single flat surface with a few raised dots has no moving parts that can confuse the user.
judge_comment: A flat panel with raised dots is plausible, but touch panels are already common and the fewer controls do not by themselves make it simpler to learn.

title: Stirring Fan Heat
new_elements: Phased-array field stirring (Electronic field phasing evens out the heat so the food needs no turning.)
rationale: Even heating without turning removes a step that users often forget or misjudge.
judge_comment: Electronic field stirring removes the turn-the-food step and is plausible, but it is costly and not very radical.

title: Sound-Only Feedback
new_elements: Tone-coded power cue (Each power step plays a distinct tone so the user hears the setting without looking.)
rationale: Hearing a tone confirms the setting without reading, which helps users with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: Tone-coded power cues are easy to build but add something to learn and don't remove the learning curve.

title: Light-Touch Latch Tap
new_elements: Capacitive tap release (A light tap on the door glass releases the latch via a capacitive touch sensor.)
rationale: Tapping the glass is intuitive and needs no moving lever or spring-loaded button to find.
judge_comment: Tap-to-open is intuitive and substitutes a mechanical latch, but it only addresses door opening and could trigger accidentally, so the benefit to operating the oven is limited.

title: Scent Bell
new_elements: Aroma cartridge (Small scented cartridge that releases a gentle smell at completion.); Signals completion by smell (Releases a pleasant aroma to indicate the cycle has finished.)
rationale: A smell is understood without any instruction, which replaces the bell with an intuitive cue.
judge_comment: Scent as a completion cue is novel, but it doesn't help with operating the microwave, and the smell could clash with food odors and fade.

title: Vertical Lift Door
new_elements: Vertical lift door (Door that rises straight up like a garage door.)
rationale: Lifting a door up is the most obvious motion there is, so no instructions are needed.
judge_comment: A lift door is intuitive but a modest change to door operation, with shielding and mechanical support issues.

title: Vendor-Preset Meal Cartridges
new_elements: Meal cartridge (Pre-packed meal sealed in a container with a tag.)
rationale: Every setting is decided before the user touches the meal, so no learning is needed.
judge_comment: Pre-programmed meal cartridges remove user decisions, but this largely duplicates idea 1, is vague about the mechanism, and limits what the user can heat.

title: Glow-in-Dark Door Handle
new_elements: Luminous handle (Handle that glows softly so its location is obvious in the dark.)
rationale: The handle is always found, so nobody searches for the opening mechanism.
judge_comment: A glowing handle is cheap and workable, but finding the handle is rarely the difficulty, and it is not very radical.

title: Food Scale Plate Edge
new_elements: Portion guide ring (Printed ring that shows the right portion size.)
rationale: The guide shows how much to put in, so no portion knowledge is needed.
judge_comment: A printed portion ring is simple and helps novices, but it is a printed marking rather than a substitution that simplifies operation.

title: Food-Safe Metal Mode
new_elements: Detects and skips metal items (Automatically cuts power when metal is detected.)
rationale: Metal is handled automatically, so no rule has to be remembered.
judge_comment: Automatic metal detection removes a rule users must remember, though reliable detection is hard and it only covers one failure mode.

title: Ultra-Simple Single-Setting Oven
new_elements: Single fixed program (Runs one program that works for almost any food.)
rationale: With no choices offered, there is nothing to learn at all.
judge_comment: Removing all choices truly eliminates learning, but it's an obvious idea and may fail to cook varied foods well.

title: Glass Door Mirror Finish
new_elements: Dual-face door glass (Glass that shows a mirror on the outside and a window inside.)
rationale: Users can see the food while the door looks like a simple, clean panel.
judge_comment: One-way mirror glass is feasible, but it's about aesthetics and has little effect on operation simplicity.

title: Popcorn Scent Alarm
new_elements: Scent cartridge (Releases a faint food smell when cooking is finished.)
rationale: A familiar smell signals the end of cooking to anyone, even without looking.
judge_comment: A scent alarm is unusual, but cartridges need replacing, smells are unreliable, and it barely helps operation.

title: Thermochromic Cool Warning
new_elements: Thermochromic casing panel (Changes colour when the outside of the oven is too hot to touch.)
rationale: A visible colour change warns the user with no buttons or moving parts.
judge_comment: Thermochromic panels are feasible and need no controls, but they only warn about heat and do nothing to simplify operation.

title: Ceramic Pizza Disc
new_elements: One-piece cooking disc (A disc that is both the turntable and the cooking dish.)
rationale: Fewer loose parts means fewer decisions and fewer things to get wrong.
judge_comment: Merging the turntable and dish reduces loose parts, but it is limited in food types and raises heating and handling concerns.

title: Rolling Shutter Door
new_elements: Sliding shutter door (A door that rolls up and down, so it never swings into the user.)
rationale: A shutter needs no pulling or pushing and cannot be opened in the wrong direction.
judge_comment: A shutter door removes the push-or-pull ambiguity and is fairly novel, but sealing against microwave leakage is hard and costly.

title: Single Warm Button
new_elements: One universal button (One button that runs a tuned warm cycle for most foods.)
rationale: A single button leaves nothing to choose, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single button removes choice and learning, but a one-size warm cycle may heat many foods poorly, and the idea is only mildly novel and vaguely defined.

title: Pre-Set Sixty Second Cook
new_elements: One-minute default cycle (Runs sixty seconds and adds more time with a single tap.)
rationale: A default minute removes the timer entirely and is hard to get wrong.
judge_comment: A default minute with a single-tap add is simple and easy to build, but many microwaves already offer quick-start, so it is barely novel.

title: Touch Handle Door
new_elements: Capacitive touch handle (A handle that opens the door when tapped, with no moving parts.)
rationale: A single tap is the natural action and needs no searching for a button.
judge_comment: A touch handle replaces a mechanical latch with a tap, but door opening is already easy, so it adds little for the learning curve and power-release safety is a concern.

title: Projected Food Window
new_elements: Door projector (Projects a live image of the food onto the door.)
rationale: The projected view replaces the lamp and works without a separate light inside.
judge_comment: A projected live image is novel but adds complexity, and it needs a camera and projector that cost more than a lamp.

title: Full-view conductive-film door
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide film (Thin conductive coating reflects microwaves while passing visible light.); Solid clear door panel (Full-view door with no holes, mesh, or lamp needed to see inside.)
rationale: Users see their food at a glance with no mesh or light to understand, so there is nothing to learn about checking the cavity.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive film is a plausible substitute for the mesh, but it only aids viewing the food and does little to remove operating complexity; the microwave-shielding and durability challenges are real.

title: Pop-up drawer cavity with no door
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Food tray slides out like a drawer; the cavity seals on closing.)
rationale: A drawer is a familiar motion that needs no instruction and no hinge awareness.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive motion and fairly novel, but sealing the microwaves around a sliding tray is hard and the door swap does not simplify the controls.

title: Top-lift lid like a slow cooker
new_elements: Top-lift lid (Whole upper cover lifts off like a rice cooker lid.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is the most intuitive kitchen action, so nothing needs learning.
judge_comment: Top-lift lid is intuitive but is awkward with heavy, hot, steaming loads, and it needs significant redesign for microwave shielding and safety interlocks.

title: Counterbalanced free-stop hinge
new_elements: Torsion counterbalance hinge (Door holds any angle and never slams or drops.)
rationale: A door that stays wherever it is left removes the worry of it swinging shut on the user.
judge_comment: A practical hinge, but it barely addresses operating simplicity or learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Magnetic levitation hinge
new_elements: Magnetic detent hinge (Magnets hold the door closed and open with a small, consistent force.)
rationale: Magnetic detents give clear, self-correcting closure, so users cannot leave the door ajar by mistake.
judge_comment: Magnetic detents are feasible and mildly helpful for closing the door, yet the name 'levitation' is misleading and the link to the need is weak.

title: Door-mounted camera screen
new_elements: Built-in camera with large display (Camera feeds a large fold-out screen showing the food inside.)
rationale: A large live view of the food removes the need to bend down or squint through a window.
judge_comment: A camera and screen aid viewing the food but add complexity rather than simplify operation, and heat and steam raise durability concerns.

title: Ready-when-green status light
new_elements: Ready status light (Single light goes from red to green when food is done.)
rationale: A single colour meaning done needs no reading at all.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and simple to build, but it only signals completion and is a common, incremental feature that does not address the operating steps.

title: Spoken done phrase
new_elements: Plain-speech alert (Speaks a short phrase such as Your food is ready.)
rationale: A spoken instruction in plain words is understood immediately by anyone.
judge_comment: Speech output is clear and cheap, but it is a common feature and covers only the done alert, not operation.

title: No power control, one smart pulse
new_elements: Auto-pulse heating (Fixed smart pulse pattern serves all foods.)
rationale: Removing the power control entirely removes the only thing users might get wrong.
judge_comment: It is radical and removes the control completely, but one pulse pattern is unlikely to heat all foods well and the pattern is not defined.

title: Fibre-optic door-edge light
new_elements: Fibre-optic light guide (Light from a door-edge LED is guided into the cavity through the glass.)
rationale: Light is delivered from outside, so no bulb sits inside to fail or get hot.
judge_comment: The light-guide mechanism is clearly described and plausible, but it only changes how the cavity is lit and does little for ease of operation.

title: Stationary cavity with mode stirrer
new_elements: Mode stirrer fan (Rotating metal fan spreads energy so no turntable is needed.)
rationale: Nothing moves in the cavity, so there is no turntable to fit, clean, or misplace.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves and mainly remove the turntable, which only slightly reduces operating complexity.

title: Pop-up lifting tray
new_elements: Lifting food tray (Tray rises to the top of the cavity when the door opens.)
rationale: Food rises to hand height, so users never reach into the back of the cavity.
judge_comment: A tray that rises on door opening is a novel ergonomic idea, but the mechanism is complex, adds hazards and cost, and is a weak fit for the SUBSTITUTE operator.

title: Phone Live View
new_elements: Cavity camera (Tiny camera that streams the inside of the cavity to the user's phone.); Remote food check (Shows food state on a phone the user already knows how to use.)
rationale: Checking food uses a familiar phone screen instead of a new interface.
judge_comment: A camera feed is feasible, but it adds an app and a setup step, which works against a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Glowing Cavity Walls
new_elements: Thermochromic cavity liner (Inner walls that change colour as the food heats, showing progress.); Heat progress display (Shows how hot the food is through colour alone.)
rationale: Colour reads at a glance, so no numbers or manual are needed.
judge_comment: A colour-changing liner gives an intuitive progress cue, but durability, cleaning, and accurate reading of food temperature are doubtful.

title: Learns Your Habits
new_elements: Usage memory chip (Stores the user's last few cycles and repeats them on demand.); Repeat last cycle (Runs the same settings the user chose before.)
rationale: After a single use, the machine already knows what the user wants.
judge_comment: Repeat-last is simple and highly feasible but common, and it does nothing for the first use or for varied foods.

title: Glowing Ring Ready
new_elements: Light ring (Light ring around the base that glows in colour to show status.); Colour status (Shows when the food is heating or done through colour.)
rationale: Colour is understood in any language, so no reading is needed.
judge_comment: Colour status helps understanding of state but doesn't simplify input, and it is a modest, obvious change.

title: Lift-Up Lid Cavity
new_elements: Lift lid (Top-opening lid that lifts like a bread bin and needs no swing clearance.); Top loading (Lets the user lift the lid and place food in.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is familiar from everyday objects, so it needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A top-opening lid is familiar and workable, but hot steam and heavy-lid handling are problems and it does little for controls.

title: Wireless Induction Base
new_elements: Induction power pad (Wireless charging-style pad that powers the cavity with no plug or cable.); Plugless operation (Powers on when placed on the pad.)
rationale: Putting the unit down is all that is needed, with no plug or switch to find.
judge_comment: Plugless power is a bold substitution, but wireless power at microwave levels (~1kW) is hard and it only removes the plug step, not the operating interface.

title: Built-In Video Tutor
new_elements: Lid projector (Projects a ten-second demo onto the counter when the lid is opened for the first time.); On-device tutorial (Teaches the basic use on the device itself.)
rationale: The machine teaches itself, so no paper manual is needed.
judge_comment: A projected demo helps first use, but it still means a learning step, which doesn't remove the learning curve, and a lid projector adds cost.

title: Hand-Shaped Handle
new_elements: Grip-shaped door pull (Door pull shaped to fit a hand, so it is obvious which way to pull.); Obvious opening (Makes the opening motion self-evident.)
rationale: The shape itself shows the user how to open the door.
judge_comment: Sensible affordance cue, but it is a trivial, common design tweak and only addresses opening the door, not operating the machine.

title: Walk-Up Auto Power
new_elements: Presence sensor (Sensor that wakes the display and offers a single default choice when the user walks up.); Wake-and-offer (Shows one clear option when someone approaches.)
rationale: Only one option is shown at a time, so the user is never faced with a panel of choices.
judge_comment: A presence sensor with a single default offer is easy to build and simplifies the interface, but a wrong default could frustrate users and the idea isn't radical.

title: Fridge Magnet Remote
new_elements: Magnetic programme card (Magnet that sticks to the fridge and programs the microwave when placed on the door.); Pre-set by magnet (Sets the cycle using a magnet kept with the food.)
rationale: The setting travels with the food, so the user never has to set anything at the microwave.
judge_comment: A magnet card that programs the microwave is a novel substitute for buttons, but the card-to-microwave link and the logistics of placing it on the fridge are unclear.

title: Grandma-Proof Single Light
new_elements: Traffic light indicator (Red, amber, and green light that shows stop, wait, and go.); Universal status (Shows the state of the machine in a way everyone understands.)
rationale: A traffic light is understood by everyone, so no training or manual is needed.
judge_comment: A traffic light is easy to understand and cheap, but it only shows status and doesn't simplify setting the cycle.

title: Dish Shape Recognition Tray
new_elements: Dish-shaped base plate (Plate with a cut-out that only fits matching dishes and locks the cycle.); Dish-locked cycle (The dish shape selects the programme.)
rationale: The dish itself selects the cycle, so wrong settings are physically impossible.
judge_comment: Dish shape selecting the programme makes wrong settings impossible, but it needs special dishes and the base plate is awkward for a microwave.

title: Wall-Mounted Single Button
new_elements: Wall plate starter (Wall plate with one button that starts the microwave in the kitchen.); Room-level start (Starts heating from a single fixed place in the room.)
rationale: Starting always happens in the same place, so no one needs to search the machine.
judge_comment: A wall button that starts the microwave is feasible, but it does not tell the user what to heat or for how long, and it separates the control from the appliance, so it only partly serves the need.

title: Self-Labelling Controls
new_elements: E-ink label (E-ink label beside each control that changes its text to suit the food loaded.); Context labels (Labels change to match the current situation.)
rationale: Labels that change to the context mean the user only sees the options that matter now.
judge_comment: Context-aware e-ink labels could simplify choices, but knowing the food loaded is hard, and changing labels may confuse users rather than remove the learning curve.

title: Haptic Done Handle
new_elements: Haptic door handle (A vibrating motor in the handle pulses when cooking ends, felt without sight or hearing.)
rationale: The end-of-cycle signal is felt in the hand, so it works for every user.
judge_comment: Haptic feedback is feasible and inclusive, but it only signals completion and may go unnoticed if the user is away from the unit.

title: Drop-Front Appliance
new_elements: Drop-front glass panel (The whole front drops forward on a counterbalance to load food, with no handle to find.)
rationale: Loading is one motion that the body already knows how to do.
judge_comment: A drop-front door with a counterbalance is plausible and intuitive, but it only addresses loading, not operation, and it is a modest change.

title: Ceramic Fuse to PTC Reset
new_elements: Resettable PTC polymer fuse (Self-resetting overcurrent device replaces the ceramic fuse, so the user never replaces one.)
rationale: A fault clears itself, so the user never has to open the oven or find a spare part.
judge_comment: PTC resettable fuse is a real substitution, but in a microwave the fuse is rarely user-facing, so it barely helps operation and is not radical; also safety fuses in HV circuits are typically non-resettable by design.

title: Self-Diagnosing Panel Light
new_elements: Single fault indicator (One coloured light shows any fault in plain terms, with no codes.)
rationale: A single colour light gives the user the next step without any codes to decode.
judge_comment: A single fault light is simple and helps users, but it is vague and adds a feature rather than substituting a part.

title: Single-Solid-State Interlock
new_elements: Solid-state door sensor (One Hall-effect sensor replaces the three microswitches and their wiring.)
rationale: One reliable sensor means fewer failures that could leave the user confused.
judge_comment: A Hall sensor replacing microswitches is concrete and plausible, but regulations require redundant interlocks and the user-facing benefit is minor.

title: Power Shield Lamp
new_elements: Cavity light sensor (Ambient light detects whether the door is open and lights the cavity only when needed.)
rationale: The light comes on exactly when the user looks, so there is no switch to remember.
judge_comment: Automatic cavity light removes a minor step, but most ovens already light on door opening, so it is an incremental improvement.

title: Snap-On Fascia Board
new_elements: Interchangeable control cartridge (A front panel snaps on as a cartridge, with the layout for the user's language or ability.)
rationale: Each user gets a panel they can understand, with no translation needed.
judge_comment: Swappable panels tailor layout to the user but add a cartridge to buy and manage, and it is not very radical.

title: Robot Reheat Assistant
new_elements: Companion robot arm (A small arm loads and unloads the cavity when the user presses one button.)
rationale: The machine does the handling, so the user only starts the job.
judge_comment: One-button robot handling simplifies use but is costly, bulky and impractical for a microwave, and it is more an add-on than a substitution.

title: Single-Mode Cooker
new_elements: Adaptive pulsing without user setting (Internal controller pulses power automatically from food feedback, so no power level is set.)
rationale: With no power setting to choose, there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Removing the power choice simplifies use, but the feedback mechanism is vague and sensing food state is hard.

title: Antenna Mode-Stirrer
new_elements: Rotating metal mode stirrer (Small metal paddle in the cavity reshapes the field so the food does not need to turn.); Mode stirring of RF field (Moving conductor redistributes standing waves.)
rationale: Food can be placed anywhere on a flat plate and it still heats evenly, so no positioning is needed.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves, and the benefit to operation simplicity is indirect.

title: Hourglass Liquid-Column Timer
new_elements: Coloured fluid time column (Column of coloured fluid that drains to show time left.)
rationale: Time is shown as a level going down, which can be read at a glance without numbers.
judge_comment: A fluid column gives an intuitive at-a-glance time display, but it is hard to build reliably in a microwave and it replaces only the display, not the input.

title: Breathing Light Ring Silent Mode
new_elements: Breathing light ring (Soft pulsing light ring around the control area that signals end of cycle.)
rationale: A visual signal works in a quiet house or for someone who cannot hear the bell.
judge_comment: A light ring is easy and helps accessibility, but it has little to do with learning to operate the oven and is not radical.

title: Top-Loading Pull-Out Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Cavity slides out like a drawer; food is placed on a flat tray.)
rationale: Pulling out a drawer is an action everyone already understands and needs no bending or reaching.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive action and eases loading, but it does not simplify the controls and has sealing and cost challenges.

title: Universal Auto-Range PSU
new_elements: Universal voltage autoranging (Power supply accepts 100 to 240 V at 50 or 60 Hz without a variant.)
rationale: One model works everywhere, so the user never picks the wrong version.
judge_comment: Autoranging power supplies are feasible and already common, and they only loosely serve operation simplicity by avoiding wrong-variant purchases.

title: One-Press Cook
new_elements: Single cook button (One large button that starts the cycle using a preset based on load and food sensing.)
rationale: A single press replaces two knobs, so the entire operating procedure is one obvious action.
judge_comment: One button is ideal for zero learning curve, but the food-sensing is vague and the idea is fairly obvious.

title: Top-Lift Lid
new_elements: Gas-strut lid (A top-opening lid lifts on gas struts and stays up without a hinge latch.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is the simplest possible way to open a container, so no latch needs explaining.
judge_comment: A gas-strut top lid is plausible and intuitive, but it only simplifies opening and does not address the controls where the learning curve sits.

title: Rotating Drum Cavity
new_elements: Self-rotating cooking drum (A cylindrical drum with a top-loading hatch tumbles food, which removes the need for both a door swing and a turntable.)
rationale: Food is heated evenly without any user action, so there is nothing to position or rotate.
judge_comment: A tumbling drum is radical and removes the positioning step, but it is impractical for liquids and plates and doesn't simplify operation of the controls.

title: Camera Preview Screen
new_elements: Door camera with large screen (A camera inside the cavity streams to a large display on the front panel.)
rationale: A large display showing the food makes the state of cooking obvious without any training.
judge_comment: A camera and screen are feasible and make cooking status obvious, but they add cost and are an obvious, non-radical feature.

title: Light-Pipe Interior
new_elements: Fibre-optic light pipe (A light pipe carries LED light from outside the cavity to the inside, with no bulb or heat source inside.)
rationale: The cavity stays lit with no hot element to avoid, so the interior is safer to look into.
judge_comment: Light pipe substitutes the bulb sensibly, but it barely affects ease of operation and fibre inside a microwave cavity has practical issues.

title: Scent Done Signal
new_elements: Scented cook-end release (A small cartridge releases a food-like aroma when cooking is done.)
rationale: Smell tells the user the food is ready even when they are in another room.
judge_comment: Novel end-of-cook cue, but it addresses notification rather than operating the microwave, and it adds cartridges that need replacing.

title: Auto-Open at Finish
new_elements: Auto-release door (The door unlatches and opens a few centimetres when cooking finishes.)
rationale: The user does not need to remember to open the door, so food is never left inside.
judge_comment: Practical and easy to build, and some microwaves already open on finish, but it only removes a minor end-of-cook step.

title: Glowing Power Bar
new_elements: Heat intensity bar (A horizontal bar of light that fills more as the power rises, shown on the front panel.)
rationale: A bar that fills with heat gives an obvious sense of power with no numbers to read.
judge_comment: A power-level bar display is easy to build and slightly clearer, but the user still has to set power and time, so it only marginally cuts the learning curve.

title: Power-by-Colour Dial
new_elements: Colour ring dial (Power is shown by a colour ring that moves from blue for gentle to red for strong.)
rationale: Colour meanings such as blue and red are understood by almost everyone without teaching.
judge_comment: A colour ring dial is intuitive and cheap, but blue-to-red is a weak substitution for numeric power and does not remove the need to set time.

title: Cheap Coin Timer
new_elements: Single-chip timer (A single microcontroller with a segment display replaces the cam timer and bell.)
rationale: A single chip is cheap to build and easy to set up on one large screen.
judge_comment: Digital timers already dominate microwaves, so this is hardly new, though a single large display could help simplicity somewhat.

title: Stationary Multi-Feed
new_elements: Multi-feed waveguide (Several waveguide feeds heat the cavity evenly, so the turntable is not needed.)
rationale: Even heating without a moving part means there is nothing to misplace or stop turning.
judge_comment: Multi-feed waveguides replace the turntable in a genuinely radical substitution, but they only loosely support learning-free operation, mostly by removing a part, and add cost and complexity.

title: Bell-Free Tone Chime
new_elements: Low-frequency done tone (A slow, low-frequency tone sounds at the end, tuned to be heard by people with hearing loss.)
rationale: An end signal tuned to older ears is heard without any setting or adjustment.
judge_comment: A low-frequency done tone is easy to build and helps older users, but it barely affects operational simplicity.

title: Door Glow Heat Meter
new_elements: Window-edge LED strip (An LED strip along the window edge shows the heat level by changing its glow.)
rationale: The heat state is visible from across the room with no labels to read.
judge_comment: A feasible, easy-to-read status indicator, but it only displays heat state and doesn't simplify operation or substitute the controls; it's also an incremental, not radical, change.

title: Hourglass Timer Window
new_elements: Sand-flow timer column (A transparent column where fine sand runs through a fixed gauge, visible through the door window.); Gravity-driven hourglass metering (Purely mechanical flow timing with no electronics.)
rationale: Users see time running out as sand falls, so no numbers have to be read or set.
judge_comment: A visual hourglass is intuitive but cannot set variable times without a user input, and it is awkward to build into a microwave door.

title: Magnetic Soft-Close Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch door (A door that closes and seals with magnets and opens with a gentle pull.); Permanent-magnet seal (Magnetic seal that holds the door shut and releases on pull.)
rationale: Closing the door is a simple push and opening it is a simple pull, with no mechanism to understand.
judge_comment: Magnetic door is simple to use, but microwave door seals need choke-based RF containment and a magnetic catch alone is questionable.

title: Sliding Drawer Door
new_elements: Sliding drawer door (A door that slides sideways like a drawer, not swinging out.); Rail-guided sliding seal (A rail system with a compressed gasket keeping the cavity sealed.)
rationale: A door that slides like a drawer needs no swing space and no understanding of hinges.
judge_comment: A sideways drawer door is plausible and saves swing space, but the microwave-sealing gasket on a sliding rail is hard and it adds little to the no-learning-curve need.

title: Stirrer-Fan Substitute
new_elements: Rotating RF stirrer (A rotating metal vane that spreads microwaves evenly so the food does not need to be turned.); Mode stirrer (A mechanical stirrer that makes the field even across the cavity.)
rationale: Even heating without a turntable means there is no plate to misplace or re-align.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves and the link to simple operation is weak.

title: Plateless Cavity
new_elements: Platform-free cavity (A flat cavity with no turntable, using the stirrer for even heating.); Removes plate handling (Eliminates putting the plate back in after washing or misaligning it.)
rationale: With no removable plate to refit, there is nothing to get wrong after cleaning.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable eliminates a misplacement issue and is plausible, though stirrer-only models already exist and the benefit is modest.

title: Ceramic Cooking Dome
new_elements: Ceramic dome cover (A dome cover of microwave-transparent ceramic that is placed over the food in its dish.); Microwave-transparent ceramic (A ceramic that passes microwaves with very low loss and handles thermal shock.)
rationale: Users lift a dome off the dish to see the food, with no door or window to understand.
judge_comment: A dome with no door is a wild idea, but it doesn't explain how the dome contains microwaves or how the user operates the unit; a ceramic dome is transparent to microwaves and would leak.

title: Counter-Level Drawer Cook
new_elements: Drawer cavity (A cooking cavity inside a counter drawer that pulls out to load food at a comfortable height.); Brings food to hand height (Places the cavity where the user can reach it without bending or lifting.)
rationale: A drawer at waist height means no bending, lifting or searching for the door.
judge_comment: Microwave drawers exist and improve ergonomics, but they don't really reduce the learning curve of operating the controls, and it isn't a substitution of a cheaper or simpler part.

title: Glass-Lift Turntable Handle
new_elements: Turntable lift grip (A grip on the turntable that lifts the plate out for cleaning, with no clip to undo.); Removes plate without tools (Lifts the plate out with one hand.)
rationale: A single grip that lifts the plate out makes cleaning as simple as the cooking.
judge_comment: It is simple and feasible, but it addresses cleaning rather than operating the microwave, so it is only tangentially relevant.

title: One-Button Heat
new_elements: Single large HEAT button (One oversized button starts a sensor-guided cook cycle.); Starts default cook cycle with one press (Device chooses time and power automatically.)
rationale: A single big button removes every setting, so there is nothing to learn before the first use.
judge_comment: Zero learning curve, but a single button with automatic cooking is vague and may cook many foods poorly.

title: Scent Cue Finish
new_elements: Aroma cartridge (Releases a toast or cinnamon scent when cooking ends.); Signals completion by smell (Scent cue for the end of the cycle.)
rationale: A smell is an instinctive cue that works without reading, timing, or pressing anything.
judge_comment: A scent cue is wild and original, but cartridges are consumable, ambiguous and impractical, with only a weak link to operation simplicity.

title: Magnetic Soft-Release Door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch (Magnets hold the door shut; a light pull opens it.); Opens door with a gentle pull (No button or lever needed.)
rationale: A door that opens when pulled needs no button to find, so first-time users open it correctly on instinct.
judge_comment: Pull-to-open is intuitive and technically easy, but it is a minor tweak, many microwaves already work this way, and it covers only door opening.

title: ITO-Coated Transparent Door
new_elements: ITO-coated glass door panel (Indium-tin-oxide film blocks microwaves and stays transparent.); Transparent conductive oxide film (Thin conductive coating on glass.)
rationale: A clear door view with no mesh or lamp leaves nothing to clean or replace, so the door is simply a window.
judge_comment: ITO glass is plausible and concrete, but it barely affects ease of operation and is not a radical substitution; it is mainly a cleaning and visibility benefit.

title: Bell-Jar Cloche Cavity
new_elements: Domed glass cloche (Dome lid sits over a plate, and its metal-lined top forms the cavity.); Contains RF with a lift-on lid (Lid lifts off to load food.)
rationale: Lifting a dome to put a plate in is as simple as any kitchen task.
judge_comment: Lift-off dome is intuitive to use, but a glass dome with a metal-lined top and RF leakage at the lift-off seam is very hard to make safe.

title: Halogen Crisp Emitter
new_elements: Halogen radiant element (Quartz halogen lamp element heats surfaces to brown them.); Browns and crisps food surfaces (Infrared radiation browns the outside.)
rationale: One mode button gives crisp results, so no one needs to learn how to combine appliances.
judge_comment: Combination browning is already common and a single crisp button helps simplicity somewhat, but it adds a feature rather than substituting a part.

title: Disposable Mica Cover
new_elements: Paper-backed mica tab (Cheap, pre-cut disposable cover slots into the waveguide.); Replaceable splatter guard for the waveguide (Changes in seconds.)
rationale: A cover you throw away when dirty removes a hard-to-clean part from the user's job.
judge_comment: Disposable mica covers are practical and concrete, and they ease cleaning, but they have little to do with operation.

title: Top-Hinged Lift Lid
new_elements: Top-hinged lift lid (Lid lifts up from the top like a toaster lid.); Opens from above (Nothing projects into the user's way.)
rationale: A lid that lifts straight up is how most people already open a box or a toaster.
judge_comment: A familiar top-lift lid is intuitive, but there are hinge, seal and ergonomics concerns and it does not simplify the control interface.

title: Thermochrome Done Plate
new_elements: Thermochromic turntable ring (Ring changes from blue to red as the food reaches temperature.); Thermochromic pigments (Pigments that change colour with temperature.)
rationale: A colour change tells the user the food is ready without any sound or reading.
judge_comment: A thermochromic ring shows when food is done, but it only reflects tray or surface temperature, not the food's, and it does nothing to simplify setting up the cook.

title: Approach-to-Open Door
new_elements: Proximity door actuator (Door swings open when a hand approaches the handle.); Capacitive proximity sensing (Detects a hand near a surface without contact.)
rationale: Opening the door works the way a person expects, with no button to find.
judge_comment: A hands-free door is intuitive, but an automatic swinging door risks accidental opening and hits people, and it solves only a minor part of operation.

title: Projected Cooking Status
new_elements: Door-face projector (Projects a large, simple progress bar onto the door glass.); Micro-projection (Small projector for showing graphics on a surface.)
rationale: Progress is shown as a large image that needs no reading ability beyond seeing a bar fill up.
judge_comment: A projected progress bar makes status clear, but it is a display add-on rather than a simpler way to operate and it adds cost.

title: Wireless Bowl Base
new_elements: Resonant coupling base (Powers any bowl placed on the base without a plug or cord.); Wireless power transfer (Transfers energy across a short air gap.)
rationale: Putting a bowl down is the only action required to start heating.
judge_comment: Placing a bowl to start is very simple, but resonant coupling only heats induction-compatible vessels, so 'any bowl' is doubtful and it isn't food heating as microwaves do.

title: Self-Stirring Plate
new_elements: Rotating food cradle (A cradle that fits any plate shape and rotates it without alignment.); Auto-centre food (Plates are automatically centred on the rotation axis.)
rationale: No alignment step means the user cannot put the food down wrongly.
judge_comment: Auto-centring removes a small step, though turntables already work without alignment and the self-centring mechanism is vague.

title: Chime-Free Haptic Pulse
new_elements: Warm vibration pad (A gentle warm vibration in the handle signals the end of cooking.); Haptic actuation (Produces touch feedback.)
rationale: A felt buzz in the hand is noticed even by people who cannot hear a bell.
judge_comment: Haptic end-of-cook alerts are helpful but only work if a hand is on the handle, and they don't simplify operation much.

title: Hand-Shape Dial
new_elements: Grip-sensing dial (A dial that reads how firmly it is held and turns power up or down.); Force-based control (Pressing harder increases heat.)
rationale: Pressing harder for more heat mirrors how people already use a stove burner.
judge_comment: Grip-force control is novel and loosely mirrors a stove, but holding a dial to cook is awkward and is arguably less intuitive than a simple start button.

title: Plate-Shaped Cavity
new_elements: Flat plate chamber (A shallow chamber shaped like a plate, with no turntable needed.); Heat-what-you-see (Food is heated in the same form it is served in.)
rationale: Putting a plate on a plate-shaped space is the most obvious action possible.
judge_comment: The plate-shaped cavity is an intuitive concept, but a flat chamber without a turntable struggles with even heating and with bowls or mugs, and it doesn't address the controls.

title: Sealed Smart Pouch
new_elements: Self-cooking pouch (A pouch with a microwave-absorbing layer that reads its own content and heats itself.); Susceptor film (Thin film that absorbs microwaves and converts them to heat.)
rationale: The food packaging itself does the cooking, so the user only places it in the oven.
judge_comment: Packaging that cooks itself would make operation effortless, but susceptor film cannot read its contents or regulate heating on its own, and the idea only works for packaged food.

title: Chalk-Mark Recipes
new_elements: Drawn-on recipe surface (Users draw a simple picture or dot pattern on a board to set cooking.); Image-based input (Recognises simple drawn marks.)
rationale: Drawing a picture of what to cook needs no manual or number entry.
judge_comment: Drawing to set cooking is unusual, but it adds a learning step and is more complex than pressing a button.

title: Ambient Cooking Mood
new_elements: Ambient glow wall (The cavity walls glow a soft colour that shifts as food heats.); Electroluminescent panel (A thin panel that lights a surface evenly.)
rationale: Colour change tells the story of cooking without any reading or setting required.
judge_comment: Colour glow is an eye-catching status cue but does not help the user operate the microwave, and it adds cost.

title: Chirping Bird Finish
new_elements: Recorded bird-song finish cue (A pleasant audio cue and gentle light flash replace the harsh bell at the end of cooking.)
rationale: A friendly, unmistakable finish signal reduces anxiety for elderly users who may miss the bell.
judge_comment: A friendlier finish cue helps a little, but it does little for operation with no learning curve.

title: Scent-Ready Alert
new_elements: Warm-aroma release at completion (A tiny heated reservoir releases a warm food scent when cooking ends, signalling completion without sound.)
rationale: Smell is an intuitive signal that needs no reading, hearing, or learning.
judge_comment: A novel completion signal, but it only covers the end of cooking and does nothing to simplify setting up; it also isn't a substitution for a part.

title: Reheat Memory Button
new_elements: Last-used memory (The microwave remembers the last setting, and one button repeats it.)
rationale: Repeating a familiar setting with one button means the user only learns it once.
judge_comment: Memory buttons already exist and the first use still requires learning, so it is neither radical nor new.

title: Touch-to-Open Glass
