new_elements: Capacitive touch panel (The whole door face is a touch surface; a firm press anywhere opens the door.)
rationale: Opening the door by pressing anywhere on it removes the need to find a small button.
judge_comment: Pressing anywhere on the door is easy to use, but a capacitive door adds cost and risks accidental opening.

title: Auto-Eject Door
new_elements: Spring-eject door (When cooking ends, the door pops slightly open by itself so the user knows the food is ready.)
rationale: A door that opens itself at the end removes the need for any action after cooking.
judge_comment: A door that pops open at the end is simple and feasible, and it signals completion, but many microwaves already open on a button press and it does little for operating simplicity.

title: Drawer Cavity
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (The whole cooking cavity slides out like a drawer, so food is placed from the front.)
rationale: Pulling out a drawer is a familiar motion that brings food to the user.
judge_comment: A drawer cavity is familiar and novel, but it is hard to build with microwave shielding and a stable turntable, and it only affects loading.

title: Projected Cavity View
new_elements: Built-in camera with screen (A small camera inside streams the cavity to a flat screen on the door.)
rationale: A screen view shows the food clearly, with no need to press the door close to the glass.
judge_comment: A camera and screen is feasible but adds complexity and cost, and replaces a window that already works, so it does little for ease of operation.

title: Thermochromic Heat Walls
new_elements: Thermochromic cavity coating (The cavity walls change color as they heat up, so the user can see when cooking is working.)
rationale: A color change tells the user the state of cooking without any display or reading.
judge_comment: The color change gives intuitive feedback, but it lags behind the food's state and cavity walls don't heat much in a microwave.

title: Magnetic Floating Hinge
new_elements: Magnetic levitation hinge (Magnets hold the door at a set angle and let it float open with a light touch.)
rationale: A door that floats open with a light touch is effortless for anyone.
judge_comment: A magnetic door is effortless to use, but levitation is impractical and costly, and a door needs to latch securely for safety.

title: Food-Touch Start
new_elements: Food-contact sensor plate (Touching the food to the plate starts a standard heat cycle automatically.)
rationale: Starting cooking by placing food removes every control step.
judge_comment: Starting by touching food to a plate removes steps, but it is unsafe and impractical with containers, and an unclear heat cycle makes it a poor fit.

title: Voice-Free Gesture Panel
new_elements: Swipe-up cooking gesture (Swiping up on the panel starts cooking and swiping down stops it.)
rationale: Simple up-and-down gestures are universal and need no labels or learning.
judge_comment: Swipe gestures are simple, but they are not self-evident without labels, and they give no way to set time or power.

title: Bell-Free Vibrating Coaster
new_elements: Vibrating finish coaster (A coaster the user can place near them that vibrates when cooking ends.)
rationale: A vibration reaches users who are hard of hearing and does not disturb others.
judge_comment: Vibrating coaster is a feasible alert, but it addresses end-of-cook notification rather than operation simplicity and isn't really a substitution that simplifies use.

title: Turntable Speed Indicator
new_elements: Turntable speed as power cue (The turntable spins faster on higher power, so the user can see the setting in motion.)
rationale: Visible motion shows power level without requiring any reading.
judge_comment: Turntable speed as a power cue is an intuitive visible signal, though it adds mechanical complexity and speed differences may be hard to read.

title: Glass Door Heat Warning
new_elements: Warm-glass warning band (A warning band on the door changes color when outer temperature is high.)
rationale: Visible heat warning keeps elderly users from touching a hot surface by accident.
judge_comment: A thermochromic warning band is cheap and feasible, but it concerns safety, not learning-free operation.

title: Proximity Door Opener
new_elements: Capacitive proximity door sensor (Detects a hand approaching the door and releases the latch.)
rationale: Walking up to the microwave and touching the door opens it, with no button to find.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but it only simplifies opening the door, which is a minor part of operation.

title: Open-to-Stop Door
new_elements: Stops heating when door opens (Opening the door is the only action needed to stop heating.)
rationale: Stopping is the same motion as taking food out, so there is nothing new to learn.
judge_comment: Microwaves already stop when the door opens via safety interlocks, so this is not new and adds little to simplicity.

title: Chime-Free Scent Alert
new_elements: Scent cartridge (Releases a mild toast or popcorn smell when cooking ends.)
rationale: The smell tells the user the food is ready without any sound to interpret.
judge_comment: A scent alert is novel but consumables add cost, and it only replaces the chime, which is not a learning barrier.

title: Haptic Door Handle Alert
new_elements: Handle vibration motor (Gently vibrates the door handle when cooking finishes.)
rationale: A buzz in the hand is noticed even in a noisy kitchen and needs no interpretation.
judge_comment: A vibrating handle is feasible and intuitive, but it addresses only the alert and adds little to ease of operation.

title: No-Turntable Phased Heating
new_elements: Phased-array field steering (Electronic control moves the hot spots around the cavity so food heats evenly.)
rationale: Nothing moves inside the oven, so there is no tray to load or clean.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with field steering is real and removes the tray, which simplifies use, but it is costly and still maturing.

title: Metal-Tolerant Cavity Coating
new_elements: Plasma-sprayed ceramic lining (A coating that stops arcing from metal items inside the cavity.)
rationale: Users can heat a metal-rimmed plate without thinking about the rules.
judge_comment: Removing the metal rule would cut a learning burden, but a coating cannot realistically stop arcing from metal in microwaves, and the plasma-sprayed ceramic is a loose fit for the need.

title: Kettle-Style Single Button
new_elements: One-press start pad (A large pad that starts cooking, with the machine picking everything else.)
rationale: Using a kettle-style pad requires no reading, so it is obvious to any user.
judge_comment: Very simple to operate, but a one-button start with the machine choosing everything is a known concept and it never explains how the oven knows what to cook.

title: Cavity Q-Factor Thermostat
new_elements: Cavity resonance sensing (Measures the cavity's resonance to tell how much food is inside and how hot it is.)
rationale: No separate thermostat is needed, so the machine has fewer parts that can fail.
judge_comment: Resonance sensing could enable auto-cooking with no settings, but it is technically hard and the stated benefit (fewer parts) is only loosely tied to ease of use.

title: Shape-Memory Latch
new_elements: Shape-memory alloy latch (A wire that bends the latch open when warmed by a small current.)
rationale: The latch opens smoothly on its own, so no lever or button needs learning.
judge_comment: A shape-memory latch is a real substitution but adds slow, power-hungry actuation, and it is unclear how it removes anything the user must learn.

title: Safe-Glass Plate Warning
new_elements: Heat-indicating glass plate (A plate with a colour panel that shows when it is too hot to touch.)
rationale: The user can see at a glance whether a plate is safe to handle.
judge_comment: Thermochromic plate is plausible and helpful, but it concerns safety after cooking rather than simple operation of the microwave.

title: Touch Anywhere Door
new_elements: Capacitive door surface (Touching any part of the door face releases the latch.)
rationale: There is no small button to find, so anyone can open the door on first contact.
judge_comment: A touch-anywhere door helps opening only and doesn't address cooking setup, the main learning burden; it also raises safety concerns about accidental opening.

title: Window Becomes Mirror
new_elements: Electrochromic door glass (The door window turns from opaque to clear when the oven is powered on.)
rationale: The glass shows the cooking state, so the user does not need a separate lamp or indicator.
judge_comment: Electrochromic door glass gives an intuitive on/off state cue and could replace a lamp, but it only weakly improves operation simplicity and the title is confusing.

title: Self-Centring Dish Well
new_elements: Bowl-shaped self-centring tray (A dished tray guides any plate to the centre and holds it steady.)
rationale: The tray places food correctly by shape, so the user never has to think about placement.
judge_comment: A dished self-centring tray is simple and plausible and removes placement thinking, but it is incremental and may interfere with the microwave pattern and with some dish shapes.

title: Cordless Induction Puck
new_elements: Solid-state RF heating (A solid-state amplifier replaces the magnetron and its high-voltage parts.)
rationale: Removing the high-voltage parts removes the need for a cord warning or a discharge procedure.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a real, radical substitution, but the stated benefit (no cord warning or discharge procedure) barely touches operational simplicity for the user.

title: Inductive Base Pad
new_elements: Wireless base station (The oven sits on a base that supplies power by induction, with no plug to insert.)
rationale: Setting the oven on a pad is the only action required to connect power.
judge_comment: Placing the oven on a pad removes plug handling, but high-power inductive transfer is tricky and only a minor part of operating a microwave.

title: Solid-State HV Free
new_elements: Low-voltage gallium nitride driver (A low-voltage driver makes high-voltage storage unnecessary.)
rationale: No stored lethal charge means the user never needs to wait or worry after unplugging.
judge_comment: A GaN low-voltage driver is plausible and novel, but the benefit is safety peace of mind, not learning-free operation.

title: Voice Phrases Only
new_elements: Plain phrase recognition (The oven responds to everyday phrases such as 'warm my soup'.)
rationale: Speaking the request in ordinary words replaces any control or manual.
judge_comment: Voice control is plausible and needs no learning, but it is already common and is not really a substitution for a cheaper or simpler part.

title: Metal-Safe Cavity
new_elements: Foil-tolerant cavity coating (The cavity tolerates metal and prevents arcing automatically.)
rationale: The user does not need to learn which containers are safe.
judge_comment: A cavity that tolerates metal would remove a major learning barrier, but it is physically implausible and the coating is vague.

title: Browning Tray Hint
new_elements: Self-browning tray (A tray with a crisping layer that browns food without any setting.)
rationale: Browning happens with no extra settings, so the user gets crisp food without learning a function.
judge_comment: A self-browning tray already exists in the form of susceptor-based crisping, so it removes a setting but adds little that is new.

title: Stop Button Only Door
new_elements: Single stop gesture (A single large pad stops and opens the oven in one action.)
rationale: One large pad with one meaning is the simplest possible stop control.
judge_comment: A single stop/open pad is simple, but it only covers stopping and does not address how to start or set cooking, and it is not very radical.

title: Lift-to-Open Glass Dome
new_elements: Counterbalanced glass dome (A transparent dome that lifts straight up like a cloche, with no latch.); Gas-spring counterbalance (Spring balance that holds the dome open at any height.)
rationale: Lifting a dome is understood immediately by anyone, so no release mechanism needs explaining.
judge_comment: A dome is intuitive to open but is a poor fit for microwave shielding and safety, and it does not simplify the actual cooking controls.

title: Wearable Done Buzz
new_elements: Wrist buzzer (A small wristband that vibrates when the food is ready.); Short-range radio pairing (Pairs automatically with the microwave out of the box.)
rationale: The user is alerted wherever they are in the home, with nothing to configure.
judge_comment: Wearable buzzer is technically easy but adds a device to own and wear, and is not a simplification of operation.

title: E-Ink Door Glass
new_elements: E-ink door panel (A door window that shows a large single icon of the cook state.); Bistable display (Keeps its image with no power draw.)
rationale: A single large icon is understood without reading or setup.
judge_comment: A single state icon helps comprehension, but e-ink refreshes slowly and the idea does nothing for input, which is where the learning curve sits.

title: Hand-Wave Stop
new_elements: Gesture sensor (A sensor that stops the cycle when the user waves a hand in front of it.); Gesture cancel (Stops cooking with a simple wave.)
rationale: A wave is instinctive, so stopping the machine needs no button hunt.
judge_comment: Wave-to-stop is easy to use, but it covers only cancelling and risks false triggers, so it does little for overall operation.

title: Open-Lid Auto Heat
new_elements: Clamshell hinge (A top-hinged lid that lifts and heats when set down closed.); Lid-based heat (The heat starts when the lid is lowered.)
rationale: Lowering a lid is a familiar motion, so the machine opens and starts without any instructions.
judge_comment: Lowering a lid to start is intuitive, but the description is muddled (it lifts and heats?), it gives no way to set time or power, and it raises safety questions.

title: Sound-Free Done Pulse
new_elements: Light pulse on counter (A pale pulse on the top surface when cooking is done.); Silent completion (Shows the end without noise.)
rationale: A visible pulse at the top works in quiet kitchens and needs no decoding.
judge_comment: A light pulse on completion is easy to build but only marginally affects operation, and it is not a substitution for an operating part.

title: Read-Aloud Done Count
new_elements: Countdown speaker (Says how many seconds are left at set points.); Spoken progress (Shares time remaining aloud.)
rationale: Spoken time means the user never needs to look at a display or dial.
judge_comment: Spoken countdown is easy to build, but it only gives output and does not simplify operation or substitute any part.

title: Glove-Proof Big Keys
new_elements: Oversized key pad (Large keys that work with oven gloves or wet hands.); Forgiving input (Keys work even with imprecise presses.)
rationale: Big forgiving keys mean that mistakes are hard to make and easy to fix.
judge_comment: Easy to use but large keys are an incremental, common improvement and not a radical substitution.

title: Ambient Light Done Glow
new_elements: Warm glow base (A base that softly glows warm orange when food is ready.); Quiet completion (Signals completion without sound or words.)
rationale: A gentle glow is understood at once and suits any room.
judge_comment: A nice completion cue, but it addresses only the end of the task and not operation itself.

title: Door-Glass Touch Pictures
new_elements: Touch-glass picture panel (Door glass that accepts taps on pictures of food.); Tap-on-door control (Controls live on the door itself.)
rationale: Controls sit where the user is already looking, so no hunting is needed.
judge_comment: Putting controls on the door is sensible, but touch glass on a hot door adds cost and heat issues, and it still needs menu navigation.

title: Wave-to-Open Door
new_elements: Proximity door sensor (Door opens automatically when a hand is held near the handle.)
rationale: The door responds to the natural gesture of reaching for it, so no button is needed.
judge_comment: Proximity-triggered opening is easy and plausible, but it risks accidental opening and only addresses door opening.

title: Hot-Plate Ring Feedback
new_elements: Thermal indicator ring (Ring on the outside of the cavity changes colour when the walls get hot.)
rationale: A visible hot-warning replaces an invisible thermostat the user can't check.
judge_comment: A simple visual hot-warning is easy to understand and feasible, but it is incremental and only peripheral to operation.

title: Ambient-Light Interior Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera module (Small camera mounted in the ceiling streams the cavity to the door display.)
rationale: Users see inside without needing a bulb or window, so they see food state at a glance.
judge_comment: A camera with a display shows food state intuitively, but it adds cost and complexity and sits awkwardly with the substitute operator, with heat and steam challenges.

title: Door Window Projection
new_elements: Door display projector (Projects a clear image of the food and timer onto the door glass.)
rationale: Status appears on the door where the user looks, without a separate panel.
judge_comment: Projecting status onto the door glass is an intuitive, panel-free idea, but brightness, the shielding mesh, and cost make it hard to realize.

title: Magnetic Gear Turntable
new_elements: Magnetic drive hub (Turntable is driven by a magnetic coupling so the plate lifts out and needs no spindle.)
rationale: The plate drops in and out without alignment, so cleaning and loading take no thought.
judge_comment: Magnetic coupling is plausible and makes the plate easier to drop in, but it mostly eases cleaning rather than operation.

title: Hand-Gesture Power Wave
new_elements: Gesture sensor (Sensor on the front detects a swipe to change power and a tap to start.)
rationale: Swipes are learned from a phone, so the controls feel familiar at first touch.
judge_comment: Gesture control adds a new interaction to learn and is less reliable than buttons with greasy or wet hands, so it does not really simplify operation.

title: Phone Cook Card
new_elements: Phone tap cooking (User taps phone to oven to send a full cooking program in one go.)
rationale: The phone holds the instructions, so the oven needs no buttons at all.
judge_comment: Phone tap programming requires a phone and an app, which adds a learning burden and dependency rather than removing it, and it replaces buttons with something more complex.

title: Cup-Shaped Microwave
new_elements: Mug-shaped oven (Mug-sized oven where the cup itself is the cavity and it heats when placed on the base.)
rationale: A cup-sized appliance needs no timer or cavity decisions for one person's meal.
judge_comment: A mug-sized single-serve oven is a plausible simplification, but it doesn't clearly remove timer decisions and it barely substitutes any part.

title: Auto-Discharge Passive Key
new_elements: Passive bleed network (Resistor network drains the capacitor within a second of switch-off.)
rationale: The charge is gone before anyone can touch it, so no warning label is needed.
judge_comment: A bleed resistor is already standard practice in microwaves and does nothing for ease of operation.

title: Ice-Cube Heat Control
new_elements: Phase-change heat sink (Wax pad absorbs excess heat so food never overcooks at any power level.)
rationale: Overcooking is physically blocked, so the user cannot make a costly mistake.
judge_comment: Wax heat sink preventing overcooking is novel, but microwaves heat food not the oven, so a pad can't absorb food heat without wasting energy; it only loosely serves simplicity.

title: Gravity Feed Door
new_elements: Self-closing gravity door (Door swings shut under spring tension after food is placed.)
rationale: The door closes itself, so there is nothing to forget or fail to latch.
judge_comment: Self-closing door is plausible and removes a small step, but it's a modest, known mechanism (and a safety/pinch concern) with limited impact on learning curve.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Capacitive door panel (Large flat panel that opens the door when pressed anywhere)
rationale: No button to hunt for, so opening the door is obvious.
judge_comment: Opening the door is already simple, so this solves a minor problem, and a touch-activated door is awkward when hands are full and could open by accident.

title: Tap-to-Add Puck
new_elements: Tap puck (Each tap adds 10 seconds and the heat stops when the puck is removed)
rationale: Counting taps is simpler than reading a dial and works for short durations.
judge_comment: Tap counting is simple, but the puck-removal stop is unclear and adds a loose part, so it is only a modest gain over existing +30s buttons.

title: Heat-Map Glass Display
new_elements: Printed heat-map film (Film on the door window that changes colour as the food warms)
rationale: Colour shows progress at a glance, with no timer to read.
judge_comment: Colour-changing film is a creative substitute for a timer display, but it is hard to make reliable for food temperature through the door and it does not control the cooking.

title: Built-In Stir Rod
new_elements: Spring stir rod (Small rod that stirs liquid when cooking starts to break up superheating)
rationale: The machine prevents eruptions by itself so users never need to know about superheating.
judge_comment: A built-in stir rod to prevent superheating removes a hidden safety concern without user knowledge, but it is mechanically awkward in a microwave cavity and only helps with liquids.

title: Crisp Floor Susceptor
new_elements: Ceramic susceptor plate (Plate that heats up and crisps the underside of food)
rationale: Food comes out browned with no setting to choose.
judge_comment: Susceptor plates exist and give browning automatically, but the link to a no-learning-curve interface is weak and it doesn't clearly substitute a part.

title: Metal Detection Ring
new_elements: Metal sensing loop (Detects metal in the cavity and blocks heating)
rationale: The machine refuses to start with metal inside, so the user never has to guess what is safe.
judge_comment: Metal detection removes a safety guess and is plausible, but reliable detection is hard and it's an addition rather than a substitution.

title: Magnetic Snap-On Cord
new_elements: Magnetic plug connector (Plug snaps into the socket and cannot be inserted the wrong way)
rationale: Plugging in is effortless and cannot be done wrong.
judge_comment: A magnetic plug is mistake-proof, but plugging in is a one-time setup, not an operating learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Ambient Glow Cavity Walls
new_elements: Electroluminescent wall film (Thin film on the cavity walls that glows softly when the cavity is in use)
rationale: The whole cavity lights evenly, so the user sees inside without a bulb in the way.
judge_comment: Electroluminescent walls are novel and plausible to a degree, but even lighting only marginally aids ease of operation, and film inside a microwave cavity faces RF and heat issues.

title: Hands-Free Foot Pedal
new_elements: Foot pedal (Floor pedal that opens the door when pressed with a foot)
rationale: When hands are full, the foot opens the door with no thought.
judge_comment: A foot pedal that opens the door is easy to grasp and feasible, but it only covers door opening and not operating the oven.

title: Sealed Door Auto-Lock Lights Only
new_elements: Door-open lockout (Heat cuts out whenever the door is open, with no interlock dial)
rationale: Safety is automatic, so the user has nothing to check.
judge_comment: Door-open lockout is already standard in every microwave, so it adds nothing new, though it does remove a safety check from the user.

title: Tray-Is-The-Controller
new_elements: Load-cell food recognition (Weight and shape of the placed dish identify the food and set power automatically.)
rationale: Placing food on the tray is the only action, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Placing the dish as the only action is simple, but weight and shape cannot reliably identify food, and the tray rotates.

title: Glass Door Becomes Touch Panel
new_elements: Proximity-sensing door (The door opens when a hand or plate approaches, with no button to find.)
rationale: A door that opens by approach removes the need to find and press a release button.
judge_comment: An approach-opening door is easy to build and removes one step, but it risks accidental opening and doesn't address how cooking is set up; the title (touch panel) doesn't match the idea.

title: Speak Your Dinner
new_elements: Plain-speech voice control (The user says 'warm soup' or 'defrost bread' and the machine does it.)
rationale: Ordinary speech needs no menus or symbols, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Voice control needs no learning and is feasible, but it is already common in appliances and the idea is described vaguely.

title: Steam Window Self-Clears
new_elements: Heated anti-fog glass (The door glass stays clear automatically so the food is always visible.)
rationale: Clear viewing needs no user action, so the user never has to wipe the glass.
judge_comment: Anti-fog glass is plausible and convenient, but it has little to do with operating the microwave without learning.

title: Phone Buzzes When Done
new_elements: Wireless done-notification (The user's watch or phone gets a gentle vibration when cooking finishes.)
rationale: The alert reaches the user wherever they are, with no need to hear a bell.
judge_comment: Phone notifications are easy to build and already common, but they add an app or pairing step and don't simplify operation.

title: Magnetic Latch Door
new_elements: Magnetic self-latching door (A magnetic seal closes and opens with a light push, with no mechanical latch.)
rationale: A light push or pull is intuitive and requires no button.
judge_comment: A push-to-open door is intuitive and simple, but it covers only a small part of operation and raises safety-interlock questions.

title: Dial Replaced by Sliding Hand Gesture
new_elements: Air-swipe gesture control (A wave of the hand left or right adjusts the cooking level.)
rationale: A wave is a universal gesture that needs no labels or instructions.
judge_comment: Air-swipe control replaces the dial, but the gesture is not self-explanatory, it lacks feedback, and it may be less intuitive than a dial.

title: Heat Is Shown as Color
new_elements: Thermochromic food indicator (A heat-reactive patch on the door changes color as the food heats.)
rationale: Color progress is understood at a glance, with no reading or timing required.
judge_comment: A thermochromic patch on the door is simple and intuitive, but it cannot reliably reflect food temperature, and it replaces a display rather than a part of the operation.

title: Microwave Explains Itself After Each Use
new_elements: Post-cook one-line summary (A short line shows what was cooked and how long, reinforcing learning without manuals.)
rationale: Clear feedback after each use builds confidence without any instruction.
judge_comment: Post-use feedback is easy to build but arrives after the task, so it barely reduces the learning curve.

title: Magnetic Snap Latch
new_elements: Magnetic door latch (Neodymium magnets hold the door shut and release it with a light tug.)
rationale: A magnet closes and opens the door in one motion, so there is no latch mechanism to understand.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch is cheap and simple, but it can't safely meet interlock requirements by itself and only covers door opening.

title: Sliding Drawer Oven
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Cavity slides out like a drawer, so food is loaded from the front without a hinge.)
rationale: A drawer is already understood by everyone, so loading the oven needs no instruction.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar interaction, but sealing microwave leakage on a sliding cavity is hard and it doesn't simplify the cooking controls.

title: Automatic Discharge Hook
new_elements: Spring grounding hook (Opening the door pulls a hook that shorts the high-voltage node to ground.)
rationale: Discharge happens automatically when the door opens, so no one has to wait or worry.
judge_comment: Discharge hooks are plausible and concrete, but they address safety rather than operation simplicity, and bleeder resistors already exist.

title: Voice-Less Sizzle Alert
new_elements: Sizzle sound cue (A short realistic sizzle sound plays when food is done instead of a bell.)
rationale: A sound people recognise from cooking needs no explanation, unlike a bell with no context.
judge_comment: It swaps a bell for a sizzle sound, which is mildly intuitive but does little for operating the oven and could be confusing.

title: Projected Door Display
new_elements: Door projector (Projects simple icons onto the door glass showing mode and time remaining.)
rationale: Information shown on the door where the food is removes the need to look at a separate panel.
judge_comment: Moves information onto the door, but the projection is hard to see through glass and the user still has to operate controls.

title: Ceramic Susceptor Plate
new_elements: Silicon carbide heat plate (A ceramic plate absorbs microwaves and gets hot enough to brown food from below.)
rationale: Browning food from below with a plate removes the need for users to know any special browning settings.
judge_comment: Susceptor plates already exist, and the idea addresses browning rather than operational simplicity.

title: Single Hall Sensor Interlock
new_elements: Hall effect door sensor (One solid-state sensor replaces three microswitches and reports door state.)
rationale: A simpler sensor cuts the chance of a confusing fault, so the oven just works when closed.
judge_comment: A Hall sensor is feasible and concrete, but safety standards require redundant interlocks and users would notice no difference in operation.

title: Thermostat Replaced By IR Spot Sensor
new_elements: Infrared spot sensor (Non-contact sensor reads food and cavity temperature to protect the magnetron.)
rationale: A sensor with no moving parts protects the oven without any user action.
judge_comment: Plausible safety substitution, but it is invisible to the user and barely affects learning curve.

title: Fridge-Door Mounted Oven
new_elements: Magnetic fridge-door microwave (Compact unit clips to the fridge door and heats food from the fridge.)
rationale: Food is reheated where it is already stored, so no counter setup or moving of plates is needed.
judge_comment: A fridge-door microwave is a radical idea that removes setup steps, but its weight, power, and safety make it hard to build and it doesn't simplify the controls.

title: Read-Your-Mind Cooking Assistant
new_elements: Single question interface (Oven asks just Hot or Cold and handles everything else.)
rationale: Reducing every choice to one plain question means there is no learning curve at all.
judge_comment: A single Hot or Cold question greatly reduces choices, but how it handles the rest (sensors, food recognition) is left unspecified.

title: Thermochromic door progress ring
new_elements: Thermochromic door ring (Heat-sensitive ink on the door window changes colour from blue to red as food heats.)
rationale: Colour progress is understood without any reading, so the user can judge doneness without knowing any settings.
judge_comment: A color-changing door ring is intuitive, but ink on a microwave door has trouble reflecting food temperature and it is hard to make reliable.

title: Inverter hides duty cycle
new_elements: Inverter-driven magnetron (Variable-frequency drive gives continuous power so the user never sees on-off cycling.)
rationale: Continuous heating removes the cycling that confused users and makes the power setting feel simple.
judge_comment: Inverter technology already exists, and hiding duty cycling does little to remove the learning curve for the user.

title: Transparent conductive window
new_elements: Transparent conductive film (Indium-tin-oxide coating on glass blocks microwaves while staying clear to view.)
rationale: A clear window shows the food without a mesh that gets dirty and confuses users.
judge_comment: ITO-coated glass is a named, plausible substitute for the mesh, but it improves visibility more than ease of operation and adds cost.

title: Sliding drawer door
new_elements: Sliding drawer front (The whole front slides out like a drawer, with no hinge or swing arc.)
rationale: A drawer is opened by pulling, which is the most obvious action there is.
judge_comment: A drawer front makes opening more intuitive, but sealing the microwaves is hard and the idea does not touch the operating controls.

title: Laptop-style clamshell lid
new_elements: Clamshell top lid (The top lifts on a hinge like a laptop screen, with a built-in handle.)
rationale: People already know how to open a laptop lid, so the gesture is instantly familiar.
judge_comment: The laptop-lid gesture is familiar, but top access has the same loading and spill drawbacks and gives only a modest simplification.

title: Pull-handle with no button
new_elements: Spring-loaded pull handle (A handle pulled outward releases the latch mechanically, with no button.)
rationale: A pull action needs no label or instruction and uses the same motion as any cupboard.
judge_comment: A pull handle is highly feasible and cheap, but microwaves already use it, so it is barely a substitution and not radical.

title: Glowing green touch pad
new_elements: Green-lit touch pad (A large capacitive pad glows green when ready and opens the door when touched.)
rationale: A green glow tells the user the machine is ready, so there is nothing to guess.
judge_comment: A ready-glow pad is clear and simple, but a touch pad that opens the door is a modest, familiar idea and it does not cover how cooking is started.

title: Reusable silicone tray with guide pattern
new_elements: Guide-pattern silicone tray (A flexible tray with a printed centre mark shows where to place food.)
rationale: A printed guide shows the user exactly where food goes without any instruction.
judge_comment: It is a simple, plausible guide for placing food, but it is incremental and may not suit microwave use, since silicone can deform and the food-placement problem is minor.

title: Thermal camera view
new_elements: Thermal-image window (A thermal camera shows the food's hot spots in colour on the front panel.)
rationale: Hot and cold areas are shown as colour, so the user sees what is done without opening the door.
judge_comment: A thermal view is novel and useful, but it adds information to interpret rather than reducing the learning curve, and it adds cost.

title: Light-pulse done cue
new_elements: Pulsing done light (A green light pulses on the top panel until the door is opened.)
rationale: A pulsing light keeps signalling until the user acts, so nobody misses that food is ready.
judge_comment: It is easy to build, but it only improves the done signal and does little for operating simplicity or learning.

title: Door-sensing cut-off replaces interlock
new_elements: Solid-state door sensor (A solid-state sensor cuts power the moment the door opens, with no mechanical interlock.)
rationale: A safety cut-off that works without any user action keeps operation simple and safe for elderly users.
judge_comment: A solid-state sensor in place of the mechanical interlock is a real substitution, but it is a safety feature the user never sees and regulations call for redundant interlocks.

title: Electroluminescent Cavity Glow
new_elements: Electroluminescent wall film (A thin, cool, low-voltage glowing film on the cavity wall replaces the 25 W bulb.)
rationale: The light is always on the surface, so the user never has to find or replace a bulb.
judge_comment: A clever bulb substitution, but it does almost nothing for ease of operation or learning.

title: Mica-Free Silicone Film
new_elements: Disposable silicone splash film (A cheap clip-in silicone sheet over the waveguide that is replaced when stained.)
rationale: A simple clip-in sheet is easier to swap than a fragile mica plate that needs careful cleaning.
judge_comment: A clip-in silicone film is feasible and concrete, but silicone near the waveguide risks heat damage and adds a maintenance chore.

title: Gesture Wave Start
new_elements: Hand-wave motion sensor (A sensor above the door starts cooking when a hand is waved across the front.)
rationale: A wave is an intuitive gesture that removes any need to find buttons.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start removes one button press but still leaves time and power selection unresolved, and it risks accidental starts.

title: Wall-Mounted Hob Unit
new_elements: Wall-mounted flat cavity (A flat unit fixes to the wall at eye height, with a door that opens at the same height as a cupboard.)
rationale: Placing the unit at comfortable height removes bending and lifting for elderly users.
judge_comment: Eye-level wall mounting helps elderly users with ergonomics, but it does not make the controls easier to operate and the installation is a burden.

title: Shape-Matching Cavity Tray
new_elements: Shaped cradle tray (A cradle tray has moulded slots that match the common food container shapes.)
rationale: Food sits in the right place by its own shape, so no positioning is needed.
judge_comment: Moulded slots remove the positioning decision and are easy to build, but they limit the container shapes that fit and don't address the controls.

title: Sealed Membrane Keypad
new_elements: Flush sealed membrane panel (A flat, sealed panel with raised bumps shows one big start key and no gaps to clean.)
rationale: A smooth panel that wipes clean removes the grooves and gaps where dirt collects.
judge_comment: A sealed membrane panel mainly addresses cleaning, and its simplicity benefit is only partial via one big start key.

title: Thermochromic Doneness Window
new_elements: Thermochromic door panel (Door glass changes colour where food reaches serving temperature.); Thermochromic pigment (Colour-changing film that needs no power.)
rationale: The door shows at a glance whether the food is ready, with no icons to read.
judge_comment: A thermochromic door is a creative passive indicator, but the door is shielded and can't directly sense food temperature, and it doesn't remove the need to set the cook.

title: Hip-Bump Door
new_elements: Soft-touch swing door (Door opens when pushed anywhere, with no button or latch to find.)
rationale: Opening the door works like any cupboard door, so there is no button to hunt for.
judge_comment: Push-open door removes a button to find, but microwave door safety latching makes it modest in impact and not very radical.

title: Rising Lid Auto-Open
new_elements: Spring-lift lid (Door pops open a few centimetres when cooking ends, announcing completion.)
rationale: The door itself signals the end of cooking and invites the user to take the food out.
judge_comment: Spring-lift door is a cheap and clear completion signal, but it only addresses the end of cooking and does nothing to simplify setting up the cook.

title: Wave-to-Start
new_elements: Proximity sensor (Waving a hand over the top starts or stops the cycle.)
rationale: A wave is more natural than finding and pressing a button.
judge_comment: A wave to start is easy, but it can trigger accidentally and gives no way to set the power or time.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Cavity is a drawer that slides out, like a dishwasher drawer, with food loaded on top.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer is an everyday motion that everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A familiar drawer motion helps loading, but it does little to simplify the controls, and sealing a drawer against microwave leakage is difficult.

title: Shape-Matched Bowl Cooking
new_elements: Bowl-fit magnetic ring (Ring in the cavity matches the bowl's base and sets the cooking zone.)
rationale: Placing the bowl sets the zone, so the user has no zone or power setting to choose.
judge_comment: Placement-based zone setting is inventive, but microwave fields don't easily map to bowl-shaped zones and a magnetic ring is questionable in a microwave cavity.

title: Plug Trigger Timer Bypass
new_elements: Standby lamp of the door (A permanent glow on the door edge that means the oven is ready.)
rationale: A ready light answers the question every user asks, which is whether the oven is working.
judge_comment: A ready lamp is simple and feasible, but the title mismatches the description, and the idea is not very radical or specific.

title: Voice-Free Stir Prompt
new_elements: Auto-stir pulse (Pauses the cycle at the halfway point and shows a stir icon on the door.)
rationale: The machine prompts the one action the user needs, so no program has to be remembered.
judge_comment: Practical stir reminder, but it only addresses one step and some microwaves already beep for stirring; not a true substitution.

title: Printed Rule Tray
new_elements: Pictogram turntable (Turntable printed with a simple picture of how much food to place where.)
rationale: The tray itself teaches the correct loading, so no manual is needed.
judge_comment: A printed turntable is cheap and easy, but it guides loading only and does not simplify operating the controls.

title: Kettle-Style Cook Lid
new_elements: Kettle-style flip lid (Lid lifts with a thumb push and lowers to start cooking.)
rationale: People already know how to use a kettle lid, so the oven needs no instructions.
judge_comment: Familiar kettle-lid metaphor makes starting intuitive, but it doesn't address time or power selection, and it isn't a real substitution.

title: Haptic Door-Handle Ping
new_elements: Haptic vibration in handle (The door handle buzzes softly when cooking ends, so the user feels the signal.)
rationale: A buzz in the hand is noticed by anyone, including people who are hard of hearing.
judge_comment: A vibrating handle is an unusual signal, but it covers only the end-of-cook alert, and the vibration motor sits awkwardly near a hot door.

title: Scent-Signal Done Cue
new_elements: Micro-cartridge scent release (A tiny cartridge releases a pleasant aroma when cooking ends.)
rationale: A scent is an instant signal that needs no reading or hearing, so anyone can tell the food is ready.
judge_comment: A scent cue is highly novel, but cartridges need replacing, aromas can clash with the food, and it does little for operating simplicity.

title: Cavity Glow Progress Band
new_elements: Thermochromic progress band (A coloured band on the cavity wall shifts from blue to red as food heats up.)
rationale: A colour band shows progress at a glance, so users know how the cook is going without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A color band is intuitive to read, but thermochromic materials in a microwave cavity are hard to get working because they don't track food temperature and they must withstand the heat and microwave environment.

title: Transparent Conductive Door
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide window (A thin coated glass pane is see-through and still blocks microwaves like a mesh.)
rationale: A clear window shows the food without any mesh to clean or misunderstand.
judge_comment: A transparent conductive window is a real, specific substitution, but it has little effect on ease of operation.

title: Radar Presence Auto-Light
new_elements: Presence-triggered LED strip (An LED strip lights the cavity when a person approaches, and it turns off otherwise.)
rationale: The light comes on by itself when needed, so nothing has to be switched on or replaced.
judge_comment: Auto light is convenient but barely affects operating the microwave, so it does little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: Hourglass Heat Bar
new_elements: Analog remaining-heat bar (A physical sliding bar shows how much heating time is left, filling as food warms.)
rationale: A visible bar that empties over time is understood instantly, without reading digits.
judge_comment: The bar makes remaining time easy to see, but it only shows status and does not simplify how the user sets the cook.

title: Sound-Only Interface
new_elements: Tone-based control feedback (Each button press plays a distinct tone, and the user confirms settings by ear.)
rationale: Audible confirmation lets users check their choice without reading the panel.
judge_comment: Audible confirmation helps somewhat, but it adds feedback rather than substituting a part, and the user still has to learn the tones.

title: Hot-Drink Button
new_elements: One-touch hot drink (A single labelled button heats a drink to the right temperature without any timing.)
rationale: A breakfast drink becomes one labelled press, so even someone half awake can use it correctly.
judge_comment: One-touch drink heating clearly removes the learning curve, but it is a common preset-button idea with little detail on how the right temperature is sensed and little that is radical.

title: Smell-to-Pause Guard
new_elements: Arc-detect camera stop (A small camera and arc sensor pauses cooking if metal sparks, and it explains the problem in plain words.)
rationale: Mistakes like metal in the cavity are caught and explained, so the user does not have to remember the rules.
judge_comment: Arc detection with a camera and plain-language explanation is a concrete safety aid, but the name mentions smell while the mechanism uses a camera and arc sensor, and it helps prevent errors more than it simplifies operation.

title: Transparent Conductive Door
new_elements: ITO-coated glass door panel (Indium tin oxide coating blocks microwaves while staying fully clear.); Transparent conductive coating (Thin conductive film on glass that reflects RF but passes visible light.)
rationale: A fully clear door lets the user see the food without any mesh, which reduces confusion about whether anything is happening.
judge_comment: ITO-coated glass is a plausible substitute for the mesh, but a clearer view does little for operation simplicity, and the cost and durability of the coating are concerns.

title: Haptic Handle Alert
new_elements: Vibrating door handle (Handle buzzes softly in the hand when cooking ends.)
rationale: A buzz in the hand is noticed even by users with poor hearing or sight, so they know when to open the door.
judge_comment: A vibrating handle is feasible and accessible but only signals completion, so its contribution to simple operation is minor.

title: Moulded Cavity Not Steel
new_elements: Laser-direct-structured plastic cavity (Plastic cavity with a laser-patterned metal layer that shields the microwaves.)
rationale: A lighter, cheaper cavity that is easier to clean makes the machine less intimidating to pick up and wipe down.
judge_comment: Laser-direct-structuring is a concrete idea, but heat, arcing, and durability are open problems, and it does nothing for ease of operation.

title: Food Goes In on Its Own
new_elements: Conveyor drop-in slot (Place food on a slot and it is drawn into the cavity and cooked.)
rationale: Loading becomes one motion with no door to open, so there is nothing to misunderstand.
judge_comment: Removes the door interaction, but a conveyor that draws food in raises safety, spill and cleaning problems, and cooking settings are still unaddressed.

title: Shaped Plate Sets Time
new_elements: Depth-sensing cavity floor (Sensor under the tray measures the food depth and sets time from it.)
rationale: Measuring the food's own size sets the time, so the user does not guess a number.
judge_comment: Depth alone is a weak proxy for cooking time (food type and water content matter), though it removes number entry.

title: Wave to Start
new_elements: Gesture sensor panel (Hand wave up or down adjusts the setting; a flat palm starts or stops.); Infrared gesture recognition (Low-cost IR sensor detects hand motion without touching.)
rationale: Waving a hand is a natural gesture with no button to find and no reading required.
judge_comment: Gesture control is feasible but adds a hidden vocabulary of gestures to learn, which works against the no-learning-curve need.

title: Two Doors, One Action
new_elements: Front-access door with open-plate (Door opens fully when you press one wide plate, no latch or button.)
rationale: A large wide plate is easier to hit than a small button, which helps users with limited dexterity.
judge_comment: A wide push plate replaces the small button and helps dexterity, but the 'Two Doors' title is confusing and it only addresses opening the door.

title: Door Closes Itself
new_elements: Soft-close damper hinge (Door is pushed near shut and the damper draws it closed with a gentle sound.)
rationale: A door that closes itself once nudged means the user never has to remember to shut it properly.
judge_comment: Soft-close dampers are common and only marginally reduce operation effort; not radical and barely addresses learning curve.

title: Ambient Scent Done Signal
new_elements: Warm-aroma cue (Gentle warm scent is released when cooking reaches the target temperature.)
rationale: Smelling that food is ready is a natural signal that needs no reading, number or sound.
judge_comment: Scent cue is a novel, reading-free signal, but releasing aroma on demand is impractical and could be unpleasant or confusing.

title: Weight-Sensing Cavity Floor
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (Measures food mass and sets energy automatically.)
rationale: Placing food on the floor is the only action needed, because mass sets the cooking profile.
judge_comment: Mass-based auto-setting is plausible, but weight alone does not determine the cooking profile and a load-cell floor is hard to integrate with a turntable and microwaves.

title: Scent Done Alert
new_elements: Aroma cartridge emitter (Releases a pleasant smell when cooking finishes.)
rationale: A familiar smell tells anyone the food is ready without reading anything.
judge_comment: A scent alert is unusual, but cartridges need replacing, scents may clash with food smells, and it adds complexity rather than simplifying operation.

title: Turntable Nudge Alert
new_elements: Tactile done alert (Turntable rocks briefly when cooking ends.)
rationale: Motion replaces the bell, so the signal works for users who cannot hear.
judge_comment: Tactile motion is accessible, but the rocking could spill food and users may not notice it or understand what it means.

title: Self-Centering Cavity
new_elements: Cavity with no fixed floor (Food sits anywhere and the field adapts.)
rationale: Users stop thinking about where food goes because placement no longer matters.
judge_comment: Placement-independent heating would be a radical improvement, but a field that adapts without a fixed floor is physically vague and implausible with current technology.

title: Auto Liquid Mode
new_elements: Automatic liquid detection (Detects liquid and adjusts power and time.)
rationale: Users stop choosing liquid settings because the oven recognises the contents.
judge_comment: Auto-detection removes a setting choice, which fits the no-learning-curve goal, but it is a familiar sensor-based idea and not a substitution.

title: Mechanical Timer Replaced By Clock Glance
new_elements: Digital countdown display (Shows remaining time in large numbers.)
rationale: A clear readout is easier to understand than a dial that is hard to set precisely.
judge_comment: Digital countdown displays are standard on microwaves, so little novelty, with modest help for simplicity.

title: Tilt-To-Start Tray
new_elements: Tilt sensor base (Tilting the tray starts cooking.)
rationale: Moving the tray is a natural action that starts cooking without any buttons.
judge_comment: Tilting a tray is an unusual trigger, but it is impractical with hot liquids and unclear about how cooking time gets set.

title: Modular Snap Cavity Tray
new_elements: Snap-fit modular tray (Tray clips in only one correct way.)
rationale: A keyed tray cannot be fitted wrongly, which removes assembly confusion.
judge_comment: A keyed tray is easy to build and prevents misfitting, but it is a minor improvement that barely touches operation and is not radical.

title: Stick-On Instruction Surface
new_elements: Single iconic front panel (One image shows how to start.)
rationale: A single picture replaces the instruction manual, so no reading is needed.
judge_comment: A single icon panel is cheap and easy to understand, but it is a labeling tweak that does not simplify the controls and is not wild.

title: Hot Plate Replaces Oven Box
new_elements: Resonant ceramic hotplate (Heats food from a flat surface.)
rationale: A flat surface needs no door, cavity or settings, so it is simpler to use.
judge_comment: Replacing the box with a hotplate removes the door and cavity, but it is no longer a microwave, heats slowly and unevenly, and still needs some control.

title: Crisp Lid Auto Mode
new_elements: Hot air crisping plate (Adds heat to brown the surface when needed.)
rationale: Crisping happens automatically, so users do not need to choose browning modes.
judge_comment: Automatic browning is a plausible and familiar air-fry combi feature, but it adds hardware and addresses only one decision.

title: Door Pull-to-Open Hinge
new_elements: Spring-assisted pull door (Door opens with a light tug on its edge; no push button required.)
rationale: A door that opens the way any cupboard does removes the button that users must find and understand.
judge_comment: A pull-open door is familiar and removes a button, but it is a modest gain and a standard door seal and latch are still required for safety.

title: Inductive Wall Dock Power
new_elements: Countertop inductive power pad (The oven sits on a pad that transfers power wirelessly, so no plug or cord is needed.)
rationale: Placing the oven on a pad is simpler than finding a socket and fitting a plug.
judge_comment: Removing the cord is easy to understand, but wirelessly transferring about 1000 W or more is impractical, costly and inefficient, and it is not cheaper than a plug.

title: Scent Done Alert
new_elements: Scented cartridge release (A small cartridge releases a warm popcorn scent when cooking finishes.)
rationale: A pleasant smell signals that food is done, which is intuitive even for someone who has never used the oven.
judge_comment: A scent alert is unusual and intuitive, but it does little for operation, needs consumable cartridges, and is unreliable as a signal.

title: Hands-Free Gesture Start
new_elements: Infrared proximity sensing (Waving a hand near the front starts or stops heating.)
rationale: A wave is a gesture everyone already knows, so no buttons need to be learned.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start is easy, but it only replaces a start button and gives no control over time or power, so it isn't radical.

title: Gravity-Shutter Safety
new_elements: Gravity-closing RF shutter (A metal shutter drops by gravity when the door opens, blocking microwave leakage.)
rationale: A purely mechanical shutter is safe even if electronics fail, so users never have to trust a switch.
judge_comment: A mechanical safety shutter is plausible and concrete, but it is invisible to the user and does little for ease of operation.

title: Sliding Drawer Oven
new_elements: Sliding drawer door (The whole front slides out like a drawer, with the food tray moving with it.)
rationale: Pulling out a drawer to load food is the most familiar motion in any kitchen.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar motion, but it only simplifies loading and does nothing for controls, which is where the learning curve sits; sealing and tray mechanics are also harder.

title: Lift-Lid Top Loader
new_elements: Gas-strut lift lid (The entire top lifts with a gas strut, so the user drops food in from above.)
rationale: Putting a bowl in from above is as natural as using a bin, so no door handling is needed.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid is intuitive and the gas strut is concrete, but microwave leakage, spill risk and the lid's safety interlock make it difficult.

title: Dead-Man Auto Stop
new_elements: Heat-proof fusible link (A fusible link breaks if the oven overheats and needs no electronics.)
rationale: A simple mechanical fuse protects the user without them ever needing to understand it.
judge_comment: A fusible link is a plausible and concrete safety part, but it does little for a no-learning-curve operating experience.

title: Glass-Free Bowl Cook
new_elements: Self-rotating cooking bowl (The bowl itself spins on a base when placed in the oven.)
rationale: The bowl is the only object used, so there is no turntable to think about.
judge_comment: A self-spinning bowl removes the turntable, but it needs a mechanism in the bowl that is hard to make microwave-safe, and it adds little to ease of use.

title: Phone Projector Cavity
new_elements: Cavity projection (A tiny projector shows the food and cooking status on the glass door.)
rationale: The oven shows what it is doing in plain words on the door, so no manual is needed.
judge_comment: Plain-language status on the door could cut the need for a manual, but it adds a component rather than substituting a simpler one, and a projector can't reliably identify the food or show status on a glass door inside a microwave cavity.

title: One-Button Cook
new_elements: Single smart button (One large button that starts a sensor-chosen cook for whatever is inside.)
rationale: One button with no settings means nothing needs to be chosen or understood.
judge_comment: Directly removes all choices, but sensor-based auto-cook for arbitrary food is hard and the idea is fairly obvious and vague about the mechanism.

title: Haptic Done Pulse
new_elements: Vibration pad (Pad under the front edge that pulses when cooking is complete.)
rationale: A felt pulse signals completion without any sound or reading.
judge_comment: A vibration pad is easy to build, but it only signals completion and does little for operating the microwave without learning.

title: Phased Heating No-Turn
new_elements: Phased heating array (Multiple emitters that heat evenly without any turning.)
rationale: Removing the turntable removes a part that can be put in wrongly or fall off.
judge_comment: Solid-state phased RF arrays are real and remove the turntable, but this only marginally reduces the learning curve and costs more rather than less.

title: Magnet-Latch Door
new_elements: Magnetic seal (A magnetic seal that holds the door closed and releases on a gentle pull.)
rationale: A pull-to-open door needs no button to find or press.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch is highly feasible and simplifies opening, but it is incremental and does not address operating the controls.

title: Hourglass Window Timer
new_elements: Sand-fill window (A window strip in the door where sand or light fills to show time left.)
rationale: A filling vessel shows elapsed time with no numbers to read.
judge_comment: A visual fill timer makes time remaining easy to read, but it only displays status and doesn't simplify setting the cook.

title: Kitchen Robot Arm
new_elements: Retrieval arm (A small arm that takes a food tray from the counter, loads it, and returns it when done.)
rationale: The user only places the tray on a pad and the machine handles the rest.
judge_comment: Removes loading steps but a robot arm is costly and complex, contradicting the SUBSTITUTE goal of cheaper/simpler.

title: Wall-Mount Shelf Mode
new_elements: Flat cooking shelf (A shallow shelf that mounts to a wall and heats only the food placed on it.)
rationale: No box or door means there is nothing to open, close, or set up.
judge_comment: Radical removal of the box, but open microwave radiation is unsafe and the idea does not say how heating starts or stops, so the simplicity gain is unclear.

title: Fold-Down Front Panel
new_elements: Single flap (Front flap that folds down; the opening reveals a single button when lowered.)
rationale: Hiding the controls until needed leaves a clean surface with almost nothing to read.
judge_comment: A single button behind a flap is simple and plausible, but it is a modest change and the flap adds a step.

title: Bell-Free Silence
new_elements: Mute-by-default signal (Signals completion through a glowing ring with no sound unless requested.)
rationale: Silent, visual completion removes any need to know what the sound means.
judge_comment: A silent glowing completion signal is easy to build, but it only touches the end of use and substitutes little.

title: Wearable Cook Cue
new_elements: Watch notification (Sends a vibration to a watch when the food is ready, so the kitchen doesn't need to be watched.)
rationale: Users are notified wherever they are, so no reading or attention is needed at the machine.
judge_comment: Notification is feasible but doesn't simplify operating the microwave itself, and it adds a watch dependency rather than substituting a part.

title: Voice-only control
new_elements: Far-field voice listener (Accepts natural phrases such as 'warm my coffee' and maps them to cook programs.)
rationale: Speaking a need requires no panel knowledge, which matches for first-time users.
judge_comment: Voice is feasible but requires speaking and phrase mapping, so it is not zero-learning for everyone, and it is neither cheaper nor simpler in hardware.

title: Scent-release done signal
new_elements: Aroma cartridge with puff valve (Releases a small puff of toasted scent when cooking ends.)
rationale: Smell is a second sense that reads as done without any learning about the bell.
judge_comment: A scent puff is very novel, but it is impractical because cartridges need replacing and the smell is ambiguous, and it does not simplify operation.

title: Thermochromic cavity glow
new_elements: Thermochromic cavity wall paint (Wall coating changes colour with temperature, showing hot and cold zones.)
rationale: Colour that appears without any bulb or switch gives feedback with no operation at all.
judge_comment: Interesting passive feedback, but it only shows heat inside the cavity (and is hidden by food and the closed door), so it does little to remove the need to set the controls.

title: E-ink progress door window
new_elements: E-ink strip in door window (Shows a large countdown or a single word such as 'Ready' in a readable font.)
rationale: A large, plain word on the door tells the user what is happening without any setting.
judge_comment: A clear status display helps understanding but does not simplify input, and it replaces a display only marginally.

title: Radar presence interlock
new_elements: Low-power radar presence sensor (Detects a hand or person near the door and cuts RF before the door opens.)
rationale: Stopping RF before anyone reaches the door protects users with no effort on their part.
judge_comment: This is a safety feature that needs no effort from the user, but it does little for operational simplicity, and the existing door interlocks already do much of the job.

title: Resettable polymer fuse
new_elements: Polymer PTC resettable protection (A self-resetting positive temperature coefficient device that trips on fault and recovers.)
rationale: No fuse to find and replace keeps the machine working with no user action after a fault.
judge_comment: Resettable PTC is a concrete, feasible substitute for a fuse, but it only helps in rare fault cases and does not change everyday operation (and is not a substitute for the thermal fuse in a safety-critical role).

title: Metal-detecting cavity lock
new_elements: Metal detection sensor (Sensor checks the cavity for metal and blocks start-up if it finds any.)
rationale: The machine simply refuses to start when something is wrong, so nobody needs to learn the rule.
judge_comment: A metal-detection lockout removes a rule users must learn and fits the need well, but it is fairly obvious and reliable detection is hard.

title: Phase-change defrost plate
new_elements: Phase-change heat-storage plate (Plate stores heat and releases it slowly, so frozen food thaws with no cycling.)
rationale: Defrosting happens with one choice and no power levels to understand.
judge_comment: A phase-change plate that makes defrost a single choice is imaginative, but it is physically doubtful in a microwave and has unclear function.

title: Kettle-style one-touch door tray
new_elements: Pull-out tray with door interlock (Tray slides out with the door and locks the food in place when it is closed.)
rationale: Pulling a tray out to load it is the same as loading a drawer, so no skill is needed.
judge_comment: A pull-out tray makes loading intuitive and is mechanically plausible, but it's an incremental change that doesn't address the controls, which are the main source of the learning curve.

title: Chime-free silent mode with light
new_elements: Ambient light ring (A soft ring of light on the top edge pulses slowly when cooking ends.)
rationale: A gentle visible glow is a clear signal that suits households with babies or night-time use.
judge_comment: A light-ring end-of-cook signal is easy to build and useful for quiet use, but it only tangentially addresses simple operation and is not a radical substitution.

title: Door-Is-the-Switch
new_elements: Door-closure magnetic reed sensor (Closing the door completes a magnetic circuit that starts the cook cycle; opening it stops cooking.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed to start cooking, so there is no start button to find or learn.
judge_comment: Door-close-to-start is simple and plausible, but it risks accidental starts and doesn't set time or power, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Ambient Scent-Feedback Door
new_elements: Warm-tinted reflective door glass (A warm reflective tint shows the cavity state through colour rather than light.)
rationale: Glance-level colour cues need no reading and work even in dim light.
judge_comment: A tinted door that signals state by colour is easy to build but only conveys status, not operation, so it barely reduces the learning curve; the 'scent' name does not match the idea.

title: No-Fault Fuse Reset
new_elements: Self-resetting polymer PTC fuse (A resettable polyfuse recovers automatically after a fault clears.)
rationale: Users never need to replace a fuse or find a spare, so a fault never leaves them stuck.
judge_comment: A resettable PTC is a concrete and plausible part, but it addresses rare faults and not normal operation.

title: Open-Lock Mechanical Gate
new_elements: Spring-loaded flip gate (A large flap that springs open when pressed anywhere on its surface.)
rationale: Pressing a large flap is a universal action, so opening never requires finding a small hidden release.
judge_comment: Press-anywhere spring door is easy to use and feasible, but it only addresses opening, not the full operation, and is only mildly novel.

title: Quiet Fanless Cooling
new_elements: Passive heat-pipe cooling (Sealed heat pipes move heat from the magnetron to the fins with no fan.)
rationale: The machine makes no fan noise that could be mistaken for a fault, so users never wonder if it is working.
judge_comment: Passive heat-pipe cooling is concrete and novel but only loosely tied to ease of use, and cooling a magnetron without a fan is technically hard.

title: Hourglass Progress Chamber
new_elements: Transparent fluid column (Coloured liquid drains from top to bottom as cooking proceeds.); Gravity-driven visual timer (Passive mechanism with no electronics.)
rationale: A draining column reads like an hourglass, so the remaining time is obvious without numbers.
judge_comment: A fluid column is a quirky, intuitive display, but it is hard to drive passively at the right rate and it does not help with setting the time.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door Open
new_elements: Pressure-sensing door panel (Pushing anywhere on the door face opens it with a gentle spring.); Push-to-open magnetic catch (Magnet catch released by a light push.)
rationale: Pushing a large door area is easier and more intuitive than finding a small button.
judge_comment: Push-to-open doors already exist; it eases opening but does not address the operation of cooking itself.

title: Sliding Drawer Door
new_elements: Side-sliding cavity drawer (Cavity slides out like a drawer on rails.); Telescopic ball-bearing rails (Smooth sliding for a food tray.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer out is understood immediately and avoids the swing arc of a hinged door.
judge_comment: A drawer is intuitive, but it adds complexity, leaks microwaves at the seal, and does little for operation simplicity beyond the door.

title: Fully Transparent Sub-Wavelength Casing
new_elements: Indium tin oxide transparent conductive coating (Conducts microwave shielding while staying clear to the eye.); Clear glass cavity wall (See-through walls with no mesh.)
rationale: A wall you can see straight through needs no lamp or mesh, so the user sees the food without any setup.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive coatings for shielding are plausible and visually striking, but they do little for operational simplicity and the coating must handle heat and durability.

title: Meal Button Tray
new_elements: Three big preset buttons with icons (Buttons for drink, meal, and dessert, each with a large icon.)
rationale: Three large icon buttons offer a choice without numbers or dial logic.
judge_comment: Simple and easy to use, but it's a common preset-button approach with little novelty and vague outcomes.

title: Presence-Based Auto Start
new_elements: Kitchen presence sensor (Detects a person near the oven and a food tray placed in the cavity.); Starts default program when food is loaded (Detects loading and begins.)
rationale: Loading a tray is enough to start cooking, which removes every control step.
judge_comment: Auto-start on loading removes controls, but it is a safety risk and a default program may not suit the food; it also does not clearly substitute a cheaper part.

title: Snap-Fit Magnetic Latch
new_elements: Rare-earth magnetic door latch (Magnets hold the door shut and release when pulled.); Magnetic door latch (Replaces the spring lever and hooks.)
rationale: A magnet closes with a click and opens with a pull, so there is no latch to press or learn.
judge_comment: A magnetic latch is a concrete, feasible substitute for the lever, but it only simplifies door opening, which is a small part of operation (and magnets near a magnetron cavity need care).

title: Hands-Free Foot Pedal Open
new_elements: Floor-level foot pedal (Stepping on the pedal opens the door.)
rationale: Using the foot removes the need to reach for a button, which helps users with limited hand strength.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is unusual and plausible, but it addresses physical access rather than operational simplicity and adds a trip hazard.

title: Ambient Radar Presence Stop
new_elements: Radar proximity door stop (Radar detects a hand near the door during cooking and pauses the oven.)
rationale: Pausing automatically when a hand approaches needs no button, which is safer and simpler.
judge_comment: Radar-based pause is somewhat novel and button-free, but it targets safety more than ease of learning and may cause nuisance stops.

title: Sealed Touch-Free Power Ring
new_elements: Continuous inverter magnetron drive (Inverter drives the magnetron for smooth continuous power.)
rationale: Smooth power needs no on-off guess, so food heats evenly with no settings to understand.
judge_comment: Inverter drive is existing technology and only indirectly reduces the need for settings, and it doesn't match the touch-free ring title.

title: Thermal Camera Inside Door
new_elements: Low-resolution thermal sensor (Shows a colour heat map of food on the door screen.); Displays food heat map (Shows cold spots so the user understands what is happening.)
rationale: A heat map shows whether food is hot in plain colour, so the user needs no interpretation skill.
judge_comment: A thermal heat map is novel and helps users see doneness, but it adds cost and information rather than simplifying operation, and it doesn't substitute a part with something simpler.

title: One-Button Cook
new_elements: Single dome start button (One large tactile dome that starts an automatic cook program)
rationale: A single large button removes every decision the user would otherwise have to learn.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible but vague about how the automatic program knows what to do, and not radical.

title: Drawer Not Door
new_elements: Pull-out cooking drawer (Shallow drawer with a fixed cavity that slides out like a kitchen drawer)
rationale: Pulling a drawer is a familiar motion, which removes the learning curve of a swing door.
judge_comment: A drawer format is a distinctive change and a familiar motion, but microwave sealing and the choke design make it hard to build.

title: Top-Lid Flip Open
new_elements: Gravity-assist top lid (Top-opening lid held by a gas strut so it stays up without hinges or latches)
rationale: A lid lifts the way a lid always does, so no one needs to be shown how to open it.
judge_comment: A top-opening lid is intuitive, but gas struts, spill risk and a top-loading cavity bring practical drawbacks, and it does nothing for the rest of the operation.

title: Clear-Glass Bowl Cavity
new_elements: Borosilicate glass bowl cavity (Single transparent bowl with metallised lid serves as cooking vessel and chamber)
rationale: Food is cooked in the same dish it is served in, so there are fewer steps and nothing to transfer.
judge_comment: Cooking in the serving dish reduces steps, but a bowl-shaped chamber with a metallised lid is hard to engineer safely and limits food types.

title: Lamp-Free Light Pipe
new_elements: Edge-lit LED light guide in door frame (LED strip feeds light across a clear acrylic light guide that floods the cavity)
rationale: The light comes on with the door and never burns out, so the user never has to change a bulb.
judge_comment: A light guide is feasible and concrete, but it barely affects operational simplicity.

title: Cavity Glows Warm Color
new_elements: Color-coded status ring (Ring around the door turns blue while cooking and green when done)
rationale: Colour gives status at a glance, so the user never has to remember what a beep meant.
judge_comment: An LED status ring that shows cooking and done states is simple and easy to read at a glance, though it is a modest and fairly common idea.

title: Mains Plug with One Orientation
new_elements: Keyed magnetic power connector (Magnet-aligned plug that only fits one way and snaps into place)
rationale: It cannot be plugged in wrong, so there is nothing to think about when connecting it.
judge_comment: Magnetic keyed plug is plausible and removes a trivial plug-in mistake, but plugs are already one-way and it does not affect cooking operation.

title: Solid-State Power Stage
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Transistor-based amplifier replaces the transformer, capacitor, diode and magnetron)
rationale: Removing the high-voltage parts also removes the lethal capacitor, so the appliance is safer to use without any instructions.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF replacing the magnetron is real and plausible but costly, and the link to no-learning-curve operation is mainly indirect safety.

title: Magnet-Free Mechanical Timer
new_elements: Crystal-clock timer chip (Quartz timing replaces the motor-driven cam and spring return)
rationale: Quartz timing is precise to the second, so short cooks behave exactly as the display suggests.
judge_comment: A quartz timer chip is a common, trivially feasible swap that does improve timing accuracy, but it is hardly new and the title is confusing.

title: Stand-Still Remote Phone Ping
new_elements: Phone notification on done (Oven sends a push notification to a paired phone when cooking ends)
rationale: The user learns that food is ready from their phone, so they never have to stand and wait beside the oven.
judge_comment: A done notification is easy to build but does little for simple operation and needs phone pairing.

title: Shared-Kitchen Lock Mode
new_elements: Tap-card access (Office card opens the door and starts the oven for an authorized user)
rationale: Only the right people can use it, and each person opens it with the card they already carry.
judge_comment: Card-tap access is feasible and specific, but it adds a step and restricts use, which works against a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Child-Proof by Design
new_elements: Safe-by-default start (Oven only starts when the door is closed and a fixed tap pattern is used)
rationale: The machine simply does not start in unsafe conditions, so the family never has to remember rules.
judge_comment: Safe-by-default start with a door interlock is feasible and reduces rule-remembering, though the fixed tap pattern is itself something to learn.

title: Silent Mode as Default
new_elements: Quiet overnight mode (Oven ignores the bell and fan at night and uses silent alerts)
rationale: Quiet behaviour happens without any setting, so the appliance fits into family life without a menu to learn.
judge_comment: Automatic quiet behavior requires no setup, but it addresses noise rather than operation simplicity, and the substitution link is weak.

title: Visible Sand-Timer Window
new_elements: Sand-fill timer strip (A clear strip on the door where a coloured band drains from top to bottom as cooking proceeds.)
rationale: A draining band is understood at a glance and needs no reading of digits, which serves users unfamiliar with timers.
judge_comment: It makes elapsed time easy to read but doesn't simplify setting the cook time, so it only partly serves the need.

title: Hip-Bump Auto Door
new_elements: Proximity door opener (A sensor on the handle side opens the door when a hand or hip approaches with a full load.)
rationale: Opening the door by approaching it requires no known gesture, which helps someone whose hands are full.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening helps, but it risks false triggers, and it addresses only door opening rather than the learning curve of operating the microwave.

title: Palm Panel Release
new_elements: Full-width soft panel (A broad, cushioned strip along the bottom of the door that opens it when pressed by any part of the hand.)
rationale: A large target that accepts any press means the user cannot miss it, so there is no need to find a small button.
judge_comment: A big forgiving press target is simple and plausible, but it is an incremental swap of the door button and not radical.

title: Lift-Lid Top Opening
new_elements: Top-lift lid (The cavity opens by lifting the top like a slow cooker lid, with the window on the top.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is a motion everyone already knows, so the door needs no explanation.
judge_comment: The familiar lid-lifting motion is intuitive, but top-opening raises ergonomic and spill concerns and does little for operating the controls.

title: Tilting Plate Finish
new_elements: Tilting turntable (At the end of cooking, the glass plate tilts gently toward the user to show that cooking is over.)
rationale: A visible movement at the end of cooking is clear without any sound or reading.
judge_comment: The visible end signal is intuitive, but a tilting plate risks spilling hot food and adds mechanical complexity.

title: Thermochromic Plate Ring
new_elements: Thermochromic indicator band (A band around the plate changes colour as the cooking zone heats and cools.)
rationale: A colour change shows whether food is still cooking, which needs no understanding of time.
